quote: The Anka prompt includes a concise syntax guide (approximately 100 lines) teaching the language from scratch. The Python prompt assumes pandas knowledge, consistent with training data distribution.
bears_on: Size of an effective in-context spec, and confounds the lotml evaluation harness must avoid.

claim: The authors state that the benchmark covers only data-transformation pipelines and that generalization to other programming tasks is not established.
quote: Benchmark Scope. Our benchmark focuses on data transformation pipelines. Generalization to other programming tasks is not established.
bears_on: Transfer of Anka's result to a general-purpose language like lotml.

claim: Three verified exemplars in the prompt left Qwen3-32B at 10.2%, far below the 47.2% it reached after fine-tuning: a few examples do not override the pretraining prior.
quote: Three-shot in-context prompting leaves Qwen3-32B at just 10.2% on PyLang (Table 4), far below its fine-tuned 47.2%, showing that a handful of exemplars cannot override the Python pretraining prior.
bears_on: Open models: lotml needs fine-tuning or a translated corpus, not few-shot prompting.

claim: For Sonnet 4, adding rules without snippets lowered the score from 12.5% to 8.2%; snippets were the single most important prompt component.
quote: Table 12 reports prompt ablation results for Sonnet 4 on PyLang. The same qualitative pattern observed for Sonnet 4.5 (Table 7) holds: code snippets are the single most important component, and rules alone without snippets actually hurt performance (8.2% vs. 12.5% base).
bears_on: How the lotml spec should be written: worked idioms over lists of prohibitions.

claim: Base Qwen3-4B writing Python under the same restrictions (no stdlib, no for, no int/split) passed about 63%, against 36.1% for the model fine-tuned on PyLang: familiarity, not expressive power, explains the gap.
quote: On the 86 problems where Qwen3-4B complied, Restricted-Python pass rate was ∼63%, versus 36.1% for fine-tuned PyLang.
bears_on: Keeping Python's syntax where semantics match: writing in the familiar surface is worth tens of points.

claim: DPO and GRPO improved Python more than the unseen language because preference tuning only reweights correct samples the model already produces, and those are rare in a new language.
quote: The asymmetry arises because preference tuning can only upweight correct solutions that already exist in the model's sample distribution.
bears_on: RL with verifiable rewards as a lever: it needs a non-trivial base pass rate, so seed with supervised data first.

claim: The whole PyLang corpus was produced by Claude Opus 4.5 in an agentic loop against the real interpreter, keeping only fully test-passing programs, with a 30.4% yield.
quote: All 2,816 PyLang training and test examples were generated by Claude Opus 4.5 in an agentic loop and kept only if they passed every test case under the actual PyLang interpreter, out of 9,269 source Codeforces problems attempted (a 30.4% yield).
bears_on: Feasibility and yield of a test-validated synthetic lotml corpus generated by a frontier model.

claim: PyLang's interpreter inherits Python's runtime semantics (scalars by value, arrays shared by reference), so its semantic distance from Python is smaller than lotml's value semantics would be; PyLang does not test semantic divergence.
quote: PyLang's interpreter is implemented in Python and inherits Python's runtime characteristics (e.g., arbitrary-precision integers, dynamic typing), so the semantic distance between the two languages is smaller than it would be for a language with fundamentally different execution semantics
bears_on: Transfer of PyLang's result to lotml, whose value semantics diverge from Python's.

claim: Moving from human-written to LLM-translated and fuzzer-generated programs collapsed accuracy by more than 40 points; data-flow and size metrics, not control flow, were the main stressors on those splits.
quote: Moving from Human-Written to LLM-Translated and FuzzerGenerated programs (Table 5) induces systematic accuracy collapses-often exceeding 40% points-highlighting the fragility of long-horizon rule composition under scale.
bears_on: Long lotml programs: the semantic compiler, not the model, must track value semantics and mutation across long traces.

claim: Generating full execution traces under supplied rules was near impossible: only four of eleven models scored above zero.
quote: PredTrace sharply exposes the fragility of longhorizon rule conditioning: only four models achieve nonzero accuracy at all, and even these remain far from reliable.
bears_on: Whether models can be trusted to simulate lotml semantics step by step from a spec.

claim: Novel symbols also cost accuracy, and a single-token control ruled out tokenization as the cause; new syntax is cheaper than conflicting syntax but not free.
quote: Even when all obfuscated symbols are atomic tokens, models still fail to reliably apply the correct operational rules and compose them over execution.
bears_on: lotml-syntax rule 2: visibly different syntax for different semantics still needs the spec and diagnostics.

claim: Even single-step rule selection, with no state to track, stayed dominated by symbol priors for most models.
quote: most systems exhibit strongly negative ∆is, implying that even when state evolution is removed, local rule selection remains dominated by symbol priors rather than formal definitions.
bears_on: Short lotml snippets are not safe either: a single assignment or call with redefined meaning is read with Python's meaning.

claim: The authors name operator overloading and DSLs as the practical cases where supplied semantics conflict with the prior.
quote: complete operational semantics are supplied and we test whether reasoning conditions on those rules when they redefine standard operator meaning-a conflict that arises in practice with operator overloading, DSLs, and proof assistants
bears_on: lotml's value semantics reuse Python's assignment and argument syntax with copy semantics, and its traits allow operator overloading: both are the swap condition.

claim: The study measures reading code - predicting final states and traces of a featherweight C - not generating it; transfer to code generation is an inference.
quote: We use program execution as a lens for analyzing formal semantic rule-conditioned reasoning in LLMs.
bears_on: Scope of the evidence for lotml's semantic-leakage risk.

claim: GPT-5 trailed Java by nearly 18 points in Haskell and 9 in OCaml, a gap wider than GPT-4o's despite higher absolute scores.
quote: Specifically, GPT4o's pass rates in Haskell and OCaml lag those of Java by approximately 16.5 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. This divergence even intensifies in GPT-5, where the performance gap widens to nearly 18 and 9 percentage points.
bears_on: Whether an immutable or functional style costs accuracy; the size of the paradigm gap.

claim: GPT-5 cut OCaml compile errors to 13.73% but stayed at 24.28% in Haskell, against 4.62% in Java.
quote: while GPT-5 successfully lowers the compilation error rate in OCaml to 13.73% and achieves a remarkably low 4.62% in Java, it fails to show similar improvement in Haskell, where the error rate remains high at 24.28%.
bears_on: Strict type systems raise compile-error rates; type-system strictness needs diagnostics with fixes.

claim: In Haskell and OCaml the imperative bias took the form of mutable references, in-place updates and effects inside pure functions.
quote: In Haskell and OCaml, we observe similar biases, such as the use of mutable references, in-place updates, or IO effects in pure function features that conflict with the declarative and immutable nature of these languages.
bears_on: Where models will break lotml's immutable-by-default rule: mutable locals and in-place updates of collections.

claim: In OCaml the static analysis also caught type errors and unintended mutation of immutable data structures, though less often than readability issues.
quote: We also observed several critical issues, including type errors and unintended mutation of immutable data structures, although these occurred less frequently.
bears_on: Semantic-compiler diagnostics for mutation of immutable values.

claim: GPT-5 passed more tests than GPT-4o but wrote less idiomatic code in all four languages, which the authors read as reward hacking.
quote: Specifically, in RQ1, we can see that GPT-5 consistently improve the pass@1 accross four studied programming languages. However, in this experiment, we found that GPT-5 consistently witness lower code style and maintainability in all these languages compared to GPT-4o.
bears_on: Tests alone will not enforce lotml idioms; the compiler must reject or flag them.

claim: GPT-4o dropped sharply after its cutoff in Java and Scala but stayed low and flat in OCaml and Haskell, so part of the paradigm gap reflects training-data frequency and contamination rather than the functional style itself.
quote: GPT-4o show show a substantial post-cutoff performance drop in Java and Scala, i.e., from 52.0% to 32.8% in Java and from 35.8% to 21.6% in Scala.
bears_on: Confound in reading the functional-language gap as a cost of immutability.

claim: SLMFix's error fixer is Qwen2.5-Coder 0.5B, trained with reinforcement learning (verl and vLLM, 70 epochs, batch size 64).
quote: For reinforcement learning approaches, we use verl (Sheng et al., 2024) and vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) to perform training with 70 total epochs and batch size of 64 on the Qwen-2.5-Coder 0.5B model.

claim: At inference SLMFix calls the small model only when the static validator reports errors, giving it the program, the original prompt and the validator's error messages.
quote: If there are no errors the program is output and otherwise the program, the original prompt, and the error messages from the validator are provided to the SLM which generates a revised program as the final output.

claim: SLMFix's GRPO reward is a weighted average of a boolean static-validator signal and a 0-to-1 semantic (AST-similarity) score against the ground-truth program.
quote: The static validator generates a boolean signal indicating if the given program contains syntactic errors, while the semantic metric will output a score between 0 and 1 representing how well the program aligns with the input query. The reward of the program is then a weighted average between these two signals

claim: SLMFix's training data starts from 20 hand-written query/ground-truth pairs per language, each sampled 10 times from five strong code LLMs to produce erroneous programs to repair.
quote: From each language-specific dataset, we manually constructed a subset of 20 diverse natural language queries along with corresponding ground truth code implementations as the example set. With this small set of curated examples, we generate 10 sample programs for each example from five strong code LLMs

claim: On the low-resource DSLs Ansible and Lean, SLMFix raised the static-check pass rate over the base LLM's output by an average of over 40%, averaged across the base LLMs tested.
quote: For Ansible and Lean, which are low-resource languages, SLMFix is able to improve the pass rate of static checking by an average of over 40%, which is higher than most baselines we compared against.

claim: With Qwen2.5-Coder 7B as generator, SLMFix reached 96.92% (Ansible) and 75.48% (Lean) validator pass rates against 59.56% and 15.96% for the base model and 73.83% and 7.31% for LoRA SFT of the 7B model, while Lean CodeBERTScore fell from 0.7320 (base) to 0.6598.
On the Spider SQL test suites (functional correctness), SLMFix left Qwen2.5-Coder 7B's score essentially unchanged at 0.702 versus 0.699 for the base model, below SFT and ICL at 0.716.
SLMFix added on average 7.35 ms per sample on the 596-example Ansible evaluation set, with latency counted as base generation plus fixing.
quote: Latency is measured as total generation time in seconds for the evaluation dataset of size 596. For program repair methods, the latency is calculated as sum of generation (Base) and fixing. SLMFix brings little additional inference latency (7.35 milliseconds per sample on average).

claim: Trained with the same RL recipe to generate Ansible directly rather than repair it, the 0.5B model reached a 48.83% validator pass rate versus 94.30% as a fixer (Ansible ablation).
The authors list as a limitation that SLMFix depends on an efficient syntactic checker for the target language, which for Ansible had to be built by hand.
quote: Third, our method relies on an efficient syntactic checker for the target language. Although this is generally available for most languages, manually implementing such a checker might be needed for certain languages like Ansible, which limits the usability of our pipeline.

claim: FLAME is a T5-small-based model with 60 million parameters, trained only on Excel formulas and compared against models of up to 175B parameters on repair and completion.
quote: FLAME is based on T5-small (Raffel et al. 2020) and has only 60 million parameters, yet it can compete with much larger models (up to 175B parameters) on last-mile formula repair and formula completion.

claim: FLAME's pre-training corpus was cut from 927M formulas to 6.1M by syntax-based (sketch) deduplication of formulas that differ only in cell inputs.
quote: To create a small but varied pre-training corpus, we reduced a corpus of 927M formulas down to 6.1M by comparing formulas based on syntax, removing near-duplicate formulas, which only vary in terms of cell inputs

claim: Deduplicating globally instead of per workbook left 591K formulas and gave a worse model, e.g. -8 points on fine-tuned repair and -19 points on exact-match completion.
quote: This results in a pre-training set of 591K formulas. Table 4 shows that training on this smaller corpus results in a worse model (e.g., -8pp on fine-tuned repair, -19pp on exact match completion).

claim: Repair fine-tuning used no human-labelled repairs: 200K well-formed help-forum formulas were corrupted with FLAME's user-inspired noise operators to make broken/fixed pairs.
quote: We create a fine-tuning dataset for all systems by taking 200K well-formed formulas from Excel help forums 3 and randomly applying our user-inspired noise operators to generate broken formulas.

claim: Across 14 repair and completion settings, FLAME (60M) outperformed Codex-Davinci (175B), Codex-Cushman (12B) and CodeT5 (220M) in 10.
quote: FLAME can outperform much larger models, such as the Davinci (175B) and Cushman (12B) variants of Codex and CodeT5 (220M), in 10 of 14 evaluation settings for the repair and completion tasks.

claim: On the Forum repair benchmark (273 real user formulas), fine-tuned FLAME scored 0.76 top-1 and 0.89 top-5, tying few-shot Davinci and trailing fine-tuned Cushman at top-1 (0.79); on the Synthetic benchmark Cushman led (0.87 vs 0.83 top-1).

Measured on a CPU to emulate client-side deployment, FLAME and CodeT5 had the lowest and comparable repair latency on the Forum set, with FLAME repairing substantially more; the latency values themselves appear only in a figure.
quote: We carry out all measurements on a CPU to emulate client-side deployment, where a GPU may not be available. Figure 5 shows each model's last-mile repair rate (with a top5 cutoff) and the average latency (seconds) to generate repair candidates for the Forum dataset. Cushman and Davinci results include network time as they are only available through an API. Davinci is used in a few-shot setting, and all other models are fine-tuned. CodeT5 (60M) and FLAME have the lowest, and comparable, latency. However, FLAME achieves a substantially higher repair rate compared to CodeT5.

claim: A 16M-parameter FLAME trained the same way scored 0.68 zero-shot and 0.73 fine-tuned top-1 on Forum repair, versus 0.71 and 0.76 for the 60M model.
The authors note that exact-match scoring misses some FLAME fixes that look more natural but differ from the user's ground-truth repair.
quote: We note that in some cases, FLAME's fixes appear to be more natural, but fail to match the user's ground truth repair.

claim: The FLAME paper carries an AAAI 2024 copyright line.
quote: Copyright © 2024, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

claim: Lean Copilot runs model inference inside Lean by wrapping it in a C++ function called through Lean's FFI, either locally via CTranslate2 or on a server.
quote: Lean Copilot makes the model runnable in Lean by wrapping its inference into a C++ function operating on strings, which can be called in Lean through FFI. As in Fig. 1, we can run the model either locally via CTranslate2 or on a server.

claim: Lean Copilot's default model is LeanDojo's pretrained ReProver, a ByT5 encoder-decoder chosen because it does both tactic generation and premise retrieval; no parameter count is given in this paper.
quote: By default, we adopt the pretrained ReProver model from LeanDojo (Yang et al., 2023) for its multi-faceted capability in not only tactic generation but also premise retrieval. ReProver is based on an encoder-decoder Transformer, ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022), that maps an input string to an output string.

claim: Running efficiently on most hardware without GPUs is stated as a design requirement, because Lean users prove theorems on laptops without GPUs; it is a goal, not a measured result.
quote: Additionally, theorem proving in Lean can work well on a user's local laptop without GPUs. Lean Copilot needs to avoid adding extra hardware constraints, so it should be able to run efficiently on most hardware even without GPUs.

claim: Each model-suggested tactic is first run by a Lean meta-program against the current goals, and candidates that raise errors are dropped before the user sees them.
quote: Instead of blindly returning all of them to users, we further check each tactic candidate via a meta-program in Lean that simulates running the tactic candidate on the current proof goals. There are three possible results. If the tactic candidate leads to errors, we drop them from the list.

claim: On the Mathematics in Lean theorems, SEARCH_PROOF needed on average 2.08 human-entered tactics versus 3.86 for AESOP and 3.11 for SUGGEST_TACTICS (Table 1 prints 3.10).
quote: When used to assist humans, SEARCH_PROOF only requires an average of 2.08 manually-entered tactics, which compares favorably to AESOP (3.86) and SUGGEST_TACTICS (3.11).

claim: Averaged per theorem, SEARCH_PROOF automated 74.2% of proof steps versus 58.4% for SUGGEST_TACTICS and 40.1% for AESOP (Table 1 prints 58.3% for SUGGEST_TACTICS).
quote: Averaging the percentage over all tested theorems, we find that SEARCH_PROOF can automate about 74.2%of the proof steps in a theorem, significantly more helpful than SUGGEST_TACTICS (58.4%) and AESOP (40.1%).

claim: Proving the 168 tactic-style textbook theorems with no human input, AESOP succeeded on 24.4%, SUGGEST_TACTICS on 45.2% and SEARCH_PROOF on 63.7%.

The human-assistance numbers come from replaying each theorem's ground-truth tactics one at a time and calling the tools after each, not from a user study, and the AESOP baseline ran with no configured rule set.
quote: To mimic a human user, we enter the ground truth tactics one by one. After each tactic, we try to prove the remaining goals using each of the automated tools: SEARCH_PROOF, AESOP, and SUGGEST_TACTICS. For AESOP, we use it out of the box, without manually configuring the rule set.

claim: The authors warn that a copilot backed by a static model soon becomes less helpful in a fast-moving project that keeps adding premises, unless the model is updated.
quote: Especially in fast-developing formalization projects, new premises can appear frequently. If the knowledge base of the LLM behind the proof automation tools is static, it would require the LLM to be updated once in a while. Otherwise it soon becomes less helpful.

claim: The paper thanks the anonymous reviewers at NeuS 2025; it has an editors line but no explicit proceedings or copyright line.
quote: We appreciate the valuable feedback from members of the Anima AI+Science Lab on an initial version of this paper, from the Lean community on the releases of our tool, and from the anonymous reviewers at NeuS 2025.

claim: JetBrains' Full Line Code Completion ships INT4-quantized LLaMA-like models of 100M parameters with a modified BPE tokenizer.
quote: In summary, for Full Line Code Completion, INT4-quantized LLaMA-like models with 100M parameters were used. The models utilize a modified BPE tokenizer implemented on top of the YouTokenToMe library.

claim: The Python model's data totalled slightly more than 50 GB, split 80%/5%/15% into train, validation and test sets.
quote: For the training of the Python model, the corresponding proportions of the train-validation-test sets of the data were 80%-5%-15%, adding up to slightly more than 50 GB of data.

claim: INT4 quantization in llama.cpp shrank the model from almost 400 MB to slightly over 100 MB and made CPU inference 2x faster on an M2 Mac and 4x faster on an Intel i9 Linux machine.
quote: Firstly, the size of the model decreased from almost 400 MB to slightly more than 100 MB, which fits within the desired restrictions. Secondly, llama.cpp allows us to shorten the CPU inference time due to more efficient usage of the registers for INT4 data: e.g., the quantized model runs 2 times faster compared to full precision model on M2 CPU on MacOS and 4 times faster on Intel i9 CPU on Linux.

claim: The IDE teams set the feature's memory budget at an upper bound of about 20-40% of the IDE's own memory footprint.
quote: Insights from the IDE development teams give us a general upper bound of about 20-40% of the IDE memory footprint (might differ between products).

claim: Measured online, the average CPU time from invoking completion to showing a suggestion was 150 ms including cache initialisation, and the cache was reused in over 90% of completion events.
quote: The average time to show for FLCC is 150 ms, which is perfect for the user's visual perception [67]. The result includes cache initialization events, as well as cache reusing. According to our observation, the cache is used in over 90% of completion events, which makes a typical time to show even lower.

claim: In A/B tests on early-access users, Python users with the feature wrote 1.3 times as much code through completion (22% vs 17% of written code) as users with standard completion only.
quote: For Python, the metric bumped 1.3 times (from 17% to 22%) for users with FLCC enabled compared to users with standard code completion only.

claim: The Python acceptance rate was about 38% (standard completion about 27%), which the authors say cannot be compared directly because suggestion lengths differ.
quote: The acceptance rate for Full Line Code Completion for Python was about 38%. For standard completion, the value is about 27%, however, no conclusions can be made from this comparison due to significantly different lengths of suggestions.

claim: Filtering out suggestions that fail the IDE's code inspections cost only 1% of valuable suggestions in the 2023.3 PyCharm Pro study, and lets the feature show only valid code.
quote: Our research for the 2023.3 PyCharm Pro release showed that FLCC benefits from filtering out incorrect code. Only 1% of valuable suggestions are lost, and as a trade-off for such a negligible loss, we establish the distinguishing feature of Full Line Code Completion - suggesting only valid code.

claim: At their model sizes the authors found knowledge distillation gave no quality improvement, so they did not use it.
quote: Unlike in many similar circumstances, we do not employ knowledge distillation [56], because we discovered that for our sizes of the models, this technique does not provide any quality improvement.

claim: The online results come only from early-access (EAP) users, who the authors say may not represent the broader IDE user base.
quote: Although the results were statistically significant, they may not fully represent the broader user base of IntelliJ-based IDEs, as EAP participants typically have a deeper understanding and engagement with the IDE's features

claim: Ansible Wisdom uses the CodeGen architecture at 350M parameters, chosen for throughput: on a single GPU the 350M model generated about 1.9x faster than the 2.7B one.
quote: We tested the architecture of CODEGEN 350M and CODEGEN 2.7B. We benchmarked the generation throughput on single GPU for both models and found that the 350M model was ∼ 1.9× faster than than the 2.7B.

claim: The curated pre-training data held about 1.1M Ansible task and playbook YAML files and about 2.2M generic YAML files.
quote: Our curated dataset contains ∼1.1M Ansible task and playbook YAMLs, and ∼2.2M other generic YAML files.

claim: WISDOM-ANSIBLE-MULTI and WISDOM-YAML-MULTI continue pre-training from a CodeGen checkpoint on Ansible and generic YAML amounting to about 1.1 billion tokens.
quote: The Ansible-YAML and generic YAML files account for about 1.1 billion training tokens in total.

claim: Recasting NL-to-Ansible generation as completion after the task's own name field beat a prefix-style prompt by about 10% BLEU, 26% Schema Correct and 16% exact match (fine-tuned CodeGen, 1024-token window).
quote: According to the results shown in Table IV, under the window size 1024, CODEGEN with the proposed prompt format largely outperforms CODEGEN-prefix, for example, 10% percent higher on BLEU, 26% percent higher on SCHEMA CORRECT, and 16% percent higher on EM.

claim: The fine-tuned 350M Ansible model reached BLEU 66.67 against 50.4 for Codex-Davinci-002, but Codex was evaluated few-shot rather than fine-tuned.
quote: We also show that after finetuning, our Ansible specific model (BLEU: 66.67) can outperform a much larger CodexDavinci-002 (BLEU: 50.4) model, which was evaluated in few shot settings.

claim: After fine-tuning, Ansible-YAML pre-training added only about 1 point over plain CodeGen-Multi at the same 350M size and 1024 window (BLEU 66.67 vs 66.03 in Table IV).
quote: By comparing the fine-tuned CODEGEN-MULTI and WISDOM-ANSIBLE-MULTI (both with window size 1024 and model size 350M) in Table IV, it shows pre-training on Ansible data can help the large language model better understand the syntax and structure of Ansible. Specifically, WISDOM-ANSIBLE-MULTI has gained 1% increase regarding Schema Correct, EM and Ansible Aware.

claim: In the few-shot setting, Codex-Davinci-002 (175B) still beat WISDOM-ANSIBLE-MULTI 350M on BLEU (50.40 vs 46.58), exact match (13.66 vs 7.35) and Ansible Aware (55.01 vs 54.51), losing only on Schema Correct (88.82 vs 96.56).
Generating a whole playbook from NL alone was weak: on 550 NL-to-playbook test samples fine-tuned CodeGen-Multi scored 0.0 exact match and 22.76 BLEU, versus 66.03 BLEU over all 50,580 samples.
All Ansible results are similarity metrics against a reference, since executing generated tasks that depend on external resources was judged impractical.
quote: Since the generated ansible task or a small playbook always has high dependency on external resources, it is not practical to evaluate the correctness of a task by executing it. For example it would be impractical to evaluate a task that installs a package on a number of remote hosts by executing it with Ansible and checking that the result is as expected. Thus, our evaluation metrics are based on the similarity between the generated ansible tasks or playbooks and the ground-truth.

claim: After fine-tuning, CodeGen-Multi 2.7B (BLEU 65.25) did no better than the 350M model (66.03) at a 1024-token window, and a 2048 window gave no gain over 1024 (66.12).

LaMirage generates a repair engine from a grammar plus domain-specific rules in which symbolic code produces every candidate repair, while neural models are used only to localize errors and rank the candidates.
quote: To tackle the challenges of localizing the errors and ranking the candidate repairs, LaMirage leverages neural techniques, whereas it relies on symbolic methods to generate candidate repairs.

claim: On the 200-formula Excel benchmark (real forum formulas, manually annotated ground truth), LaMirage's top-1 candidate matched the ground truth for 174 formulas versus 147 for the next best system, Codex-Edit.
quote: In Excel, LaMirage's top repair candidate matched the ground truth repair in 174 out of 200 formulas, compared to 147 for the next best system, Codex-Edit.

claim: On the 200-formula Power Fx benchmark (100 forum and 100 telemetry formulas), LaMirage's top-1 candidate matched the ground truth for 170 formulas versus 106 for Codex-Edit, the next best system.
quote: 170 out of 200 formulas, compared to 106 for Codex-Edit. We also motivate our design with ablation studies.

claim: Moving from Excel to Power Fx, whose public corpus the authors note is much smaller, LaMirage repaired 4 fewer formulas at top-1 while Codex-Edit repaired 41 fewer.
quote: LaMirage, which combines symbolic and neural benefits, experienced the smallest drop in performance (4 fewer formulas repaired at top-1 cutoff) compared to the next best approach (Codex-Edit, which repaired 41 fewer at top-1 cutoff).

claim: Median time to produce all repair candidates per formula was 32.1 ms (Excel) and 134.4 ms (Power Fx) for LaMirage against 5806.6 ms and 6417.6 ms for Codex-Edit, whose times include OpenAI API network time.

In the top-1 ablation (full system 174 Excel, 170 Power Fx, of 200 each), removing the domain-specific strategies dropped Excel to 138 and Power Fx to 153, while removing the neural ranker left Excel at 173.9 but dropped Power Fx to 150.9.

Replacing the symbolic candidate enumerator with neural enumeration lowered top-1 repairs to 135 (Excel) and 125 (Power Fx) with CodeBERT and to 128 and 112 with Codex, versus 174 and 170 for full LaMirage.

The authors advise that training the neural ranker requires a corpus of at least tens of thousands of well-formed programs in the target language; without it the engine falls back to purely symbolic ranking.
quote: To train the ranker successfully, the language developer's corpus should contain at least 10s of thousands of well-formed programs.

claim: The pointer-network error localizer was trained only on synthetic corruptions of well-formed formulas: 480,572 well-formed/buggy pairs for Excel and 60,802 for Power Fx.
quote: We train pointer network independently for Excel with 480572 synthetically generated well formedbuggy formula pairs and Powerfx with 60802 synthetically generated well formed-buggy formula pairs.

claim: The price of LaMirage's speed and low compute is a one-time manual cost: the language developer must supply an annotated grammar (which tokens are unreliable) and the domain-specific strategies.
quote: LaMirage can quickly (and cheaply, in terms of compute resources) produce effective repairs, but at the one-time cost of the language developer providing an annotated CFG and DSS.

claim: The RING paper carries a 2023 copyright line of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI).
quote: Copyright © 2023, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

claim: RING uses Codex with no training at all, splitting repair into three prompted stages: fault localization (a compiler or analyzer message in the prompt), code transformation (few-shot examples retrieved by error similarity) and candidate ranking (mean token log-probability).
quote: To do this effectively, we break down program repair into the same three phases as symbolic automated program repair systems: fault localization, code transformation, and candidate ranking

claim: RING's Excel benchmark is 273 tasks: LaMirage's 200 forum formulas plus 73 newly collected formulas that each contain at least one type error.
quote: We also collect a set of 73 tasks where the Excel formula contains at least one type error and annotated each such formula with a ground truth repair. The final collection consists of 273 Excel repair tasks.

claim: On the 273 Excel tasks, RING (davinci-code-002 at temperature 0.7, abstracted error message, error-vector shot selection) reached exact-match pass@1 0.82 against 0.71 for LaMirage.
quote: Excel | RING (Abstracted Message, Error Vector) | 0.82 | 0.89 | 0.92 | Exact Match | 26 ±14 | | | LaMirage (Bavishi et al. 2022) | 0.71 | 0.76 | - | Exact Match | 26 ±14

claim: On the 200 Power Fx tasks, LaMirage beat RING at exact-match pass@1 (0.85 vs 0.71); RING's pass@3 of 0.85 only matched LaMirage's pass@1.
quote: Power Fx | RING (Compiler Message, Message Embedding) | 0.71 | 0.85 | 0.87 | Exact Match | 29 ±19 | | Power Fx | LaMirage (Bavishi et al. 2022) | 0.85 | 0.88 | - | Exact Match | 29 ±19

claim: Of RING's 6 languages, it beat the language-specific engine at pass@1 in 3 (Excel, Python, C); for Power Fx only its pass@3 was comparable to LaMirage's pass@1.
quote: RING outperforms the state-of-the-art repair engines in pass@1 for Excel, Python, and C. For Power Fx, we find that RING's pass@3 rate is comparable to the pass@1 rate for LaMirage.

claim: On 200 JavaScript ESLint tasks, TFix on its original windowed snippets beat RING at exact-match pass@1 (0.59 vs 0.46), though TFix fell to 0.09 on the extended whole-function snippets that RING was given.
quote: Javascript | RING (Compiler Message, Error Vector) | 0.46 | 0.59 | 0.64 | Exact Match | 163 ±106 | | Javascript | TFix (extended code snippets) (Berabi et al. 2021) | 0.09 | - | - | Exact Match | 163 ±106 | | Javascript | TFix (original dataset) (Berabi et al. 2021) | 0.59

claim: On the new PowerShell benchmark (208 StackOverflow task pairs, no prior engine), RING reached only 0.10 exact-match pass@1 against 0.06 for zero-shot Codex, which the authors attribute to presumed scarcity of PowerShell in Codex's training data.
quote: Powershell | RING (Compiler Message, Message Embedding) | 0.10 | 0.19 | 0.27 | Exact Match | 24 ±30 | | Powershell | Codex (Chen et al. 2021) | 0.06

claim: In the JavaScript configuration study, adding only the compiler/linter error message to the zero-shot prompt raised exact-match pass@1 from 0.19 to 0.35 before any few-shot examples were added.

Error-similarity shot selection raised pass@1 over fixed shots from 0.76 to 0.82 in Excel but only from 0.70 to 0.71 in Power Fx, which the authors attribute to imprecise Power Fx compiler messages adding noise to retrieval.
RTLFixer was published at the 61st ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC 2024).
quote: In 61st ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC '24), June 23-27, 2024, San Francisco, CA, USA.

claim: On VerilogEval-Human, syntax errors made up 55% of the errors in GPT-3.5-generated Verilog, more than simulation (functional) errors.
quote: The VerilogEval-Human benchmark statistics show that syntax errors constitute a significant 55% of errors in GPT-3.5 generated Verilog code, surpassing simulation errors.

claim: RTLFixer uses an off-the-shelf gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613 with no fine-tuning, after a rule-based pre-fixer, as a ReAct agent limited to 10 Thought-Action-Observation iterations at temperature 0.4, where actions can call the compiler.
quote: We specifically used gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613. A simple rulebased syntax fixer is applied to every LLM-generated verilog code, which avoids simple errors such as misplaced timescale derivatives. In all experiments, we set the sampling temperature to 0.4. For ReAct prompting, we restrict the LLM to a maximum of 10 iterations of Thought-Action-Observation, where Action might involve interactions with the compiler.

claim: On the 212-implementation VerilogEval-syntax set with GPT-3.5 and Quartus compiler messages, the compile-error fix rate was 98.5% with ReAct plus RAG versus 79.9% for ReAct alone, and 89.9% versus 58.7% for one-shot prompting with and without RAG (mean of 10 runs).
quote: The results with Quartus compiler in Table 1 show that RAG improves the fix rate by 31.2% (58.7% to 89.9% ) for One-shot and 18.6% (79.9% to 98.5%) when using ReAct.

claim: With GPT-3.5 and ReAct, the fix rate was 73.1% (no RAG) and 82.0% (RAG) with the terse open-source iverilog messages versus 79.9% and 98.5% with the more informative commercial Quartus messages; GPT-4 with Quartus reached 92% and 99%.

Fixing only syntax errors raised VerilogEval-Machine simulation pass@1 from 0.467 to 0.799 (pass@5 from 0.691 to 0.891), an absolute gain of 33.2 points by the table although the paper reports it as 32.3%.
On VerilogEval-Human, fixing only syntax errors raised simulation pass@1 from 26.7% to 36.8%, i.e. the reported 10.1% gain is in absolute percentage points.
quote: With just addressing syntax errors using our approach (shown in the inner circle), the pass rate increases from 26.7% to 36.8%.

claim: The RAG database is hand-written human expert guidance keyed by compiler error tags and retrieved by exact match: 7 error categories with 30 entries for iverilog and 11 categories with 45 entries for Quartus.
quote: We collected 7 common error categories with 30 entries for iverilog and 11 common error categories with 45 entries for Qaurtus in total.

claim: With GPT-4 and Quartus feedback, ReAct improved on one-shot prompting by only about 1%, which the authors read as GPT-4 fixing syntax errors without needing reasoning, planning or iteration.
quote: When comparing the results of GPT-4 between One-shot and ReAct, we observe minor improvements of approximately 1%, suggesting that GPT-4 is already a robust agent proficient in fixing syntax errors without the need for reasoning, action planning, and iterative refinement.

claim: On RTLLM, with no new guidance entries, RTLFixer raised GPT-3.5's syntax success rate from 73% to 93% but simulation pass@1 only from 11% to 16%.
HDLdebugger's ACM reference format places it in the proceedings of KDD 2024 (13 pages).
quote: 2024. HDLdebugger: Streamlining HDL debugging with Large Language Models. In Proceedings of (KDD'24). ACM, New York, NY, USA, 13 pages.

claim: Training pairs are synthesized by applying LLM-derived modification functions to clean industrial HDL and compiling the results to capture real error messages, so the faults and fixes are known by construction and no manual diagnosis is needed.
quote: Given that our instructions systematically brought the errors, we can employ reverse engineering to identify the faults and produce solutions directly. This bypasses the need for manual error diagnosis

claim: The data are 92,143 generated (buggy code, compiler error messages, correct code) instances from Huawei HDL files, split 8:2 into train and test, so the test set comes from the same mutation generator as the training set.
quote: Based on these HDL code files, we use the data generation in Sec. 2.1 to generate 92,143 distinct HDL training code instances. Each HDL training code instance consists of the buggy HDL code, error messages, and the correct HDL code. Specifically, in the experiments, we split the data into training and testing sets at a ratio of 8:2, respectively.

claim: HDLdebugger fine-tunes CodeLlama-13b, a size the authors chose to balance training and deployment cost against performance.
quote: Specifically, we selected CodeLlama-13b as our base model from the available code LLMs.

claim: On the held-out synthetic Huawei test split, HDLdebugger reached an 81.93% pass rate versus 71.57% for the strongest of its 13 baselines, WizardCoder fine-tuned on the same data.
quote: WizardCoder w/ SFT | 71.57% | 1.04 | 1.06 | | HDLdebugger(ours) | 81.93% | 1.00 | 1.00

claim: The ChatGPT and GPT-4 baselines (3.01% and 6.35% pass rate) were run with certain code specifications omitted for privacy, so they did not see the same inputs as the other systems.
quote: Due to privacy concerns, certain code specifications have been omitted for testing purposes when using ChatGPT or GPT4.

claim: In the CodeLlama ablation on the same test split, direct prompting scored 4.01%, adding RAG 15.05%, SFT 70.56% and SFT with generated thoughts 74.91%, versus 81.93% for the full RAG plus SFT-with-thoughts system.
The Verilog-specialized VeriGen scored under 1% raw and 1.34% with RAG on Huawei's HDL, but 67.55% after supervised fine-tuning on the synthetic pairs.

The explanatory thoughts used as fine-tuning targets are written by an LLM shown both the buggy and the corrected code, sampled several times, and the one whose resulting fix has the smallest edit distance to the ground truth is kept.
quote: The core principle of our approach involves submitting both the buggy code and its corrected version to the LLM, subsequently prompting the model to generate instructive guidance.

claim: In deployment the authors found compile-passing fixes insufficient, since compiling code may still hurt chip performance and engineers often want hints rather than exact rewrites, for which they have no metric.
quote: Code that successfully compiles may not necessarily optimize chip design performance. Additionally, exact solutions are not always required; engineers often benefit from suggestive "hints" that inspire solutions to complex issues.

claim: The study distills code repair from a GPT-3.5-Turbo teacher into three 7B students (CodeLlama-7b-Instruct, CodeLlama-7b, Mistral-7b), fine-tuned with LoRA.
quote: Our teacher model is GPT-3.5-Turbo (Ouyang et al., 2022; OpenAI, 2022), while our student models are CodeLlama7b-Instruct (Rozière et al., 2024), CodeLlama-7b (Rozière et al., 2024), and Mistral-7b (Jiang et al., 2023).

claim: Each per-language fine-tuning set has only about 400 examples, from an 800-question MBXP split, each pairing a student's failing answer and its test-execution error with a teacher repair that passed the tests, with no human labeling.
quote: Although the original train split starts with 800 examples, our construction pipeline results in fine-tuning datasets with around 400 examples.

claim: Relative to the initial generation without any repair, four rounds of distilled repair raised CodeLlama-7b-Instruct's mean HumanEval pass@1 by 99.5% for Perl, 112.8% for Golang and 144.5% for Swift.
quote: We see a relative increase in the average pass@1 of CodeLlama-7b-Instruct by 99.5% for Perl, 112.8% for Golang, and 144.5% for Swift after four rounds of repair on HumanEval.

claim: Against rationale-only distillation (teacher rationale in context), rationale-plus-code distillation raised CodeLlama-7b-Instruct's Perl HumanEval pass@1 from 0.360 to 0.439 (+21.9% relative; initial generation 0.220).

On high-resource languages the benefit of distilling code vanished: CodeLlama-7b-Instruct's HumanEval pass@1 went from 0.499 to 0.495 for JavaScript and from 0.464 to 0.457 for Java (rationale-only to rationale-plus-code).
On low-resource languages, rationale-only repair models produced a rationale judged correct (by GPT-4) 91.1% of the time but correct code only 10.0% of the time.
quote: On LRPLs, rationale-only repair models generate a correct rationale 91.1% of the time, but only generate correct code 10.0% of the time, exposing a weak correlation between rationale correctness and code correctness.

claim: Rationale quality in the 91.1%/10.0% analysis was judged by GPT-4 rather than people, because recruiting programmers fluent in Perl and Swift proved hard.
quote: Although human evaluation would be preferred, crowdsourcing participants well-versed in programming languages like Perl and Swift and capable of solving the coding problems found in HumanEval is challenging.

claim: Averaged over Perl, Golang and Swift, CodeLlama-7b-Instruct repair runs ended with 16.9 syntax errors for rationale-plus-code models versus 30.9 for rationale-only models.
quote: Averaging over the 3 LRPLs, rationale-plus-code models finish with 16.9 errors, while rationale-only models finish with 30.9 errors.

claim: Across all 6 languages, four rounds of distilled repair (5 inference calls in total) outperformed the initial generation's pass@5 from independent sampling.
quote: Across all languages, four rounds of distilled code repair outperforms the initial pass@5.

claim: The study's low-resource languages still appear in pretraining data: Perl and Golang are 0.1% and 0.32% of DeepSeek-Coder's corpus, against 15.12% and 18.63% for Python and Java.
quote: containing high-resource languages like Python and Java at rates of 15.12% an 18.63%, while other languages like Perl and Golang are at much lesser rates of 0.1% and 0.32%.

claim: Break-It-Fix-It (Yasunaga and Liang) was published at ICML 2021 (PMLR 139).
quote: Proceedings of the 38 th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139, 2021.

claim: BIFI learns a fixer from unpaired code plus a critic (the Python AST parser or the C compiler) by keeping only fixer outputs on real bad code that the critic accepts, and by training a breaker on those real pairs to generate realistic bad code, instead of relying only on heuristic corruption.
quote: (i) we use the critic to check a fixer's output on real bad inputs and add good (fixed) outputs to the training data, and (ii) we train a breaker to generate realistic bad code from good code.

claim: Without any labelled data, BIFI reaches 90.5% repair accuracy on GitHub-Python (+28.5 points absolute over its initial fixer trained on random perturbations, 62.0%) and 71.7% on DeepFix (+5.6 points over DrRepair, 66.1%, on BIFI's 20% held-out split).
quote: BIFI outperforms state-of-the-art methods, obtaining 90.5% repair accuracy on GitHubPython (+28.5%) and 71.7% on DeepFix (+5.6%). Notably, BIFI does not require any labeled data

claim: GitHub-Python is 3M Python 3 snippets of 10-128 tokens labelled only by the AST parser as critic: 38K are bad, of which 15K real bad snippets are the test set and the remaining 23K are the only real bad examples BIFI trains on.
quote: Using this critic, we obtain 38K snippets of bad code and 3M snippets of good code. From the 38K bad examples, we holdout 15K as the final test set, and make the remaining 23K bad examples available for BIFI.

claim: On GitHub-Python a repair counts as successful when the output parses and lies within a Levenshtein distance of under 5 tokens from the input; the authors note that semantic preservation is not checked automatically, so the edit-distance bound stands in for it.
quote: We acknowledge that while we want f(x) to be semantics-preserving, it is nontrivial to ensure this automatically, so we rely on the edit distance.

claim: On GitHub-Python the BIFI fixer and breaker are each a small encoder-decoder Transformer with 4 layers, 8 attention heads and hidden size 256, trained on one GTX Titan X GPU; the paper gives no parameter count or inference speed.
quote: (Vaswani et al., 2017) with 4 layers, 8 attention heads, and hidden states of size 256. The model parameters are optimized by Adam

claim: BIFI's initial GitHub-Python fixer is trained purely on synthetic corruption: 1-3 tokens dropped, inserted or replaced uniformly, applied 8 times to each of 2.6M good snippets.
quote: which drops, inserts, or replaces 1-3 tokens in code with uniform distribution. We apply bsynthetic 8 times to each of the 2.6M good code snippets to prepare the initial training data Psynthetic.

claim: Training the initial fixer for as many extra rounds on synthetic perturbations only gave no improvement (62.7% versus 62.0% on GitHub-Python), which the authors read as a performance ceiling for synthetic-only training.
quote: however, this did not provide an improvement, suggesting that there is a performance ceiling if we only train on synthetic data.

claim: With only 10% of the 23K real bad GitHub-Python examples available, critic-verified self-training (FixerOnly) still reaches 78.5% against 62.7% for continued synthetic-only training.
quote: making FixerOnly perform better than using synthetic data alone (i.e., 78.5% vs 62.7%).

claim: On GitHub-Python, removing the critic's verification drops BIFI round 2 from 90.5% to 84.0%, and removing both the critic and training on real bad code (plain backtranslation) drops it to 80.1%.
quote: | - critic | Round-2 | 84.0% | | - both (backtranslation) | Round-2 | 80.1% |

claim: Error categories that random perturbation rarely produces are where synthetic training fails: on GitHub-Python indentation errors the initial fixer repairs about 39%, rising to about 85% after BIFI rounds 1-2.
quote: but it achieves significantly higher performance in round 1, 2 (e.g., 39%→85% for indentation errors).

claim: DrRepair (Yasunaga and Liang, graph-based self-supervised repair from diagnostic feedback) was published at ICML 2020 (PMLR 119).
quote: Proceedings of the 37 th International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, Austria, PMLR 119, 2020.

claim: DrRepair reports a 68.2% full repair rate on the DeepFix raw test set (+22.9 points over the prior best, SampleFix at 45.3%) and a 48.4% synthesis success rate on SPoC (+3.7 points), although the SPoC table in this version does not list a 48.4% entry for DrRepair.
quote: 68.2% full repair rate on DeepFix (+22.9% over the prior best), and 48.4% synthesis success rate on SPoC (+3.7% over the prior best).

claim: DrRepair's program-feedback graph takes every identifier in the code and every symbol quoted in the compiler message as nodes and links identical symbols, so graph attention can jump from the message to the declaration that caused it.
quote: it takes all identifiers (e.g. a, b) in the source code and any symbols in the diagnostic arguments (e.g. a, char) as nodes, and connects instances of the same symbols with edges to encode the semantic correspondence

claim: DrRepair is a small LSTM-plus-graph-attention model (bidirectional LSTM encoders, 2 graph-attention layers, a pointer-generator decoder) with state size 200 and 200-dimensional token embeddings, trained on one GTX Titan X; no parameter count or inference speed is given.
quote: We set the dimension of input token embeddings and position embeddings to be 200 and 100. The LSTMs and graph attention networks have a state size of 200.

claim: DrRepair conditions on only the first compiler message and must predict which line to edit itself, because the line the compiler reports is often not the line that needs the fix.
quote: If the compiler returns multiple error messages, we use only the first one.

claim: For self-supervised pre-training, DrRepair corrupts 310K compiling Codeforces C++ programs about 50 times each and keeps the variants that fail to compile, yielding about 1.5M (broken code, compiler feedback, fix) examples with no human labels.
quote: For each program, we then create roughly 50 corrupted versions by applying DrPerturb and keeping ones that fail to compile. This yields ∼1.5M extra training examples

claim: The corruption is not random token noise but DrPerturb: 1-5 heuristic edits from four modules (syntax, identifier type, identifier typo, keyword), sampled with probabilities 0.3/0.5/0.15/0.05 to match compiler-error statistics.
quote: samples 1-5 modules fromM (with replacement) and applies them to an input program sequentially. We sample each module with probability 0.3, 0.5, 0.15, 0.05, respectively, motivated by the distribution of errors found in our analysis (Table 1).

claim: Without the compiler message as input, the base model scores about the same on synthetic dev data but only 34.0% full repair on the real DeepFix test set, against 62.5% with the message: it learns superficial patterns of the synthetic data.
quote: We find that while it attains comparable scores to "our base" on the synthetic dev, the performance drops a lot on the raw test set: 34.0% acc., similar to the prior work (30-40% acc.).

claim: The same base model trained on DrPerturb data repairs 62.5% of the DeepFix test set, against 49.4% when trained on random token dropout, although random dropout produces more distinct compiler-error types (170 versus 156).
quote: while Random produces more distinct types of compiler errors than DrPerturb in terms of the number (170 vs 156), models trained by DrPerturb outperform Random by more than 10%

claim: On DeepFix full repair, the program-feedback graph adds about 3 points (62.5% to 66.4%) and self-supervised pre-training about 2 more (to 68.2%).
quote: provides a 3% boost over "base" in full repair rate, and self-supervised pre-training ("base + graph + pre-train") provides a further improvement of 2%

claim: Pre-training is not uniformly positive: on SPoC dev the 'request for member' error class falls from 56.9% with the graph model to 48.4% after pre-training, while the rare 'expected initializer' class (2.1% of training data) rises from 50.1% to 93.0%.
quote: | request for member '@@@' in '@@@', ... (e.g. Figure 1) | 2.9 % | 37.9 | 56.9 | 48.4 | | expected initializer before '@@@' | 2.1 % | 48.8 | 50.1 | 93.0 |

claim: SynShine (the arXiv 2104.14671 version) is a three-model pipeline for Java syntax errors: BLOCKFIX repairs brace nesting, javac then localises the faulty line, LINEFIX edits that line given the javac message, and UNKFIX fills identifiers with a masked language model.
quote: The second stage (LINEFIX) in SYNSHINE uses the line-location of the error, as detected by the standard javac compiler, together with the actual error message, and generates relevant fixes for delimiters, operators, and keywords

claim: LINEFIX and UNKFIX build on a RoBERTa-base-sized model: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 heads, with a byte-level BPE vocabulary capped at 25K subtokens.
quote: Our RoBERTa architecture consists of 12 attention layers, 768 hidden dimensions, and 12 self-attention heads in each layer. We applied Byte Level BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) tokenizer [23] limiting the subtoken vocabulary size to 25K.

claim: SynShine's masked-language-model pre-training uses 1.2 billion tokens from the 5000 most-starred Java projects on GitHub.
quote: we collected 5000 most starred Java projects from GitHub (since our end-goal is to correct Java syntax errors). We tokenized the files, yielding 1.2 billion tokens for the pre-training.

claim: Fine-tuning is supervised on real novice error/fix pairs from the Blackbox dataset (1.7M pairs in total); after holding out 100K test samples and dropping brace-imbalanced programs, about 540K examples train LINEFIX.
quote: We discarded the programs with imbalanced curly braces from the training set, and after tokenization, we found around 540K examples to train the model.

claim: Instead of autoregressive generation, LINEFIX classifies: one multi-label head picks token positions and another picks among 154 edit commands (insert, delete or substitute a delimiter, keyword, operator or the placeholder unk).
quote: LINEFIX outputs one of 154 possible editing commands, to insert/delete/substitute delimiters, keywords, operators, or identifiers. We limit its output vocabulary to 154.

claim: On a random sample of 100,000 Blackbox single-token-error programs up to 1000 tokens, scored by top-1 exact match with the human fix, SynShine reaches 74.89% against 56.91% for BF+FF, 63.25% for DeepFix (short) and 56.89% for SequenceR.
On programs needing 2 or 3 edits, SynShine's accuracy falls to 29.4% and 14.4% (single-token errors are 57% of Blackbox).
quote: We also applied our model on files that required 2 and 3 edits to fix the program and observed 29.4% and 14.4% accuracy, which is much higher than the reported accuracy by Ahmed et al. (19% and 9%).

claim: On 10,000 javac-flagged lines, adding the javac message to LINEFIX's input raises complete correction from 86.71% to 89.39% and localisation F-score from 90.75% to 93.58%; the authors stress that javac's line localisation, not the message, is the large win.

In a sample of 50 programs, the javac message alone was not that helpful in roughly 60% of cases, and the model learned to ignore or reinterpret misleading messages rather than translate them into fixes.
quote: We observed that in roughly 60% cases, the javac warning is not that helpful, and the model learns to respond in fairly nuanced ways to address the error.

claim: Integrated into VS Code as a CPU-only local correction server, SynShine answered 200 randomly chosen erroneous programs in 0.88 s on average (standard deviation 0.49 s, maximum 2.2 s).
quote: The average response time is 0.88 seconds (standard deviation 0.49s, maximum 2.2s).

claim: The SynShine correction server ran on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X CPU and occupied 1.765 GB of memory.
quote: The CPU we used for the experiment is "AMD Ryzen 7 2700X". The code correction server occupies 1.765 GB of the memory.

claim: Exact match with the human fix undercounts: 13% to 45% of SynShine's failures (depending on program length) still compile, but in a manual sample of 50 such cases only about 18% were semantically correct.
quote: We randomly collect 50 cases where the model generates a compilable fix, that fails to match the user fix recorded in Blackbox. We found that about 18% of programs are semantically correct.

claim: SynShine's accuracy falls with program length, from 82% for 1-100 tokens to 55% for 901-1000 tokens, and on the shortest programs DeepFix (short) at 77% is close behind.
quote: Our overall accuracy ranges between 55% to 82%, and always outperforms DeepFix long (18%-74%), and short (9%-77%), SequenceR (54%-59%) and BF+FF (29%-65%).

claim: DeepBugs frames name-based bug detection as binary classification and needs no human-labelled bugs: negative examples come from simple AST transformations (swapping arguments, replacing an operator or an operand) applied to presumed-correct code.
quote: To address the challenge that effectively learning a bug detector requires examples of both correct and incorrect code, we create likely incorrect code examples from an existing corpus of code through simple code transformations.

claim: Each DeepBugs detector is a tiny feedforward network with a single hidden layer of 200 units over concatenated Word2Vec (CBOW, 200-dimensional) identifier embeddings.
quote: a single hidden layer of size 200, and an output layer with a single element that represents the probability computed by D.

claim: DeepBugs trains on 100,000 deduplicated JavaScript files and evaluates on another 50,000 (68.6 million lines of code in total).
quote: In total, the corpus contains 68.6 million lines of code. We use 100,000 files for training and the remaining 50,000 files for validation.

claim: The 89.06%-94.70% accuracy figures for DeepBugs' three detectors are measured on artificially seeded bugs in the 50,000 validation files, not on real bugs.
quote: The accuracy ranges between 89.06% and 94.70%, i.e., all bug detectors are highly effective at distinguishing correct from incorrect code examples.

claim: On real code, the authors manually inspected the top 50 warnings of each of the three detectors: 95 of the 150 were bugs and 7 code-quality problems, so 68% pointed to a real problem.
quote: Out of the 150 inspected warnings, 95 warnings point to bugs and 7 warnings point to a code quality problem, i.e., 68% of all warnings point to an actual problem.

claim: Precision on real code varies a lot by detector: the swapped-arguments detector's top 50 warnings held 23 bugs and 27 false positives.
quote: | Swapped arguments | 50 | 23 | 0 | 27 |

claim: A trained DeepBugs detector takes on average under 20 ms per JavaScript file to predict, and training plus prediction over all 150,000 files takes 36-73 minutes per detector.
quote: Running both training and prediction on all 150,000 files takes between 36 minutes and 73 minutes per bug detector. The average prediction time per JavaScript file is below 20 milliseconds.

claim: Learned embeddings add only modestly over random identifier vectors: accuracy on seeded bugs goes from 93.88% to 94.70% (swapped arguments), 89.15% to 92.21% (binary operator) and 84.79% to 89.06% (binary operand).
quote: | Swapped arguments | 93.88% | 94.70% | | Wrong binary operator | 89.15% | 92.21% | | Wrong binary operand | 84.79% | 89.06% |

claim: At the default probability threshold of 0.5 the three detectors emit 116,941 warnings on the validation files, about one per 196 lines, so in practice only top-ranked warnings are usable.
quote: For a threshold of t = 0.5, the three bug detectors report a total of 116,941 warnings, which corresponds to roughly one warning per 196 lines of code.

claim: The authors name an inherent limitation: name-based detection fails when developers use unconventional names, which is the main source of DeepBugs' false positives.
quote: These false positives illustrate an inherent limitation of name-based bug detection: Because the approach relies in reasonable names that are in line with common practice, it may fail when developers choose to diverge from the norm.

claim: Ray et al. study 266 snapshots of 10 Java projects (202.6M non-comment lines, 38,003 commits), of which 8,296 commits are classified as bug fixes.
quote: These snapshots contain 38,003 distinct commits, of which 8,296 were marked as bug fixing changes

claim: Bug-fix commits, and therefore buggy lines, are labelled automatically from commit-message keywords rather than by humans, which the authors list as a source of false positives and false negatives.
quote: We mark a commit as bugfix, if the corresponding commit log contains at least one of the error related keywords

claim: The model is a cache n-gram language model: a global n-gram model interpolated with a cache built on the current file, with maximum n-gram order 10 and minimum back-off order 4, scoring each line's average token cross-entropy.
quote: We follow Tu et al. [36] to set the maximum order of cache ngrams to 10.

claim: Buggy lines are more entropic than non-buggy lines, but the effect shrinks with fix size: 1.67-1.80 bits higher (Cohen's d 0.56) for commits deleting at most 2 lines, and only 0.80-0.84 bits (d 0.26) at up to 30 deleted lines.
quote: for a max\_delete size of 2, the entropies of buggy lines are on average 1.67 to 1.80 bits higher, with a high effect size of 0.56.

claim: For commits deleting at most 5 lines, the entropy of buggy code drops by 1.19-1.26 bits once it is fixed (95% confidence).
quote: On average, entropy of the buggy lines drop after the bugfixes, with a drop of 1.19 to 1.26 bit, with 95% confidence.

claim: Raw cache-LM entropy is a weak line ranker at small inspection budgets: only 17% better than random at 5% of lines inspected; it needs a syntax-type normalisation and a bug-history weight ($gram+wType) to exceed twice random.
quote: Indeed, average performance of $gramwas significantly better than random at 20% (nearly twice as good) but only marginally so at 5% (17% better than random).

claim: On Rahman et al.'s Apache release data, the entropy-based finder and the static bug finders PMD and FindBugs perform comparably; the slight edge for entropy vanishes under full credit or without the bug-size threshold.
quote: SBF and NBF performed comparably; NBF performed slightly better when using both partial credit and the specified threshold for bug-sizes, but when dropping the threshold, and/or with full credit, no significant difference remains between NBF and SBF.

claim: Ordering static-bug-finder warnings by tool priority and then by entropy gives the most cost-effective inspection order the paper tests.
quote: Result 5: Ordering SBF warnings by priority and entropy significantly improves SBF performance.

claim: Naturalness misses bugs that look familiar: a copy-paste error reusing an existing statement had low entropy, and its correct fix raised entropy by 5.75 bits.
quote: Since, the statement related to maxChunkSize was already present in the existing corpus, the line was not surprising. Hence, its entropy was low although it was a bug.

claim: The authors concede that a surprising line is less informative than a static-analysis warning, since entropy only flags a line as surprising while a static bug finder says what is wrong.
quote: NBF just marks a line as "surprising", whereas SBF provides specific warnings.

claim: As a sanity check on 3 C/C++ projects (2,518 bug-fix commits), buggy lines were 0.87-1.16 bits more entropic than non-buggy lines at a 15-line threshold.
quote: we found that buggy lines were between 0.87 and 1.16 bits more entropic than non-buggy llines when using a threshold of 15 lines

claim: dcc --help wires gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 (via the OpenAI API) into the Debugging C Compiler, at both compile time and run time, consuming source code, error messages and error locations to produce novice-facing explanations.
quote: We introduce a new toolflow whereby DCC uses the OpenAI ChatGPT 3.5 API (model: gpt-3.5-turbo-0301) at compile- and run-time to consume source code, error messages, and locations

claim: The hidden dcc --help prompt contains a base prompt, the program source, DCC's enhanced error message (not the raw compiler message), the error line number, and, for run-time errors only, the GDB stack-frame values.
quote: Program source code, - DCC enhanced error message, - Error line number, and, - Values in the stack frame at error time (run-time only).

claim: Deployed in CS1 and CS2 courses at UNSW, dcc --help was used by 2,565 students over 64,000 times in ten weeks.
quote: dcc --help was deployed to our CS1 and CS2 courses, with 2,565 students using the tool over 64,000 times in ten weeks.

claim: On a random sample of 400 logged error/explanation pairs rated by four teaching reviewers, gpt-3.5-turbo's explanations were conceptually accurate in 90% of the 200 compile-time cases but only 75% of the 200 run-time cases.
quote: At compile-time, 90% conceptual accuracy was observed, as compared to 75% at run-time.

claim: Only 78% of sampled compile-time explanations and 53% of run-time explanations were free of any inaccuracy, as judged by the four reviewers.
quote: No inaccuracy was present in the generative explanation for compile-time errors in 78% of cases. Lower inaccuracy was observed at run-time, with only 53% of explanations having no inaccuracy.

claim: Guidance was technically correct in 93% of sampled compile-time cases versus 66% of run-time cases, and complete in 72% versus 39%.
quote: specifically noting 93% correctness at compile-time as compared to 66% at run-time. Generative explanations were consistently deemed relevant to the error, with 92% relevancy at compile-time and a reduced 75% at run-time. There is a large difference in how complete the explanations are between compile-time explanations at 72%, as compared to run-time, reduced 39%.

claim: Despite a prompt forbidding code, 48% of sampled compile-time and 49% of run-time explanations contained code blocks that reviewers considered too much help.
quote: Despite the prompt instructing that no code be given out with the explanation, 48% of the explanations at compile-time and 49% of run-time explanations contained blocks of code that reviewers considered too much help.

claim: dcc --help does not validate the model's output before showing it; its safeguards are a warning that the explanation may be wrong, a rate-limit warning, and removal from the exam environment.
quote: dcc --help warns students that AI-generated explanations may not be correct. The tool also detects if a student is generating many dcc --help explanations in a short amount of time

claim: The paper's quality numbers are reviewer judgements only: it did not measure whether the explanations actually helped students understand or fix their errors.
quote: Currently, we have not assessed students' interpretations of generative explanations, nor the tool's efficacy in assisting students to understand and solve errors.

claim: The paper identifies itself as a preprint of a SIGCSE'24 paper (March 20-25, 2024, Portland, OR).
quote: Preprint - SIGCSE'24, March 20-25, 2024, Portland, OR

claim: The SFT training set is 40,000 DCC Help examples from the first two teaching sessions, with target explanations written by gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 at temperature 0 (distillation, not human-written targets).
quote: Using this prompt strategy, we generate responses for the 40,000 examples using gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, via OpenAI's batch completions API, with a temperature of 0.

claim: Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-4B were each fine-tuned with QLoRA (4-bit quantised base plus adapters) for one epoch on a single 80GB A100.
quote: We train all our models using QLoRa [4], a Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning technique (PEFT) that quantises a language model to 4-bit and adds on top a set of trainable parameters called adapters, while the base model remains frozen.

claim: The automated evaluation set is about 8,000 examples (about 5,600 compile-time and 2,400 run-time) with eight model responses each, 64,000 responses in total, though Section 3.7 describes the same set as 32,000 responses.
quote: This produced an evaluation set of approximately 5,600 compile- and 2,400 run-time examples, each of which contains the student code and error context, and eight model responses (total evaluation responses: 64,000).

claim: The 8,000-example set was labelled by a three-judge LLM ensemble (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Qwen3-32B) under a strict unanimity rule, two of which are also candidate models or the training-data generator.
quote: Rather than relying on a single judge, we use a panel of three strong LLMs: GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Qwen3-32B.

claim: Before fine-tuning, base Qwen3-4B scored 0.74 expert-judged and 0.70 LLM-judged Correctness, and 0.61 / 0.65 Selectivity.
After SFT, Qwen3-4B scored 0.89 expert-judged and 0.86 LLM-judged Correctness, but satisfied all eight criteria in only 0.24 (expert) of compile-time and 0.30 of run-time responses.
On the 100 expert-annotated examples, SFT-Qwen3-4B stayed within 0.10 of GPT-4.1 on every expert-judged metric, with a mean rank 1.03 worse.
quote: When compared to GPT-4.1, SFT-Qwen-4B performs within a margin of 0.10 in all expert-judged metrics, and achieves a mean ranks score worse by only 1.03.

claim: In expert rankings (n = 100), SFT-Qwen3-4B beat GPT-4.1 in only 0.34 of compile-time and 0.36 of run-time comparisons, while beating the original DCC Help responses in 0.68 / 0.78.
Every fine-tuned model beat the deployed DCC Help responses on almost all metrics, with gains of at least 20% in Clarity and No Overhelp and higher expert rankings in 68%-82% of cases.
quote: Additionally, each of the fine-tuned models exceed the performance of DCC Help on almost all metrics, demonstrating gains of ≥20% in Clarity and No Overhelp, and with responses ranked higher in 68%-82% of cases.

claim: The authors note that because the training targets came from GPT-4.1, results are bounded by GPT-4.1's quality, style and biases, and using GPT-4.1 as a judge may reward imitation.
quote: Our SFT training dataset was generated using GPT-4.1, therefore our results are inherently bounded by the quality, style and biases of GPT-4.1.

claim: Leinonen et al. evaluated 81 Codex (code-davinci-002) generations: 9 Python 3.6 error messages, 3 author-written programs each, and 3 outputs per program (one at temperature 0, two at 0.7).
quote: This led to a total of 9 × 3 × 3 = 81 unique combinations of programming error message, program category, and temperature value, which we subsequently evaluated.

claim: Across 81 Codex outputs rated by two researchers (162 ratings, Cohen's kappa 0.83), outputs were comprehensible 88% of the time and contained an explanation for 84% of inputs, but only 57% of those explanations were correct, 48% of all inputs.
quote: Overall, the explanations created by Codex were quite comprehensible (88%). Codex produced an output with an explanation to 84% of the provided codes and error messages, but only about half (57%) of these explanations were deemed correct (48% of all inputs).

claim: 70% of Codex outputs proposed a fix, but only 47% of those fixes were correct, 33% of all inputs.
quote: Although 70% of the outputs had a proposed fix, a little less than half (47%) of those were deemed correct (33% of all inputs).

claim: Explanation correctness varied by error message from 11% ("unexpected EOF while parsing") to 83% ("can't assign to function call").
quote: The range of correct explanations ranged from 11% for "unexpected EOF while parsing" to 83% for "can't assign to function call".

claim: Temperature 0 did markedly better: outputs were judged an improvement over the original message in over 70% of cases at temperature 0 versus at most 50% at 0.7 (54% overall).
quote: For example, the output was considered an improvement in over 70% of the cases with a temperature value of 0, while only up to 50% of the cases with a temperature value of 0.7.

claim: Even at temperature 0, proposed fixes were correct in only 42%, 56% and 61% of cases for function-with-strings, simple and library programs respectively.
quote: they were still correct in only around half of the cases - 42%, 56%, and 61% of the cases for functions with strings, simple programs, and library related programs respectively.

claim: Wrong Codex outputs sounded as confident as right ones, and a common failure was blaming indentation for errors actually caused by incomplete code or miscapitalised keywords.
quote: seem similarly confident in their tone, which could potentially mislead students. In both of the examples where the output is incorrect, Codex suggests that the issue is related to indentation.

claim: The authors conclude that LLM-generated error explanations and fixes were not yet ready for production use in introductory programming classes.
quote: The key implications of this work are that programming error message explanations and suggested fixes generated by LLMs are not yet ready for production use in introductory programming classes

claim: The authors propose a two-step system that inspects the error message and code complexity before deciding whether to use the LLM or a traditional support mechanism.
quote: highlighted a potential way around this by having a two-step system that would look into the error message and the complexity of the source code before deciding whether to use LLMs or other more traditional support mechanisms.

claim: All evaluated programs were short, single-error snippets written by the authors rather than student code, and the prompt was zero-shot.
quote: Regarding the code snippets used in the analysis, they were created by the authors and were not student code.

claim: PyFiXV uses Codex in three stages: Codex-Edit (code-davinci-edit-001) produces the fixed program, Codex-Complete (code-davinci-002) writes the explanation, and Codex-Edit then validates the (fix, explanation) pair before anything is shown.
quote: (1) generating a fixed program Pf by editing Pb using Codex-Edit; (2) generating natural language explanation X using Codex-Complete; (3) validating feedback (Pf,X) using Codex-Edit to decide whether the generated feedback is suitable for sharing.

claim: Stage 1 samples 10 candidate fixes at temperature 0.5 and keeps the syntactically correct one with the smallest token-level edit distance to the buggy program.
quote: PyFiXV selects Pf as the program that is syntactically correct and has the smallest edit-distance to Pb.

claim: The explanation prompt includes the buggy program, the fix as a line diff, and three expert-annotated few-shot examples chosen first by matching the parser's error type.
quote: The primary criterion is to pick examples where the error type of buggy program in the example is same as that of Pbthe underlying parser/compiler provides error types

claim: Validation feeds the generated explanation to Codex-Edit as a simulated student and accepts the feedback only if enough of n3 samples reproduce the fix exactly (AST-normalised, syntax-error-free).
quote: Then, out of n3 generated programs, PyFiXV counts the number of programs that don't have syntax errors and have an exact-match with Pf.

claim: Evaluation used 240 Python 2 student programs from TigerJython and 240 Python 3 programs from Codeforces, all with syntax errors and the Codeforces ones submitted after Codex's training cut-off.
quote: As our second dataset, namely Codeforces, we curated 240 distinct Python 3 programs from the Codeforces website using their public APIs [13]

claim: Feedback quality was rated by a single expert after two experts reached Cohen's kappa 0.72 on 100 calibration instances.
quote: we obtained Cohen's kappa reliability value 0.72 indicating substantial agreement between experts [37]. Afterward, one expert (with experience in tutoring Python programming classes) did these feedback ratings for the evaluation results.

claim: Pairing the generated fix with the stock Python error message as the explanation gave only 5.0 precision on TigerJython (Python 2.7 messages) and 35.0 on Codeforces (Python 3.12 messages).
quote: For our baseline PyFi-PEM, we see a big jump in precision from 5.0 for TigerJython (Python 2) to 35.0 for Codeforces

claim: Without validation, PyFiXV's generator (selected few-shots) reached only 38.9 precision at 92.5 coverage on TigerJython and 55.2 precision at 98.8 coverage on Codeforces.
Calibrated for precision of at least 70, PyFiXV achieved 76.0 precision at 31.2 coverage on TigerJython and 72.4 precision at 64.2 coverage on Codeforces.
An oracle validator with access to expert ratings could reach only 47.1 coverage on TigerJython and 75.0 on Codeforces at PyFiXV's precision, the ceiling for the generated feedback.
quote: the coverage numbers (47.1 for TigerJython and 75.0 for Codeforces) indicate the maximum possible achievable coverage.

claim: Santos and Becker ran a within-subjects study with n = 106 second-semester CS1 students, each fixing six buggy C programs that produce compile-time errors only, under stock GCC, expert-handwritten or GPT-4 messages.
quote: We ran a within-subjects study with 𝑛 = 106 participants in which students were tasked to fix six buggy C programs.

claim: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, temperature 0) explanations were pre-generated from a prompt containing the verbatim GCC error message and the full source of the buggy program.
quote: The prompt used was identical to that in Santos et al. [39], providing both the error message verbatim from GCC as well as the full source code of the buggy program.

claim: Every GPT-4 response reproduced the full corrected source code, the fix was equivalent to the expert's in all six tasks, and there were no major inaccuracies or hallucinations, so the null result is not explained by wrong output.
quote: every response consistently had a line saying something similar to "here ' s the corrected code: " followed by a full reproduction of the source code with the problem resolved. In all six problems, GPT-4 generated a solution equivalent to the one suggested in the handwritten explanations. In addition, GPT-4' s error message explanations were devoid of any major technical inaccuracies or "hallucinations " [18].

claim: Measured by students' time-to-fix, GPT-4 explanations beat stock compiler messages in only 1 of the 6 tasks.
quote: we found that GPT-4 generated error messages outperformed conventional compiler error messages in only 1 of the 6 tasks, measured by students ' time-to-fix each problem.

claim: On the missing-parameter task, students were slower with GPT-4's explanation than with the stock GCC message.
quote: In fact, in one of the tasks (" missing parameter "), students were slower when using GPT-4' s explanation.
