claim: The conclusion reports expert-handwritten messages more effective than stock messages in four of six tasks and more effective than GPT-4 in five of six tasks.
quote: Handwritten error messages were more effective than the control in four of six tasks, and more effective than GPT-4' s error message explanations in five of six tasks.

claim: Table 1 shows no significant handwritten-vs-GPT-4 difference on the missing-parameter task (p = 0.157), so the per-task tests support handwritten beating GPT-4 in four tasks, not the five stated in the conclusion.
quote: | | Handwritten | GPT-4 | -15.61s | 0.157 |

claim: Students still rated GPT-4 messages above stock GCC messages (+0.69 points on a -2 to 2 scale) and handwritten messages higher still (+1.27), both p < 0.001.
quote: Using a handwritten message results in a 1.27 point increase in opinion compared to traditional compiler error messages (𝑝 < 0.001); whereas using a GPT-4 generated message results in a 0.69 point increase in opinion compared to the control (𝑝 < 0.001).

claim: The winning handwritten messages followed a structured Error/Help/Note layout with source excerpts modelled on the Rust compiler's diagnostics, and were written so that a real compiler could plausibly generate them.
quote: The structure of the messages was greatly inspired by the diagnostics emitted by the Rust compiler, with source code excerpts mimicking the structure of Rust' s "diagnostic windows " [38]. The handwritten explanations were written in such a way that they can plausibly be generated by an actual compiler, given sufficient context.

claim: The paper appeared at UKICER 2024 (United Kingdom and Ireland Computing Education Research), September 5-6, 2024, Manchester.
quote: United Kingdom and Ireland Computing Education Research (UKICER 2024), September 5-6, 2024, Manchester, United Kingdom.

claim: Pankiewicz and Baker's study of GPT-4 hints for compiler errors was published at ITiCSE 2024 (Milan).
quote: In Proceedings of the 29th annual ACM conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE'24), July 8-10, 2024, Milan, Italy.

claim: The experiment compared 48 control and 49 experimental self-reported novices in a first-semester C# course (pre-test medians 24% vs 21%, no significant difference), with the experimental group receiving hints from gpt-4-0613.
quote: a control group (N=48), and an experimental group (N=49). No significant difference was identified between the median pre-test score of the experimental group (Mdn=21%) and the control group (Mdn=24%) for a nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test (W=1181.5. p=0.971). In the experimental condition, GPT hints (GPT-4 model: gpt-4-0613)

claim: Each GPT-4 hint was generated once per submission that failed to compile, took about 15-20 seconds, and was shown directly to the student as a pop-up, with no verification step described between generation and display.
quote: The hint was generated immediately after the submission (it took approximately 15-20 seconds to generate it) and was presented as a pop-up.

claim: Among the 25 experimental-group students who answered the usefulness survey (213 responses), 56% gave hints a median rating of very or extremely useful, while 20% rated them not useful at all or only slightly useful.
quote: The majority of students (56%) generally rated the hints as very or extremely useful - this shows a generally positive reception of the GPT hints feature by students. However, 20% of students generally rated hints as not useful at all or slightly useful.

claim: The higher focus after a hinted compiler error (median 0.9 vs 0.25, 15 vs 13 students) had p=0.0152 against a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted alpha of 0.0125, so the paper itself reports it only as marginally significant, despite the abstract's 'significantly higher'.
quote: For focused, students in the experimental group (N=15) reported marginally higher rates (Mdn=0.9) than those in the control group (Mdn=0.25, N=13), (W=153, adjusted α=0.0125, p=0.0152

claim: Confrustion (confusion plus frustration) reported right after a hinted compiler error was lower in the experimental group (median 0 vs 0.0167, p=0.0157 against an adjusted alpha of 0.025).
quote: For confrustion (described in section 2), students in the experimental group reported lower rates (Mdn=0) than those in the control group (Mdn=0.0167), (W=48, adjusted α=0.025, p=0.0157

claim: While GPT-4 hints were available, the hinted group did not consistently make fewer compiler errors than the control group on the six most frequent C# errors, and did worse on several of them.
quote: The results of the student performance analysis for different compiler errors were mixed, indicating that the availability of GPT hints did not consistently lead to improved performance across tasks with GPT hints enabled. Contrary to our expectations, we observed lower performance in the experimental condition for several error types.

claim: On the harder second-half tasks where hints were switched off, the previously hinted group had a lower cumulative compiler-error fraction over the first five attempts than control for 5 of the 6 most frequent errors, a descriptive comparison of charts without a reported significance test.
quote: However, for more challenging tasks in the second half of each module where GPT hints were disabled, the performance of the experimental group was consistently higher for 5 out of 6 analyzed errors

claim: The one exception was CS0266 (implicit type conversion), the only conceptual type error among the six, where GPT-4 hints did not appear to help students learn to resolve it.
quote: However, addressing the CS0266 error, which necessitates a more profound comprehension of data types, did not follow this trend. It appears that the provided GPT assistance, may not have been helpful to students in learning to resolve more complex errors.

claim: The authors limit their findings to three months of one C# course at one Polish university, with a small number of participants.
quote: The limited number of participants in this study, and its focus on a single university and course, also represents a limitation to the robustness and external validity of the findings.

claim: Moraru et al. generated every error-message rewrite participants saw with a small self-hosted model, llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
quote: All participant-facing rewritten messages were generated using llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The model was selected because it could be self-hosted

claim: The rewrites used zero-shot prompting at temperature 0, because one-shot and few-shot prompts biased outputs toward the examples in pilot testing.
quote: We used zero-shot prompting and set temperature to 0. This setting was chosen to improve consistency and reproducibility across generated messages. In pilot testing, one-shot and few-shot prompts biased outputs toward the examples and reduced generality.

claim: The main Prolific experiment had 103 valid participants (35 standard, 35 pragmatic, 33 contingent messages; 38 lower and 65 higher assessed proficiency), each fixing one of four short buggy Python snippets.
quote: 35 participants were assigned to the standard condition, 35 to the pragmatic condition, and 33 to the contingent condition. The sample included 38 participants in the lower assessed proficiency group and 65 in the higher assessed proficiency group.

claim: With 103 participants, LLM-rewritten Python error messages were rated clearer and less cognitively demanding than the interpreter's own, but produced no statistically significant improvement in fix rate, attempts or time-to-fix.
quote: Our results show that while LLM-rewritten messages significantly improved subjective evaluations, with pragmatic messages rated as clearer and less cognitively demanding, these perceived gains did not translate into statistically significant improvements in objective debugging performance.

claim: Fix rates within three attempts, pooled over snippets, were 46% / 54% / 42% (standard / pragmatic / contingent) for the 38 novices and 68% / 82% / 90% for the 65 experts, so the scaffolded contingent style scored below the plain interpreter message for novices.
Novice time-to-fix favoured LLM messages descriptively, but only 6, 7 and 5 novices succeeded per condition and statistical tests found no significant effect; for experts results were inconclusive.
quote: statistical tests found no significant effects, though the current pattern seems to favor LLM explanations. As for experts, results remain inconclusive.

claim: The clearest LLM benefit came on snippet A, an unterminated string whose interpreter message points to a non-offending line (53% overall fix rate, the lowest): rewrites that named the right line and cause generally raised fix rates, except the pragmatic style for novices.
quote: For snippet A, LLMenhanced PEMs, which do correctly identify the offending line and root cause, generally increase fix rates, with the pragmatic style among novices as the main exception. However, across snippets, style effects vary widely, so we refrain from making any conclusions.

claim: On Likert ratings (Kruskal-Wallis with Holm-adjusted Dunn tests), experts rated the concise pragmatic rewrites lighter in cognitive load, less authoritative and more useful than the standard interpreter message.
quote: Overall, adaptive style, especially Pragmatic, are consistently rated by experts as lighter in cognitive load, less authoritative, and more useful than the Standard baseline.

claim: The longer scaffolded (contingent) explanations did not consistently help lower-proficiency participants; the authors attribute this to the reading cost of their verbosity in short repair tasks.
quote: Contingent messages provided additional explanatory context, but their greater verbosity may have reduced their usefulness in short repair tasks, particularly for lower assessed proficiency participants.

claim: The evidence rests on four short synthetic single-fault Python snippets in a web editor, which the authors say limits ecological validity for real IDE debugging.
quote: The four Python snippets were short, synthetic, and designed to contain a single primary fault. This made the study feasible and controlled, but it limits ecological validity.

claim: CORE pairs GPT-3.5-Turbo as the proposer that writes code revisions with GPT-4 as the ranker that scores them.
quote: We obtain promising results that bear witness to practical utility of CORE using GPT-3.5Turbo [41] as the proposer LLM and GPT-4 [40] as the ranker LLM.

claim: CORE uses no training or fine-tuning: the proposer is prompted zero-shot with the static checker's own documentation and fix recommendation, the warning location and message, and the flagged code.
quote: We use an instruction-based LLM in zero-shot setting (i.e., no ⟨before code, after code⟩ examples needed) without finetuning.

claim: Of 10 sampled candidate revisions per file, CORE re-runs the static check and drops any candidate that still has a violation or a syntax error, before the ranker sees the rest.
quote: We run the static analysis check (that CORE is configured with in 1 ) against the candidate revisions and filter out the ones where the code quality issue continues to persist (i.e., non-zero violations detected). In this process, we de-duplicate identical code revision suggestions as well as ensure the syntactic validity of code revisions, and reject the ones with syntax errors.

claim: On 765 Python files flagged by 52 CodeQL checks (CQPy), 81.57% had at least one GPT-3.5-Turbo revision that passed the static checker with zero violations, judged by the tool alone.
quote: First, we observe that 81.57% of the flagged files get fixed entirely as validated by the static analysis tool, i.e., they have at least one revision that completely passes the static checker with zero issues flagged.

claim: Passing the static checker was far from sufficient: in the user study, reviewers rejected 1321 of 2397 CodeQL-passing revisions (55.11%) as incorrect or carrying unintended changes.
quote: However, from the last column, we see that this high acceptance rate comes at a high cost of 1321 false positives, i.e., 55.11% of the revisions that CodeQL passed were rejected by users.

claim: Human acceptance in CORE was judged only on the CQPyUS subset (10 files per check) by 15 intermediate Python developers with 1-3 years of experience, with one label per revision.
quote: Our user group consists of 15 Python developers (intermediate level, with 1-3 years of software engineering experience). Each revision was labeled by only one user

claim: CORE's headline is 59.2% of Python files across 52 CodeQL checks revised to pass both the tool and a human reviewer; this equals (298+10)/520 files of the CQPyUS user-study subset with a ranker-accepted revision that the reviewer accepted, not a result on all 765 files.
quote: CORE could revise 59.2% Python files (across 52 quality checks) so that they pass scrutiny by both a tool and a human reviewer.

claim: Keeping only GPT-4 strong-accept revisions cut the human rejection rate from 55.11% to 47.55% (1321 to 835 rejections, a 36.8% cut that the text calls 'close to 25%'); the abstract's 25.8% matches dropping only the 341 rejections among ranker-rejected revisions.
quote: if we surface only the candidates strongly accepted by the Ranker LLM, the rejection rate drops to 47.55%. In an absolute sense, the number of rejections drops to 835 from 1321, which is close to 25% reduction.

claim: The ranker's rejections agreed with humans: for the 26 files where GPT-4 accepted no revision, reviewers also rejected 82.57% of those revisions.
quote: if we consider only the files for which no revision was (strong- or weak-) accepted by Ranker LLM, the users also rejected over 82% of those revisions

claim: On 483 Java files with 10 SonarQube checks, CORE fixed 76.8% of files (passing SonarQube and accepted by the GPT-4 ranker, with no human review) against 78.3% for the hand-built rule-based Sorald, configured in under a week with fewer than 100 changed lines.
quote: CORE produced revisions that passed the static analysis tool in 76.8% Java files (across 10 quality checks) comparable to 78.3% of a specialized program repair tool, with significantly much less engineering efforts.

claim: AutoCommenter (Google) was published at the 1st ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software, AIware 2024.
quote: In Proceedings of the 1st ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software (AIware '24), July 15-16, 2024, Porto de Galinhas, Brazil.

claim: AutoCommenter is one task of a multi-task T5X model (size not disclosed, 2048-token context) trained on over 3 billion examples, of which about 800k are best-practice comments mined from human code reviews that cite a style-guide URL.
quote: The training corpus consists of over 3 billion examples, of which the best practice analysis dataset contributes about 800k examples.

claim: A single confidence threshold of 0.98 suppressed many correct predictions (about 80% of several hundred sampled below-threshold predictions were correct), and per-language thresholds also failed, so AutoCommenter moved to per-URL thresholds set from validation data.
quote: We manually sampled several hundred results and observed that around 80% of predictions below the threshold were still correct-that is, the false-negative rate was very high at t = 0.98. Additionally, we observed that predictions in Python showed a significantly different distribution of confidence scores, which were disproportionately impacted by thresholding. We conjecture that the training dataset composition (number of distinct URLs and URL frequencies) and specificity of the best practice documents are reasons, but leave a deeper investigation to future work. An attempt to deploy per-language thresholds proved ineffective as a single threshold per language still did not adequately capture the model's ability to correctly predict hundreds of diverse best practices. This led to a lack of diversity in predicted URLs as the model tended to produce higher scores for some URLs vs. others, irrespective of correctness. These observations led to the first major change to AutoCommenter: per-URL thresholds computed based on the intrinsic evaluation on the validation dataset.

claim: Beam search (n=4) tripled posting frequency but had a 2-second median latency, too slow for the IDE, so AutoCommenter uses beam search in code review and greedy decoding for sub-second IDE diagnostics.
quote: While beam search increased the posting frequency and diversity, inference became noticeably slower (median latency of 2 seconds). Given that this latency is prohibitive for interactive use in the IDE, we ultimately decided to use beam search for the code review system and greedy search for the IDE.

claim: After several months with about 3 thousand early adopters the developer-feedback useful ratio plateaued at 54%, and 15 independent raters scored the same ~370 comments 60% useful, both below the 80% target set for wider deployment.
quote: The useful ratio from the rater evaluation was 60%, slightly higher than the 54% from the developer feedback on the same comments, but well below our target of 80% for wider deployment.

claim: The useful ratio reached the 80% target not through thresholds but by suppressing 17 (then 5 more) non-actionable best-practice URLs, which raised it from 54% to 66% on historical developer feedback, and by manually rewriting the summaries of frequently posted URLs.
quote: First, the rater study identified 17 non-actionable URLs, whose suppression increased the historical useful ratio from 54% to 66% on developer feedback, and from 60% to 74% on rater feedback. We further analyzed comments linked to similar, unrated URLs and suppressed an additional 5. Second, we reviewed and manually updated summaries for all frequently posted URLs. Together, these changes were sufficient to reach our target useful ratio of 80% for the next stage of deployment.

claim: When a Python import best practice changed in 2022 but the training data predated it, the model kept posting outdated advice, and AutoCommenter suppressed those predictions with regular-expression filters rather than wait for a retrain.
quote: We opted for suppression of specific best-practice predictions, using conditional filtering (matching regular expressions on the source code) for two reasons. First, it can be dynamically deployed and immediately applied.

claim: In a July 2023 A/B experiment over about half of Google's developers, AutoCommenter produced no statistically significant change in code-review duration, active review time or review iterations, only a slight coding-speed improvement.
quote: We did not detect any statistically significant change in any of the following: total duration of code reviews, time developers actively spent on the code review, the number of comment-response iterations between the author and the reviewer.

claim: About 40% of AutoCommenter comments are estimated to be resolved: the comment disappeared in 50% of 6000 snapshot pairs, and in a manual sample of 40 such pairs 80% were direct fixes by the author.
quote: We found that in 80% of cases, a change made by the author directly resolved the issue described by the posted comment. Therefore, we estimate that the commentresolution rate is about 40%

claim: Of the 50 most frequently predicted best-practice URLs, three of the authors judged 33 (66%) beyond what a traditional linter detects or could easily be built to detect.
quote: For 33/50 (66%) of these best practices, violation detection is beyond the scope of traditional static analysis.

claim: Eiffel-tools targets Eiffel as a low-resource language with little public code but a built-in specification language and a static verifier, AutoProof.
quote: Eiffel is a low-resource language; it has a first-class support for specifications and a static verifier AutoProof, but the low amount of public code makes LLM code generation more challenging.

claim: Eiffel-tools, an LSP language server, runs AutoProof with timeouts on every LLM suggestion and reverts LLM-generated code to its last stable state when verification fails.
quote: Eiffel-tools uses AutoProof to verify existing code or LLM-generated suggestions. Because AutoProof may not terminate on some inputs, Eiffel-tools runs it with timeouts: any verification exceeding a time limit is killed, and if the code was LLM-generated, the tool reverts it to its previous stable state upon failure.

claim: The interactive fix-feature-body code action loops LLM candidate, AutoProof, retry, and applies no edit to the user's code unless a candidate verifies.
quote: If a candidate body passes verification, Eiffel-tools copies that body into the original feature; otherwise, the loop continues until a candidate passes or a maximum number of attempts is reached. Unless a candidate succeeds, no changes are applied to the original feature.

claim: For LLM-suggested contracts, the server parses each candidate and drops contracts that are redundant, not usable by the verifier, reference invalid identifiers, or call with the wrong number of arguments, before inserting the rest.
quote: Are redundant - Are not model-based, and thus unusable by AutoProof - Contain invalid top-level identifiers - Contain calls with the wrong number of arguments

claim: The bug-fixing evaluation used 539 bugs (513 from buggy-java-jml-eiffel, 26 from maple-recursive-eiffel) with correct contracts, three LLMs (GPT-5 Nano, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Poolside Laguna XS) and two prompt ablations, allowing at most 10 attempts per feature.
quote: In total, the experiment used 539 bugs to be fixed by 3 LLMs using 2 prompt ablations. At most 10 attempts were allowed per feature.

claim: Measured as passing AutoProof within 10 attempts, Sonnet 4.6 fixed 95% (full prompt) and 90% (minimal), Laguna XS 85% and 76%, and GPT-5 Nano 82% and 77%, which is the source of the 76-95% range.
quote: Sonnet 4.6 solved the most tasks in both ablations (95% full, 90% minimal). Laguna XS was better than GPT-5 nano in "full" (85% vs. 82%) while GPT was better than Lagune in "minimal" (77% GPT vs. 76% Laguna).

claim: The tool-built 'full' prompt (syntax guide, feature template, available identifiers, verifier error) raised success by 6.4 percentage points on average over the 'minimal' prompt, and by 8.9 points for the small open-weights Laguna XS.
quote: Using "full" gives 6.4 pp improvement on average. Extended prompts helped Laguna to improve the most (8.9 pp).

claim: The 'minimal' ablation that still reached 76-90% withholds the verifier's error message and the identifier list from the model, so models fixed most bugs from the code and its contracts alone, with the verifier acting as the accept/reject gate; the diagnostic context added only the 6.4-point average gain.
quote: User message omits the list of available variables and the error itself. Model is only told in the system message that there is a problem, but the exact problem is not specified in the user message.

claim: Among bugs eventually fixed, 67.9% (Laguna, minimal) to 83.5% (Sonnet, minimal) were fixed on the first attempt, with diminishing returns from each further retry.
quote: The majority of fixes happen on the first attempt (from 67.9% for Laguna "minimal" to 83.5% for Sonnet "minimal"). Every next attempt increases the success rate less and less.

claim: The only stated threat to validity is that both public benchmarks exist in other languages and may have leaked into the models' training data, so models might reproduce known fixes rather than repair the bug.
quote: It is possible that those benchmarks leaked in the training data of some LLMs and the models could reproduce the solution they were trained on instead of "fixing" the bug.

claim: GRPO drops PPO's critic (value model) and estimates the baseline from the scores of a group of outputs sampled for the same question, which cuts training resources.
quote: GRPO foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group scores, significantly reducing training resources

claim: Under outcome supervision, GRPO normalizes a group's rewards by subtracting the group mean and dividing by the group standard deviation, and gives every token of an output that output's normalized reward as its advantage.
quote: Subsequently, these rewards are normalized by subtracting the group average and dividing by the group standard deviation. Outcome supervision provides the normalized reward at the end of each output 𝑜𝑖 and sets the advantages ˆ𝐴𝑖,𝑡 of all tokens in the output as the normalized reward

claim: The original GRPO keeps a KL penalty against a reference policy, added directly to the loss rather than folded into the reward as PPO-RLHF does; the beta=0 recipe the survey adopts is a later departure from GRPO as defined, not part of it.
quote: instead of adding KL penalty in the reward, GRPO regularizes by directly adding the KL divergence between the trained policy and the reference policy to the loss, avoiding complicating the calculation of
bears_on: GRPO definition and the beta setting

claim: DeepSeekMath's GRPO run used a learned reward model (initialized from DeepSeekMath-Base 7B, LR 2e-5), not a rule-based verifier, and a policy LR of 1e-6, KL coefficient 0.04, 64 samples per question, max length 1024, batch size 1024, and a single policy update per exploration stage (strictly on-policy).
quote: We train our initial reward model based on the DeepSeekMath-Base 7B with a learning rate of 2e-5. For GRPO, we set the learning rate of the policy model as 1e-6. The KL coefficient is 0.04. For each question, we sample 64 outputs. The max length is set to 1024, and the training batch size is 1024. The policy model only has a single update following each exploration stage.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters and reward source

claim: Already in the GRPO paper, RL on DeepSeekMath 7B improved Maj@K but not Pass@K on GSM8K and MATH, sampled at temperature 0.7; the RL gain was in voting accuracy, not in the set of problems the model can solve.
quote: Figure 7 | The Maj@K and Pass@K of SFT and RL DeepSeekMath 7B on GSM8K and MATH (temperature 0.7). It was noted that RL enhances Maj@K but not Pass@K.
bears_on: whether RL adds capability; pass@k evaluation

claim: In the paper's Figure 5 comparison on a small DeepSeekMath-Instruct model, GRPO beat online rejection-sampling fine-tuning (which itself beat offline RFT), which the authors attribute to GRPO also penalizing wrong responses and scaling updates by reward; process supervision (GRPO+PS) beat outcome supervision (GRPO+OS).
quote: As demonstrated in Figure 5, GRPO surpasses online RFT, thereby highlighting the efficiency of altering positive and negative gradient coefficients. In addition, GRPO+PS shows superior performance compared to GRPO+OS
bears_on: rejection-sampling SFT versus GRPO for a small model

claim: DAPO decouples PPO's clip range, keeping epsilon_low at 0.2 and raising epsilon_high to 0.28, to leave room for low-probability exploration tokens and avoid entropy collapse.
quote: As for the Clip-Higher mechanism, we set the clipping parameter εlow to 0.2 and εhigh to 0.28, which effectively balance the trade-off between exploration and exploitation.

claim: DAPO's dynamic sampling over-samples and drops prompts whose group accuracy is exactly 1 or 0, so every prompt in the batch carries a non-zero gradient and the number of prompts per batch stays constant.
quote: we propose to over-sample and filter out prompts with the accuracy equal to 1 and 0 as illustrated in Equation 11, leaving all prompts in the batch with effective gradients and keeping a consistent number of prompts

claim: DAPO averages the loss over all tokens instead of per sample first; the authors report it brought less accuracy than the other techniques but stabilized training and made length growth healthier.
quote: For token-level loss, although it brings less performance improvement, we find it enhances training stability and makes the length increase more healthily.

claim: DAPO's overlong filtering masks the loss of truncated samples instead of giving them the default punitive reward, which stabilized training and improved performance.
quote: To investigate the impact of this reward noise, we first apply an Overlong Filtering strategy which masks the loss of truncated samples. We find that this approach significantly stabilizes training and enhances performance

claim: On DAPO's 32B Qwen base, AIME24 avg@32 rose from 30 (naive GRPO) to 50 (DAPO), against 47 for DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B, as techniques were added one after another: overlong filtering 36 (+6), clip-higher 38 (+2), soft overlong punishment 41 (+3), token-level loss 42 (+1), dynamic sampling 50 (+8). The increments are cumulative steps in one fixed order, not isolated ablations, so dynamic sampling's +8 is the largest step in that order.
quote: | Model                      |   AIME24avg@32 | |----------------------------|----------------| | DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B  |             47 | | Naive GRPO                 |             30 | | + Overlong Filtering       |             36 | | + Clip-Higher              |             38 | | + Soft Overlong Punishment |             41 | | + Token-level Loss         |             42 | | + Dynamic Sampling (DAPO)  |             50 |

claim: Masking truncated samples (overlong filtering) took DAPO's AIME score from 30 to 36 as the first step over a punitive default, but DAPO did not conclude that truncation should go unpunished: its final recipe adds soft overlong punishment, a length penalty growing over a band beyond the expected maximum length, which was worth 38 to 41. DAPO masks and then punishes softly.
quote: | Naive GRPO | 30 | | + Overlong Filtering | 36 | | + Clip-Higher | 38 | | + Soft Overlong Punishment | 41 |
wiki_says: Truncated samples should be masked rather than punished. That change alone was worth six AIME points in DAPO's ablation.

claim: DAPO's settings: constant LR 1e-6 with a 20-step linear warm-up, 512 prompts per rollout with 16 responses each, and a mini-batch of 512, i.e. 16 gradient updates per rollout step, so the run is substantially off-policy (the Skywork Open Reasoner report found that several updates per rollout accelerate entropy collapse). Generation allowed 16,384 tokens plus a 4,096-token soft-punishment band.
quote: For hyper-parameters, we utilize the AdamW [39] optimizer with a constant learning rate of 1 × 10-6 , incorporating a linear warm-up over 20 rollout steps. For rollout, the prompt batch size is 512 and we sample 16 responses for each prompt. For training, the mini-batch size is set to 512, i.e., 16 gradient updates for each rollout step. For Overlong Reward Shaping, we set the expected maximum length as 16,384 tokens and allocate additional 4,096 tokens as the soft punish cache.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters and on-policy updates

claim: In DAPO's runs the final training-set reward often had little correlation with validation accuracy, which the authors read as overfitting to the training set; training reward is not a progress metric on its own.
quote: However, we find that the final reward on the training set often exhibits little correlation with the accuracy on the validation set, which indicates overfitting to the training set.
bears_on: what to monitor during RL; held-out evaluation

claim: To keep the rule-based reward accurate, DAPO rewrote every problem so the expected answer is an integer (DAPO-Math-17K, 17K prompts); all of DAPO's evidence is on math with one base model, and transfer to other tasks is asserted, not tested.
quote: After selection and transformation, we obtained the DAPO-Math-17K dataset, which consists of 17K prompts, each paired with an integer as the answer.
bears_on: reward design: make outputs mechanically checkable

claim: DAPO reports that dynamic sampling needs more samples but did not significantly change overall training time in its synchronous system, where generation time is dominated by long-tail samples; Yue et al. measured the extra sampling as several-fold per batch.
quote: When applying Dynamic Sampling, although more data needs to be sampled due to the filtering out of zero-gradient data, the overall training time is not significantly affected.
bears_on: cost of dynamic sampling under a small budget

claim: Dividing each response's loss by its length makes GRPO penalize long incorrect responses less than short ones, so the policy drifts toward longer responses among the incorrect ones.
quote: longer responses are penalized less due to their larger |oi |, causing the policy to prefer lengthier responses among incorrect ones

claim: Dividing the centered reward by the per-question reward std gives questions whose rewards are almost all 1 or almost all 0 (too easy or too hard) higher weight in the update.
quote: Questions with lower standard deviations (e.g., those that are too easy or too hard, with the outcome rewards being almost all 1 or 0) are given higher weights during policy updates.

claim: Dr. GRPO removes both the 1/|o_i| length normalization and the std normalization, and implements the masked mean with a constant denominator such as the generation budget instead of the per-response token count.
quote: we propose to simply remove the 1 |oi | and std({R(q, o1), . . . , R(q, oG)}) normalization terms. Meanwhile, to faithfully implement the unbiased optimization objective, we could replace the mask.sum(axis=dim) with a constant value (e.g., generation budget)

claim: On a small Qwen base model RL-tuned on MATH questions, Dr. GRPO substantially reduced the length of incorrect responses on the evaluation benchmarks compared with GRPO.
quote: Moreover, on evaluation benchmarks, the length of incorrect responses is substantially reduced by Dr. GRPO compared to the baseline (Plot 4), suggesting that an unbiased optimizer also mitigates overthinking

claim: In the appendix ablation on a small Qwen base model, removing either bias term alone (length or std) already beat vanilla GRPO in training reward and evaluation accuracy; the length term drives response length more than the std term.
quote: In terms of performance, Dr. GRPO and the other ablated variants consistently outperform vanilla GRPO in both training rewards and evaluation accuracy.
bears_on: choice of loss_type for a small model

claim: Every open-source PPO implementation the authors examined, trl and verl among them, normalized the loss by response length, a mismatch with the PPO objective of their Eq. (2); which loss a framework's default computes has to be checked, not assumed.
quote: To our surprise, all of these implementations normalize the loss by response length (see Listing 1 and Table 2), which misaligns with the PPO objective as defined in Eq. (2).
bears_on: framework loss defaults (TRL loss_type)

claim: With a Qwen math base model, a prompt template mismatched to the model first destroyed capability the model already had, and much of the RL gain was rebuilding it; the authors warn against crediting such gains to pure RL.
quote: Applying templates in fact destroys the capability before RL reconstructs it. This implies that we should be more conservative in claiming the huge gains brought about by pure RL.
bears_on: prompt format before RL; reading RL gains

claim: On Llama-3.2-3B, RL with Dr. GRPO moved the five-benchmark math average only from 3.3 to 6.8; after continual pretraining on FineMath it went 6.0 to 14.8, and after further continual pretraining on concatenated NuminaMath question-answer text 0.14 to 20.7. Domain pretraining before RL raised the RL ceiling of a weak base.
bears_on: continued pretraining in a new language before RL

claim: With the Qwen-Math template on a small Qwen math base, RL on the much simpler GSM-8K questions gave the best final performance and nearly doubled accuracy on harder benchmarks; with a mismatched template, narrow question coverage lowered the plateau instead.
quote: However, when using the Qwen-Math template, the best final performance is attained by RL on GSM-8K, demonstrating that training on much simpler (and o.o.d.) questions can largely improve (nearly double) the test accuracy on harder questions.
bears_on: task difficulty of the RL pool

claim: The authors use the base policy's pass@k over a few samples as a readiness check: if it cannot sample a single correct trajectory, RL cannot improve it, because there is no reward signal.
quote: if a base policy cannot even sample a single trajectory that leads to the correct final answer, it is impossible for RL to improve the policy because there is no reward signal
bears_on: pre-RL check of the starting model

claim: RLVR-trained models beat their starting models at small k, but as k grows the starting models catch up and surpass them on every benchmark tested, i.e. they cover more solvable problems.
quote: However, as k increases, with steeper curves, base models consistently catch up to and eventually surpass RL-trained models across all benchmarks, indicating their broader coverage of solvable problems.

claim: The code experiments evaluated released GRPO-trained models, Code-R1 (from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and DeepCoder (from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B), on LiveCodeBench and HumanEval+; the six-algorithm comparison is a separate math experiment. On code the reference model is an instruction-tuned or distilled model, not a base model.
quote: | Code Generation | Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B | Code-R1 DeepCoder | GRPO | LiveCodeBench HumanEval+ |
wiki_says: Yue et al. tested six RL algorithms and found that base models overtake their RL-trained versions at large k on code benchmarks including HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench.

claim: In the paper's controlled math comparison (one Qwen base model, an Omni-MATH-Rule split), PPO, GRPO, Reinforce++, RLOO, ReMax and DAPO had similar sampling-efficiency gaps (the base model's large-k pass rate minus the RL model's single-sample pass rate): from 43.9 for GRPO to 42.6 for RLOO on the in-domain test set, all above 40 points.
quote: Different RL algorithms yield slightly different ∆SE values (i.e., ranging from GRPO's 43.9 to RLOO's best 42.6 on the in-domain test set). Furthermore, we observe that ∆SE remains consistently above 40 points across different algorithms

claim: The distillation evidence is one model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (DeepSeek-R1 distilled into Qwen2.5-Math-7B), whose pass@k curve stayed consistently and significantly above the base Qwen2.5-Math-7B, unlike the RL-trained Oat-Zero.
quote: We focus on a representative model, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, which distills DeepSeek-R1 into Qwen2.5Math-7B. We compare it with the base model Qwen2.5-Math-7B and its RL-trained counterpart Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Oat-Zero and include Qwen2.5Math-7B-Instruct as an additional baseline. As shown in Figure 7, the pass@k curve of the distilled model is consistently and significantly above that of the base model.

claim: Over GRPO training of Qwen2.5-7B, Omni-MATH-Train pass@1 rose from 26.1 (step 150) to 42.5 (step 450) while pass@256 fell from 66.3 to 64.3, below the base's 67.2; on the held-out Omni-MATH-Test pass@256 fell from 69.1 (base) to 63.9. Narrowing shows only when pass@k at large k is compared with the starting model.

For code (and visual reasoning) the open-source RLVR work starts from instruction-tuned models, because pure zero-RL from a base model was unstable and of limited effect; this supports fine-tuning before RL for code.
quote: However, for coding and visual reasoning tasks, open-source work typically uses instruction-tuned models as starting points, primarily due to the training instability and limited effectiveness of using a pure zero-RL setting.
bears_on: training order: SFT before RL for code

claim: Adding a KL term with coefficient 0.001 to GRPO left pass@1 about the same but gave a much lower pass@128.
quote: We ablate this by applying a KL term with coefficient 0.001. As shown in Figure 16, the KL-regularized model achieves similar pass@1 to GRPO without KL, but with a much lower pass@128.
bears_on: the beta setting

claim: Raising rollouts per prompt from 8 to 32 at the same prompt batch (more compute per step) gave a higher pass@128 even though the run was cut at 220 steps, before pass@1 had converged.
quote: For increasing n from 8 to 32, we keep the prompt batch size unchanged, which results in increased computation per training step. Due to resource constraints, we train for only 220 steps under this setting, leading to lower pass@1 as the model has not yet converged. Nevertheless, the model with n = 32 achieves a higher pass@128, highlighting the positive effect of larger rollout numbers in improving pass@k at higher values of k.
bears_on: generations per prompt

claim: In the controlled comparison DAPO had slightly higher pass@1 but its dynamic sampling needed about 3-6x more samples per batch and it dropped significantly at k = 256; RLOO and Reinforce++ did well across k from 1 to 256 at efficient training cost.
quote: First, DAPO achieves slightly higher pass@1 scores across all three datasets; however, its dynamic sampling strategy requires approximately 3 ∼ 6× more samples per batch during training compared to other algorithms. Moreover, its performance drops significantly at k = 256. Second, RLOO and Reinforce++ perform consistently well across the entire k range (from 1 to 256), while maintaining efficient training costs
bears_on: cost of dynamic sampling under a small budget

claim: The authors argue that because RL stays within the base model's prior, starting RL from a distilled model may help, since distillation injects a better prior: distillation first, then RL.
quote: From this perspective, training RL models from a distilled model may temporarily provide a beneficial solution, as distillation helps inject a better prior.
bears_on: training order: distillation then RL

claim: Pass@k at large k is trusted for code because a compiler and predefined unit tests serve as the verifier, whereas in math an incorrect chain of thought can reach the right answer by luck as k grows; the guarantee rests on the tests being strong.
quote: For coding tasks, where a compiler and predefined unit test cases are used as verifiers, the pass@k value can accurately reflect whether the model can solve the problem. In mathematics, the issue of "guessing" can become pronounced as k increases, where a model may generate an incorrect CoT but still accidentally arrive at the correct answer.
bears_on: pass@k validity depends on test strength

claim: Taking more SGD steps per rollout batch, whether by splitting it into more mini-batches or reusing it, significantly accelerated entropy collapse and generally degraded test performance, which the authors attribute to off-policy data.
quote: Increasing the number of SGD steps per training step - whether by using more mini-batches or increasing data reuse - significantly accelerates entropy collapse and generally results in degraded test performance due to the introduction of off-policy data.

claim: Skywork sets the rollout temperature to 1 because at 0.6 the policy entered a low-entropy state immediately on math data and quickly on code data.
quote: High-Temperature Sampling. We set the rollout temperature to τ = 1 to enhance the model's exploration capability and improve learning plasticity. This decision was motivated by our observation that the sampling policy either immediately enters (in the case of math data) or quickly transitions into (in the case of code data) a low-entropy state when using a smaller sampling temperature (e.g., τ = 0.6).

claim: With temperature 0.6, entropy either started extremely low or collapsed to near zero within about 100 steps, which first slowed learning and then stalled it.
quote: when a low temperature is used (e.g., 0.6), the model either begins with extremely low entropy or its entropy quickly collapses to near zero within approximately 100 steps. This behavior initially slows learning progress and ultimately leads to stagnation.

claim: High-temperature sampling gave lower test accuracy in the early steps but larger improvements in the end, so early checkpoints under-rate it.
quote: High-temperature sampling results in lower test accuracy during the early training steps but ultimately yields greater performance improvements

claim: In an off-policy run (several SGD steps per rollout) on a distilled long-CoT model, raising the upper clip to 0.25 or 0.265 prevented premature entropy collapse and improved test performance, but DAPO's 0.28 made entropy rise sharply with poor test performance; the authors conclude the right upper clip is task-dependent.
quote: Our results, shown in Figure 22, indicate that using a properly chosen higher-clip ratio - e.g., 0.25 or 0.265 - can prevent premature entropy collapse and lead to better test performance. However, it is worth noting that when the higher-clip ratio is set to 0.28, as suggested in [34], entropy increases sharply, resulting in poor test performance. This suggests that the optimal higher-clip ratio is task-dependent.
bears_on: epsilon_high setting

claim: Skywork tested masking the advantage of truncated responses and dropped it: giving truncated samples negative advantages improved token efficiency and preserved later-stage scaling, so the final recipe applies no mask.
quote: However, our findings show that assigning negative advantages to truncated samples not only improves token efficiency but also preserves the model's scaling ability in later stages. As a result, we did not apply any mask strategies in our final training pipeline.
bears_on: truncation: mask or penalize

claim: Excluding truncated responses from the group baseline and zeroing their advantage (Adv-Mask-Before) raised accuracy within the context window while overall training accuracy fell and the truncation ratio climbed steadily, which the authors call a form of reward hacking.
quote: We observe that although the response quality within the context length (i.e., the accuracy of non-truncated responses) increases as expected after applying the Adv-Mask-Before strategy, the overall training accuracy continues to decline, and the clip ratio increases steadily. This appears to be a form of reward hacking from our perspective.
bears_on: truncation masking as a hackable reward

claim: A short context cap in the first RL stage did not cap later performance: Skywork's math model trained at 8K in Stage I kept comparable AIME24 accuracy when evaluated at 32K while its average response length fell from about 12.5K to 5.4K tokens, and later stages with longer caps raised both length and accuracy.
quote: In Figure 5(b), we observe that training with an 8K context length in Stage I maintains comparable AIME24 accuracy under a 32K context length while significantly improving token efficiency (reducing the average response length from approximately 12.5K to 5.4K tokens).
bears_on: completion-length cap

claim: For code RL data, Skywork kept a problem only if its reference solution passed every one of its test cases, which validates the tests themselves before they serve as a reward.
quote: We programmatically verify all test cases using the provided original solutions. A sample is marked as valid only if the solution passes all corresponding test cases perfectly.
bears_on: task pool and test quality

claim: Incomplete or invalid problems still passed the pass-rate difficulty filter, because the model produced the expected answer at least once in its rollouts; a pass-rate filter does not check that a task is well posed.
quote: Interestingly, these problems passed the difficulty estimation procedure (i.e., a model can produce a correct answer even when the problem is invalid or incomplete).
bears_on: task pool validation

claim: In an offline analysis on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (responses sampled by the inference engine, then re-scored with the same weights in the DeepSpeed training engine), the sequence-level log-probability ratio between inference and training policies stayed approximately 24 times smaller under FP16 than under BF16; the BF16 mismatch grew with response length. This is a measurement of the mismatch, not of an RL run.
quote: The results clearly indicate that BF16 introduces an exponentially larger mismatch, which worsens with longer responses due to cumulative autoregressive errors, whereas FP16 maintains the mismatch at a much milder level (approximately 24× smaller).

claim: RL frameworks sample rollouts from the inference engine's policy but compute the gradient under the training engine's policy; ignoring the numerical mismatch between the two biases the policy gradient, so nominally on-policy training is in fact off-policy.
quote: In practice, we sample the responses from the inference policy µ, instead of the training policy π. As noted by Yao et al. [2025] and Liu et al. [2025a], the policy gradient would become biased if simply ignoring this mismatch.

claim: LoRA GRPO (token-level TIS) on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B with the MATH dataset, LoRA on all layers with rank 32 and alpha 64 and a learning rate of 4 × 10-5: the BF16 run collapsed after roughly 600 steps while the FP16 run stayed stable throughout.
quote: we train Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B models on the standard MATH dataset using GRPO-Token-TIS (Equation (9)). LoRA is applied to all layers with a rank of 32 and scaling factor α = 64. Following Schulman and Lab [2025], we adopt a slightly larger learning rate (4 × 10-5 ) than that used in full fine-tuning. As shown in Figure 1 (h), BF16-based LoRA training collapses after roughly 600 steps, whereas FP16 maintains stable training throughout.
bears_on: precision for a LoRA GRPO run at 1.5B

claim: The paper reports that computing the language-model head in FP32 (the fix ScaleRL adopts from MiniMax) was shown to be insufficient to prevent training collapse; it treats the head-only fix as a partial engineering patch and switches the whole model to FP16 instead.
quote: Early attempts, such as using an FP32 language model head by Chen et al. [2025], is shown to be insufficient to prevent training collapse [Yao et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025a].
bears_on: which precision fix to use against train-inference mismatch

claim: The importance-sampling corrections for the mismatch, as implemented on top of GRPO (token-level TIS, sequence-level MIS), need an extra forward pass costing about 25% more training compute (assuming a backward pass costs twice a forward pass); FP16 removes the need for them.
quote: This extra step incurs approximately 25% computational overhead during training, assuming a backward pass is twice as costly as a forward pass [Qi et al., 2023].
bears_on: cost of the importance-sampling correction versus an FP16 run

claim: On the sanity-test set with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, the only BF16 correction that did not collapse, GRPO with sequence-level MIS, converged slowly and peaked at 95% training accuracy and 34% on AIME 2024, against 99% and 39% with FP16: algorithmic corrections stabilize BF16 but leave a ceiling.
quote: Among all the algorithmic corrections in BF16, only GRPO with sequence-level MIS [Liu et al., 2025a] maintains stable training without collapsing. However, this stability is costly. The method suffers from slow convergence due to the high variance of its sequence-level importance ratio (see Figure 2). More importantly, even at its peak, it exhibits a significant deployment gap compared to our FP16 approach. It achieves a maximum training accuracy of only 95% (vs. 99% in FP16) and a score of 34% (vs. 39% in FP16) on the AIME 2024 benchmark, demonstrating a clear performance ceiling.
bears_on: whether algorithmic mismatch corrections can replace FP16

claim: The paper validates an RL setup on a 'perfectible' set: sample 40 responses per MATH problem, keep only problems the initial model solves between 20% and 80% of the time (1,460 questions for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B), and require training accuracy on that set to converge to a high threshold; a setup that cannot fit problems known to be within reach is treated as unreliable.
quote: Specifically, we unroll 40 responses for each problem in the MATH dataset [Hendrycks et al., 2021], and only keep problems where the initial accuracy is between 20% and 80%. This process yielded a targeted dataset of 1,460 questions for the DeepSeek-R1-DistillQwen-1.5B model [Guo et al., 2025].
bears_on: validating the RL pipeline on a solvable task pool

claim: Runs that later collapsed showed a growing training-inference mismatch beforehand, so logging the mismatch during training gives an early warning of collapse.
quote: Our experimental results reveal an interesting phenomenon: algorithms that eventually collapse consistently exhibit a growing training-inference mismatch beforehand, making it a potential early-warning signal (see Figure 3).
bears_on: what to monitor during a GRPO run

claim: In the forward ablation on the paper's dense-model math baseline (before the ScaleRL recipe was assembled), computing the LM head in FP32 on both generator and trainer raised the fitted asymptotic pass rate A from 0.52 to 0.61.
quote: MiniMax et al. (2025) identified that these mismatches are especially pronounced at the language model head, and mitigate this by FP32 computations at the head for both the generator and trainer. As shown in Figure 5b, the precision fix dramatically improves the asymptotic performance A from 0.52 to 0.61.

claim: The FP32-head gain was measured on the pre-ScaleRL baseline (PipelineRL with a DAPO-clipped GRPO-style loss), not on ScaleRL. Inside the full ScaleRL recipe the FP32 fix makes little difference on the dense 8B model; it gives large gains with GRPO/DAPO-style losses, and a leave-one-out on the Scout MoE showed it improves scalability. ScaleRL's own fitted asymptote is a separate number.
quote: For example, while the FP32 precision fix makes little difference with dense 8B trained with ScaleRL (Figure 7), it provides large gains in GRPO/DAPOstyle losses by mitigating numerical instabilities.
wiki_says: an FP32 output layer raised ScaleRL's ceiling from 0.52 to 0.61

claim: ScaleRL keeps a history of each prompt's pass rate and permanently removes any prompt whose pass rate reaches 0.9 or more from later epochs (No-Positive-Resampling); against uniform resampling of all prompts, this curriculum improved scalability and the asymptotic reward.
quote: We implement this by maintaining a history of pass rates and permanently removing any prompt with pass rate ≥ 0.9 from subsequent epochs-we call this No-Positive-Resampling. In Figure 6b we compare this curriculum against the default setting where all prompts are resampled uniformly throughout training. We see that the curriculum improves scalability and the asymptotic reward A.

claim: At batch size 768, truncation rates of 10-15% (generations cut at the length budget) typically destabilized training, and performance degraded without recovering unless someone intervened; the authors treat a rising truncation rate as a warning signal.
quote: At batch size 768, we observed that truncations in the range of 10-15% typically destabilized training, with performance degrading and not recovering without intervention.
bears_on: length budget and what to monitor during RL

claim: With a DAPO-style loss the upper clip ratio epsilon_max sets the asymptotic reward, not only the convergence speed: A rises with epsilon_max up to an optimal range and then falls again.
quote: As ϵmax increases, the terminal reward A increases until an optimal range is reached, after which A decreases again. This is a striking effect: unlike many hyper-parameters that merely shifts the convergence speed, ϵmax governs the asymptotic error itself.
bears_on: tuning clip-higher in GRPO

claim: Methods that look better at small compute budgets can be worse when extrapolated to large compute, so a short pilot run can rank recipes wrongly.
quote: Embracing theBitter Lesson: Methods that appear superior at small compute budgets can be worse when extrapolated to large-compute regimes (Figure 2).
bears_on: reading short pilot runs

claim: At a fixed total batch, sweeping 8, 16, 24 or 32 generations per prompt (and adjusting the number of prompts) left the fitted scaling curves essentially unchanged: at moderate batch the split between prompts and generations is second-order.
quote: Sweeping generations per prompt 8,16,24,32 and adjusting prompts to keep total batch fixed leaves fitted scaling curves essentially unchanged (Appendix A.13), suggesting that, at moderate batch, this allocation is a second-order choice for both A and B.
bears_on: group size per prompt

claim: Three independent ScaleRL runs (batch 768, 14k generation length) gave fitted asymptotes A that varied by at most ±0.015, so the authors take 0.02 as the error margin; two runs whose A differ by less than that are not distinguishable.
quote: To estimate the error margin of our fits, we trained three independent ScaleRL runs with a batch size of 768 and generation length of 14k (as used in Section 4), shown in Figure 8a. We found that the fit values of A varied by at most ±0.015, suggesting 0.02 as a reasonable error margin on the estimates of asymptotic performance.
bears_on: comparing a main run with a control run

claim: Entropy fell consistently in every run but did not predict downstream performance: a larger-batch run with far better downstream results followed nearly the same entropy trajectory.
quote: Overall, our findings suggest that while entropy decreases consistently during training, it is not necessarily a reliable predictor of downstream performance.
bears_on: what to monitor during RL

claim: ProRL's Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B reaches 41.99 APPS pass@1 against 20.95 for its starting point DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, roughly double (41.99 / 20.95 = 2.0). APPS here is part of the PRIME validation set, and the RL mix covered math, code, STEM, logic puzzles and instruction following, not code alone.

ProRL reports continued improvement after 2k training steps, kept stable with a KL penalty, periodic hard resets of the reference policy and optimizer, and DAPO's decoupled clipping and dynamic sampling.
quote: More importantly, ProRL demonstrates continued performance improvements after an unprecedented 2k training steps (Figure 1, Left), suggesting that RL training scales effectively with increased compute.

claim: ProRL reports many tasks on which the distilled base model produces no correct solution however much it samples, while the RL-trained model reaches 100% pass rates.
quote: Most strikingly, we identify many tasks where the base model fails to produce any correct solutions regardless of the amount of sampling, while our RL-trained model achieves 100% pass rates (Figure 4).

claim: ProRL's boundary expansion is task-dependent: where the base model already has a high pass@128 (many math benchmarks), RL brings minimal or even negative pass@128 gains, the narrowing Yue et al. report; expansion is largest where the base model starts weak, and code benchmarks fell in the sustained-gain group. The paper compares an intermediate checkpoint with the final model; it does not show that newly solved tasks require thousands of steps.
quote: Specifically, tasks where the base model already performs well (i.e., high pass@128) tend to exhibit minimal or even negative gains in reasoning breadth post-RL.
wiki_says: ProRL counters that prolonged, stabilized RL does solve tasks the base model never solved at pass@128, but only after thousands of steps

claim: ProRL's code reward was the fraction of test cases passed (all tests run, no stop at the first failure), with zero for submissions that fail to compile, have syntax errors or exceed a 5-second total timeout: its APPS gain came with partial credit, not a binary all-tests-pass reward.
quote: To support continuous reward feedback, we improve code execution environment to run all test cases rather than terminating on the first error and assign rewards based on the fraction of test cases passed. Submissions that fail to compile, contain syntax errors, or exceed a 5 second total timeout are assigned a reward of zero.
bears_on: binary versus fraction-of-tests code reward

claim: ProRL trained on 4 nodes of 8 H100-80GB GPUs for approximately 16k GPU-hours, with batch size 256, mini-batch 64 (4 gradient updates per rollout step) and a constant learning rate of 2 × 10-6.
quote: We set batch size to 256 and mini-batch size to 64 (equating to 4 gradient updates per rollout step). For training we use the AdamW [20] optimizer with a constant learning rate of 2 × 10-6 . We conduct training on 4 8 x NVIDIA-H100-80GB nodes, and the whole training runs for approximately 16k GPUs hours.
bears_on: budget of a ProRL-style run

claim: ProRL's 1.5B settings: epsilon_low 0.2 and epsilon_high 0.4, dynamic sampling that drops prompts with accuracy 1 or 0, 16 responses per prompt, an 8096-token context limit and a high rollout temperature of 1.2.
quote: We adopt enhancements of GRPO [16] proposed by DAPO [4], decoupling clipping hyperparameters with ϵlow = 0.2, ϵhigh = 0.4, and dynamic sampling for filtering prompts that are too easy or difficult (with accuracy equal to 1 and 0). For rollout, we sample n = 16 responses for each prompt with a context window limit of 8096 and use a high sampling temperature of 1.2.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters at 1.5B

claim: ProRL argues that dropping the KL penalty suits base models before supervised fine-tuning; starting from a distilled checkpoint that already produces coherent chains of thought, keeping a KL penalty (with periodic reference resets) helped stability and kept entropy up.
quote: We observe that this perspective often applies to base models prior to any supervised fine-tuning. In contrast, we begin from a well-initialized checkpoint (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) already capable of generating coherent CoT outputs. In this context, retaining a KL penalty is still beneficial for both stability and sustained entropy.
bears_on: KL penalty when RL starts from a fine-tuned checkpoint

claim: On easy Reasoning Gym tasks the base model's low scores came largely from answering in the wrong format, which RL fixed; the authors conclude formatting is relatively easy to learn, so part of a large RL gain can be format rather than skill.
quote: Despite poor initial formatting behavior, the model is able to achieve high accuracy on these easier tasks post training, suggesting that formatting is relatively easy to learn.
bears_on: format gains inflating RL improvements

claim: Mid-campaign, response length jumped because the model repeated answers and failed to terminate; ProRL's later stages added reward shaping that penalizes responses that do not end correctly.
quote: This stage proceeds until we observe a sudden increase in response length, primarily due to the model repeating answers and failing to terminate
bears_on: failure modes to monitor in long GRPO runs

claim: With GRPO on DeepScaleR training data, Qwen2.5-Math-7B gained 21.4 absolute MATH-500 points under random rewards (independent of the answer) against 29.1 under ground-truth rewards.
quote: For example, RLVR training with GRPO improves MATH-500 performance for Qwen2.5Math-7B in absolute points by 21.4% using randomly assigned rewards, nearly matching the 29.1% gained with ground truth rewards.

claim: The paper attributes the random-reward gain to a bias of GRPO's clip term, which amplifies behaviors that are already high-probability after pretraining even when rewards carry no information; for Qwen2.5-Math the amplified behavior is reasoning in Python without executing it, which rose from 65% to over 90% of responses.
quote: we show that GRPO exhibits a clipping bias arising from the clip term, which can amplify high-prior behaviors learned during pre-training even without informative rewards. As a case study, we identify one such high-prior behavior for Qwen2.5Math models, which we term code reasoningreasoning in code without actual code execution; code reasoning frequency increases from 65% to over 90% with spurious rewards.

claim: The effect is model-dependent: spurious rewards that work on Qwen models often fail to produce gains for other families such as Llama3 or OLMo2.
quote: However, the presence of such amplifiable behaviors is highly model-dependent. In practice, spurious rewards that are effective for Qwen models often fail to produce gains for other model families, such as Llama3 or OLMo2.

claim: The authors recommend confirming RLVR results on other model families and running spurious rewards as dummy baselines.
quote: Thus, we suggest that future RLVR research should be confirmed on other models and using spurious rewards as dummy baselines.

claim: The paper does not explain random-reward gains as format drift: it traces them to clipping amplifying pre-existing reasoning strategies (code reasoning in Qwen2.5-Math), and notes that even under a spurious prompt the model follows the format 84.1% of the time and that format-following does not obviously explain much of the performance. Its controls are random and format rewards as separate baselines, plus several model families.
quote: Even with a spurious prompt, the model is able to follow the format 84.1% of the time. It is not obvious that much of the performance can be explained by format-following.
wiki_says: A random-reward control run, which detects gains from format drift

claim: At 1.5B the random-reward effect was weaker: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B gained only after about 100 steps and only 4.9 points on AMC.
quote: One exception is that Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B sees gains with random rewards much slower (after 100 steps) and less so on AMC (only 4.9%).
bears_on: random-reward control at 1.5B

claim: Random rewards carry a training signal only through clipping: with clipping disabled, or with a single gradient update per rollout (mini-batch equal to rollout batch, so the policy ratio never leaves its starting value), the expected objective is zero and random rewards give no consistent gain. A random-reward control is comparable to the main run only with the same updates per rollout.
quote: When clipping (the red term in Eq. 1) is removed and rewards are sampled independently of the responses, the expected training objective is zero, yielding no meaningful learning signal. To demonstrate this, we consider three separate no-clipping variants of GRPO: disabling clipping in the implementation, increasing the minibatch size to match the rollout size, or reducing the rollout size so that only a single gradient update is performed per rollout.
bears_on: designing the random-reward control run

claim: Models that had already been through RL post-training (Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) improved minimally under every reward type, ground truth included.
quote: As shown in Figure 20, Qwen Instruct models show minimal improvement from RLVR training across different reward types in our setup, even when using ground-truth rewards.
bears_on: choosing a base or an RL-tuned instruct checkpoint

claim: A reward for merely containing the string "python" pushed Qwen2.5-Math-7B to over 99% code usage within 20 training steps: a surface-pattern reward term is optimized almost at once.
quote: To induce code reasoning with RLVR, we assign a positive reward if and only if a response contains the string "python" (a Python reward). This rapidly increases code usage in Qwen2.5-Math-7B to over 99% within 20 training steps
bears_on: surface-pattern bonus terms in the reward

claim: Before any RL, Qwen2.5-Math-7B's MATH-500 accuracy ranged from 49.4 with the default prompt to 68.8 with a lorem-ipsum spurious prompt: the prompt alone moved the baseline by 19.4 points (68.8 - 49.4).
bears_on: fixing prompt and template before measuring RL gains

claim: Spurious-reward gains on AIME 2024 largely vanished on AIME 2025, which post-dates the models: an evaluation set the model cannot have seen separates elicitation from learning.
quote: Intriguingly, we find that any AIME24 gains achievable from training Qwen models with spurious rewards largely vanish when evaluating on AIME 2025.
bears_on: held-out evaluation of RL gains

claim: On RandomCalculation, generated arithmetic problems that post-date the model, RLVR on Qwen2.5-Math-7B improved steadily and passed the base model's boundary only with the correct reward; random and incorrect rewards gave no reliable improvement (unstable training), and inverted rewards collapsed performance.
quote: Using this leakagefree dataset, we show that only accurate reward signals yield steady improvements that surpass the base model's performance boundary in mathematical reasoning, whereas random or incorrect rewards do not.

claim: Given the first 60% of each MATH-500 problem, Qwen2.5-Math-7B regenerated the remaining 40% exactly 54.60% of the time and answered 53.6% of the truncated problems correctly, against 3.8% and 2.4% for Llama3.1-8B: evidence the benchmark is in Qwen's pretraining data.
quote: Furthermore, prompting with the first 60% of each MATH-500 problem, Qwen2.5-Math-7B regenerates the remaining 40% with a 54.60% exact-match rate and answers 53.6% of these incomplete problems correctly. In contrast, Llama3.1-8B scores 3.8% and 2.4% on both metrics.

claim: Measured against the base model's best greedy score without the chat template, the MATH-500 'RL gains' of Qwen2.5-Math-7B largely reflect adaptation to the template format and only converge to that baseline: a format change can pass for learning.
quote: gains' of Qwen2.5-Math-7B largely reflect adaptation to the template format and merely converge to the Greedy (w/o Template) baseline, indicative of memory recall rather than genuine mathematical generalization.

claim: The follow-up accepts the clipping (exploitation) bias but disputes which pretrained behavior it amplifies: on contaminated MATH-500, outputs after spurious-reward RL stay closer to the pre-RL outputs than after correct-reward RL, which the authors read as retrieval of memorized answers rather than the code reasoning Spurious Rewards proposed.
quote: Therefore, performance surge under spurious rewards arises because GRPO inadvertently triggers Qwen to retrieve memorized answers, rather than stimulating Qwen's existing reasoning patterns like codes as explained in Shao et al. (2025).

claim: The contamination extends to code: given 80% of a LiveCodeBench problem, Qwen2.5-Math-7B reproduced the rest exactly 56.59% of the time and Qwen2.5-7B 85.71%, against 4.40% for Llama3.1-8B. Python benchmark problems translated into a new language may still be recalled from their Python originals by a Qwen base.
bears_on: translating Python benchmarks into a new language

claim: On long generated arithmetic problems the binary reward was almost never positive, which made training unstable and prone to divergence; the authors switched to a continuous reward from 0 to 1 penalizing absolute and relative error.
quote: When using the standard RLVR framework, which only provides binary feedback, the model rarely receives positive reinforcement, making training unstable and prone to divergence. To overcome this, we design a continuous reward function that ranges from 0 to 1 and penalizes both absolute and relative errors between the model's prediction and the reference answer.
bears_on: binary versus partial-credit reward when pass rates are near zero

claim: A procedurally generated pool of 1,000 problems per difficulty (5-step and 10-step arithmetic), 700 for training and 300 held out, was enough for steady RLVR gains on Qwen2.5-Math-7B with the correct reward.
quote: Specifically, experiments are conducted on two sub-datasets comprising 5-step and 10-step calculation problems. Each dataset contains 1,000 problems, with 700 used for training and the remaining 300 reserved for validation. As shown in Fig. 7, the performance improves steadily throughout training under correct rewards.
bears_on: size of a generated task pool for a new language

claim: The clipping bias that lets random rewards help only pushes tokens the model already rates highly; mid-probability tokens, typical of the clean arithmetic problems, get almost no random-reward gradient. On a new language where the model is unsure, a random-reward control should stay flat, so a gain there points to a harness or format effect.
quote: Overall, clipped objective introduces systematic exploitation bias for high-probability tokens, whereas mid-probability tokens are less optimized.
bears_on: what a random-reward control can show on a new language

claim: The official chat template cut Qwen2.5-Math-7B's greedy MATH-500 accuracy from 72.20 without it to 50.60 with it, so an RL 'gain' on a base model can be recovery from a template mismatch.
quote:
| Qwen2.5-Math-7B | Greedy (w/o Template) | 72.20 | 63.80 | 53.60 | 41.20 |
| Qwen2.5-Math-7B | Avg@16 (w/o Template) | 68.53 | 57.25 | 45.51 | 31.03 |
| Qwen2.5-Math-7B | Greedy (w/ Template) | 50.60 |
bears_on: evaluation template for base models

claim: Starting from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, math-only RL (8K to 24K response length) raised LiveCodeBench v5 avg@8 from 37.6 to 44.4, and the following code-only RL (24K to 32K) raised it to 51.8; v6 went 34.1, 37.6, 44.1.
The code-RL set is about 8.5K problems: after dropping problems DeepSeek-R1 failed in all 8 attempts, decontaminating and deduplicating, 8,520 problems remained.
quote: Problems where the model failed all 8 attempts (level 8) were excluded. Finally, we performed careful benchmark decontamination and problem deduplication across platforms using n-gram context analysis and original URL matching (see App. A.4 for details). After such aggressive filtering process, 8,520 problems remained, forming our final training set.

claim: AceReason is strictly on-policy (a single gradient update per group of rollouts) and sets the KL coefficient beta to 0, so its GRPO objective reduces to REINFORCE with group-normalized rewards.
quote: Our experiments strictly adhere to on-policy training by performing a single gradient update after generating a group of 𝐺 rollouts. This approach ensures stable RL training and helps prevent entropy collapse. Consequently, the policy used for data collection matches the current policy, i.e., 𝜋𝜃old (· | 𝑞) = 𝜋𝜃(· | 𝑞), and the importance weight 𝑟𝑖,𝑡(𝜃) = 1. Additionally, we eliminate the KL divergence term by setting 𝛽 = 0, thus the GRPO objective becames REINFORCE objective (Williams, 1992) with group-normalized rewards,

claim: AceReason uses the token-level policy-gradient loss variant of GRPO introduced by DAPO (Yu et al., 2025).
quote: We employ the token-level policy gradient loss variant of GRPO, as introduced by Yu et al. (2025)

claim: Math RL used batch size 128, G = 8 rollouts per prompt at the 8K stage and 16 otherwise, learning rate 1 × 10-6 with AdamW, and both the entropy and KL coefficients at 0.
quote: We used a batch size of 128, sampling 𝐺 = 8 responses per prompt for 8K length training and 16 responses otherwise. We adopted a learning rate of 1 × 10-6 with AdamW (Kingma, 2014), and set both the entropy loss coefficient and KL loss coefficient 𝛽 to 0.

claim: Maximum response length was extended stage-wise 8K, 16K, 24K, 32K; starting directly at 16K or 24K gave suboptimal results.
quote: Based on this, we adopted a stage-wise length extension strategy (8K → 16K → 24K → 32K) to enable more efficient training, as directly starting from 16K or 24K resulted in suboptimal results (see Figure 3b).

claim: With a 64-worker process pool, math verification took about 3.9 s per 1,024 instances and code verification (binary: pass all tests within the time limit) about 552.4 s per 1,024 instances, roughly 142 times slower (552.4 / 3.9).
quote: Using a process pool with 64 workers, the average verification time is approximately 3.9 seconds per 1,024 instances. - For coding problem verification, we utilize a local sandbox verifier, following the code execution tools implemented in the LiveCodeBench repository (Jain et al., 2024). Given the model's output, we extract the code generated within '''python[code]''' code block that follows <\think> token. Binary rewards are then assigned based on code execution outcome on full set of test cases. A positive reward will be granted if and only if the extracted code successfully passes all test cases within the specific time limit. Using a process pool with 64 workers, the average verification time for code is approximately 552.4 seconds per 1,024 instances.

claim: Math-only RL, before any code RL, raised LiveCodeBench v5 to 44.4% (+6.8) at 7B and 58.9% (+5.8) at 14B, already above DeepCoder-14B's 57.9%.
quote: In Table 1, we show performing math RL not only improves math reasoning on AIME24/25 but also boosts LiveCodeBench v5 score to 44.4% (6.8% ↑) for 7B and 58.9% (5.8% ↑) for 14B, which already outperforms the very recent code RL model DeepCoder-14B (57.9%)
bears_on: training order: reasoning RL before code RL

claim: Ablations showed both false-positive rewards (incorrect code passing all tests) and false-negative rewards (incorrect tests failing correct code) harm code RL, causing early convergence on sub-optimal policies or complete training collapse.
quote: To highlight the importance of eliminating false positive reward (incorrect code passing all tests within time constraints) and false negative reward (incorrect test cases that fail correct code) in RL Training, we conduct two ablation experiments, showing that both types of errors can be harmful to RL training, resulting in early convergence on sub-optimal policies, or even complete training collapse.
bears_on: test-suite quality in the RL verifier

claim: Applying 2 or 4 gradient updates per rollout batch caused rapid entropy collapse around 100 steps; exactly one update per batch consistently prevented it.
quote: In early experiments, we found applying multiple (2 or 4) gradient updates after model generation with a group of 𝐺 rollouts per prompt led to rapid entropy collapse around 100 steps (see Figure 3c). In contrast, using exactly one gradient update after model generation, as in original DeepSeek-Math's GRPO implementation (Shao et al., 2024), consistently prevented collapse.
bears_on: GRPO updates per rollout batch

claim: At 7B, RL on a distilled model only matched the distillation-only OpenCodeReasoning-7B on code and trailed OpenMath-7B on math; the authors conclude distillation versus RL depends on model size and domain, with RL's clearer edge at 14B and beyond.
quote: model scale, AceReason-Nemotron-7B performs competitively with OpenCodeReasoning-7B on coding tasks, while OpenMath-7B appears to have bigger advantage than RL-trained AceReason-Nemotron-7B on math reasoning. In all cases, AceReason-Nemotron models significantly outperform the general-purpose reasoning model Llama-Nemotron-8B/49B, which is trained via distillation. This indicates that the effectiveness of distillation versus RL still depends on model size and task domain, though RL offers the potential for significantly higher accuracy at the 14B scale and beyond.
bears_on: distillation versus RL at small scale
