claim: Code RL stage 1 trained the 7B model only on problems up to difficulty level 5 (14B: up to 7) at 24,000 tokens, temperature 0.6 and 8 rollouts; stage 2 used all problems at 32,768 tokens, dropped problems easy for the previous epoch's checkpoint, and raised temperature 0.6 to 1.0 and rollouts 8 to 16; batch 128, learning rate 5 × 10-6.
quote: In Stage 1, training data is constructed by difficulty: problems with difficulty up to level 5 are used for 7B model, while problems up to level 7 are used for 14B model. We set maximum response length as 24,000, temperature as 0.6 and number of rollouts as 8 for Stage 1 training. - Stage 2 employs the full set of training problems with 32,768 maximum response length. In this stage, we implement an epoch-wise filtering strategy by filtering out relatively easy problems w.r.t. prior epoch checkpoints and gradually increasing the sampling temperature from 0.6 to 1.0, number of rollouts from 8 to 16 across epochs. This aims to encourage policy convergence while encouraging exploration. We set batch size to 128 and learning rate to 5 × 10-6 with AdamW, continuing training in both stages until policy converges.
bears_on: task-pool curriculum for code RL

claim: Seed-Coder's RL additionally filtered out simple problems with correctness rates above 87.5%, because thinking on them was redundant; the paper presents this as an addition to GRPO's in-training removal of all-correct and all-wrong groups and does not say the rate is measured once on the starting model.
quote: While GRPO inherently incorporates curriculum learning by filtering entirely correct or incorrect samples, we identified two areas for improvement: For simple problems, the model's thinking process contained significant redundancy, including repetitive examples and superficial logic. Since thinking patterns play a crucial role in scaling capabilities, we further filtered simple problems - those with correctness rates above 87.5% - to encourage more efficient utilization of thinking tokens.

claim: Seed-Coder-8B-Reasoning's GRPO run used batch size 128, initial learning rate 1e-6, temperature 0.6, no KL loss, clip-high 0.28, overlong filtering and token-wise loss.
quote: The training configuration included a batch size of 128, an initial learning rate of 1e-6, a temperature of 0.6, and we removed the KL loss. We set the clip ratio high at 0.28, filtered overlong samples, and applied the token-wise loss during training.

claim: RL ran 250 steps: 90 steps at 16K sequence length with 16 samples per prompt, then 160 steps at 32K with 32 samples per prompt.
quote: Specifically, we first trained for 90 steps with a 16K sequence length and 16 samples per prompt, followed by 160 steps with a 32K sequence length and 32 samples per prompt, totaling 250

claim: RL raised Seed-Coder-8B's overall LiveCodeBench pass@1 by 14.6 points to 53.6%, i.e. from 39.0% (53.6 - 14.6) for the warmup-only model.
quote: After RL training, our model Seed-Coder-8B-Reasoning markedly improves the overall pass@1 score on LiveCodeBench by 14.6 points. With an overall pass@1 score of 53.6%, our model surpasses larger models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and even slightly outperforms Claude-3.7-SonnetThinking.

claim: The RL starting point is a long-CoT SFT model: Seed-Coder-8B-Base fine-tuned on thousands of warmup LongCoT samples at learning rate 2e-5.
quote: Before proceeding to reinforcement learning (RL) training, we fine-tuned Seed-Coder-8B-Base on thousands of collected warmup LongCoT samples using a learning rate of 2e-5.

claim: Warmup started from the base model, not the instruct model, although the instruct model scored higher right after warmup: the instruct model frequently collapsed into SFT data patterns during RL, degrading post-RL performance.
quote: We initiated the warmup process from the base model rather than the instruct model, despite the latter achieving higher scores immediately following warmup completion. This decision stemmed from our observation that the instruct model frequently collapses into typical SFT training data patterns during RL, ultimately degrading its post-RL performance.
bears_on: which checkpoint to start RL from

claim: Warmup gains grew with the amount of distillation data, but the authors deliberately kept it small to preserve the base model's exploration space for RL; this is a design choice, not an ablated result.
quote: During the warmup phase, we observed that model performance improvements were positively correlated with the amount of distillation data used. However, as pointed out by Yue et al. [2025], a large volume of distillation data may exceed the inherent capabilities of the base model and thus fail to accurately reflect its true potential. To preserve the model's own exploration space, we chose not to further scale up the distillation data.
bears_on: how much distillation before RL

claim: Growing sequence length and rollout count progressively gave final results comparable to the full setting but trained much more efficiently early on; preliminary observations suggest rollout sizes of 64 or more could help further.
quote: Through empirical comparison, we found that expanding the sequence length and the rollout number yielded comparable final results, but the progressive schedule significantly improved training efficiency during the early stages. Preliminary observations also suggest that further increasing the rollout size to 64 or higher could potentially lead to even better performance.
bears_on: RL compute budget schedule

claim: RL gains concentrated on harder problems: pass@1 rose 22.8 points on medium and 14.0 on hard LiveCodeBench questions.
quote: Notably, during the RL training, our model exhibits substantial pass@1 improvements for medium and hard questions, increasing by 22.8 and 14.0 points, respectively.
bears_on: where RL helps

claim: In the same LiveCodeBench table, Qwen3-8B in thinking mode scores 57.4 overall against 53.6 for Seed-Coder-8B-Reasoning, with a large gap on easy problems (98.0 vs 87.8 in the first easy column).
bears_on: distillation versus RL at 8B

claim: To keep hard SFT examples that quality filtering would drop, the model generated solutions plus unit tests, ran them in a sandbox, and revised failures until all tests passed or a revision limit was hit.
quote: Specifically, we prompted the model to generate solutions along with corresponding unit tests, evaluate the outputs within a sandbox environment, and iteratively refine any failed solutions until all tests passed or a maximum number of revision attempts was reached. This iterative refinement process allows us to retain more challenging examples and enrich the difficulty distribution of the training corpus.
bears_on: synthesizing verified SFT data

claim: MiMo's strict test-difficulty reward pays a difficulty level's reward only if the solution passes all tests in that level's group and in every lower-difficulty group.
quote: (1) Strict Reward. Under the strict reward scheme, a solution receives the reward corresponding to a difficulty level only if it passes all tests in that group as well as in all lower-difficulty groups.

claim: MiMo assigns test difficulty from pass rates: several models roll out each problem, each test's pass rate is computed over all generated solutions, and tests are clustered into levels, lower pass rate meaning harder.
quote: We utilize several models to perform multiple rollouts on each problem, and calculate the pass rate for each test case across all model-generated solutions. We then cluster the test cases into different difficulty levels according to their pass rates, with lower pass rates indicating higher difficulty.

claim: For math, MiMo rolled out its SFT model 16 times per problem and removed problems with pass rate above 90%, which removes approximately 50% of easy problems from the original problem set.
quote: For the remaining problems, we rollout an SFT version of MiMo-7B 16 times, eliminating problems with a passrate exceeding 90%. Notably, this process removes approximately 50% of easy problems from the original problem set.

claim: For code, MiMo's easy-problem filter removed only problems its SFT model solved in all 16 of 16 rollouts (pass rate 100%), leaving 30K code problems; the lower threshold the survey quotes belongs to the math filter (see the math-filter claim).
quote: Similar to math data, we utilize an SFT version of MiMo-7B to filter out easy problems that are perfectly solved in all 16 rollouts. This rigorous cleaning process yields 30K code problems.
wiki_says: In the code-RL task-pool paragraph: MiMo dropped those solved over 90% across 16 rollouts but kept an easy pool.

claim: During RL, problems that reach a perfect pass rate (and so drop out under dynamic sampling) are kept in an easy pool sampled with probability 10% per rollout, which stabilized updates and improved sampling efficiency; the pool holds problems solved during training, not the problems pre-filtered before RL.
quote: During the training process, we maintain an easy data pool, where problems with perfect pass rates are stored. When performing rollouts, there is a probability 𝛼 (10% in our experiments) to sample data from this easy data pool. This strategy effectively stabilizes the policy update while improving sampling efficiency, especially in the later phases of RL training.

claim: Simply removing problems that reach a perfect pass rate from the training data caused significant instability in policy updates in MiMo's preliminary studies, the reason for the easy pool.
quote: A straightforward approach to address this efficiency issue would be to entirely remove problems with perfect pass rates from the training data. However, our preliminary studies show that this method introduces significant instability in policy updates.
bears_on: retiring solved prompts from the pool

claim: MiMo also defined a soft scheme that splits each difficulty group's score equally over its tests and sums passed tests; the text compares strict and soft only in Figure 5 and does not state which one the final model used.
quote: (2) Soft Reward. In contrast, the soft reward scheme distributes the total score of each group equally among its tests. The final reward is the sum of the scores for all passed tests. The right part of Figure 5 compares the performance achieved by two reward schemes against the baseline without test difficulty driven reward.
bears_on: partial-credit reward design

claim: From the same 7B base, RL directly on the base reached 49.1 on LiveCodeBench v5 (from 32.9), SFT alone 52.3, and SFT followed by RL 57.8.
bears_on: distill first, then RL

claim: In RL from the base model, the policy hacked the math reward, while the test-case-based code verifier made reward exploitation significantly harder.
quote: Analysis of the model outputs reveals that the base model, with its strong exploration capabilities, tends to hack the reward for mathematics problems. For code problems, however, the test-case-based verifier makes reward exploitation significantly harder.
bears_on: test-based verifiers resist hacking

claim: MiMo-7B-RL used batch size 512, actor mini-batch 32, 16 gradient updates per training iteration and learning rate 1e-6, with 32,768 max tokens and temperature and top-p 1.0, i.e. off-policy updates unlike AceReason's single update.
quote: In our experiment, we employed a training batch size of 512, with an actor mini-batch size of 32. We executed 16 gradient updates per training iteration at a learning rate of 1e-6. The maximum sequence length was set to 32,768 tokens to facilitate complex reasoning tasks. During the training phase, both temperature and top-p parameters were configured at 1.0 to promote output diversity.
bears_on: GRPO updates per rollout batch

claim: For a later MiMo release, vanilla GRPO was markedly prone to premature performance saturation; switching to on-policy RL was remarkably stable with sustained growth.
quote: Our prior empirical investigations indicated that a vanilla implementation of GRPO was markedly prone to premature performance saturation. To mitigate this, we adopted an on-policy RL algorithm, drawing parallels with the approach used in MiMo-VL-7B-RL Team et al. (2025a). Training with on-policy RL proved to be remarkably stable, while also enabling sustained growth in model efficacy throughout the learning process.
bears_on: on-policy versus off-policy GRPO

claim: In Klear-Reasoner's ablation, a soft code reward equal to the test pass rate reached 61.0 on LiveCodeBench V5 against 59.2 for a hard all-tests-pass reward, a 1.8-point gain.
quote: As shown in Figure 3(a), the model trained with soft reward achieves a LiveCodeBench V5 score of 61.0, outperforming the 59.2 achieved with hard reward. This 1.8-point gain confirms that addressing reward sparsity and variance not only improves learning dynamics, but also boosts generalization in code RL.

claim: Klear's soft code reward is proportional to tests passed: 4 of 16 tests yields 0.25.
quote: For example, if generated code passes 4 out of 16 test cases, it receives a proportional reward of 0.25 (4/16).

claim: The soft-versus-hard comparison ran only 100 steps at 16K tokens from an early long-CoT SFT checkpoint, and its hard arm gives a negative (not zero) reward unless all tests pass.
quote: Models are initialized from an early long CoT SFT checkpoint and trained for 100 steps with a sequence length of 16K tokens. In the soft reward setting, the reward equals the test case pass rate; in the hard reward setting, a positive reward is given only if all test cases pass and a negative reward otherwise.
bears_on: strength of evidence for pass-rate rewards

claim: Klear dropped code problems with fewer than 16 tests as prone to false positives, and kept only prompts where DeepSeek-R1 reached pass@16 above 0.5 over 16 completions, to remove faulty or insufficient tests.
quote: We first remove examples with fewer than 16 test cases, as these are more susceptible to false positives. For each retained prompt, we generate 16 completions using DeepSeek-R1-0120 4 . Only those prompts for which DeepSeek-R1-0120 achieves a pass@16 greater than 0.5 are kept, reducing noise introduced by faulty or insufficient test cases.
bears_on: minimum tests per task and test validation

claim: Adding an SFT loss on correct rollouts with weight alpha = 0.1 gave AIME2024 79.37 against 78.13 for plain GRPO (alpha = 0) after 100 math RL steps at 32K.
quote: Table 6: Performance on AIME2024 (avg@32) and AIME2025 (avg@32) with varying α values when training with SFT loss. Here, α = 0 corresponds to the standard GRPO loss. All models are trained for 100 steps on mathematical RL data with a sequence length of 32K tokens. | | AIME2024 | AIME2025 | |---------------------|------------|------------| | Starting Checkpoint | 73.51 | 64.62 | | α = 0 | 78.13 | 68.02 | | α = 0.05 | 77.81 | 69.48 | | α = 0.1 | 79.37 | 70.42 |
bears_on: auxiliary SFT loss during RL

claim: With the same prompts, SFT students reached LiveCodeBench V5 44.44 with a QwQ-32B teacher, 50.90 with DeepSeek-R1-0120 and 53.05 with DeepSeek-R1-0528 (an early-stage SFT model).
quote: Table 3: Impact of different teacher models on supervised fine-tuning performance. Bolded values indicate the best performance across teacher models. Note that results under DeepSeek-R1-0528 correspond to an early-stage SFT model. | Benchmark | QwQ-32B | DeepSeek-R1-0120 | DeepSeek-R1-0528 | |------------------|-----------|--------------------|--------------------| | AIME 2024 | 62.71 | 67.71 | 73.54 | | AIME 2025 | 53.13 | 50.00 | 64.58 | | LiveCodeBench V5 | 44.44 | 50.90 | 53.05 |
bears_on: teacher choice for distillation

claim: In math SFT, correct-only traces won on easy problems (+4.78 on AIME 2024) but mixing in incorrect traces won on hard problems (+1.66 on the AIME 2024 Hard subset).
quote: For easy tasks, training solely on correct data consistently yield superior results. For instance, on the AIME 2024 benchmark, using only correct data resulted in a 4.78% performance improvement compared to training with mixed responses. This suggests that when the underlying reasoning is relatively straightforward and aligns well with the model's prior capabilities, exposure to incorrect paths acts primarily as detrimental noise, interfering with the model's grasp of established, correct patterns. In contrast, for hard tasks, incorporating incorrect examples alongside correct ones surprisingly improved performance. On the AIME 2024 Hard subset, training with mixed data achieved a 1.66% higher accuracy than using only correct samples.
bears_on: filtering SFT traces by correctness

claim: Klear's RL was off-policy with constant learning rate 1e-6 and mini-batch 16 for math, but 5e-7 and mini-batch 32 for code, 8 rollouts per prompt, and the test pass rate as the code reward.
quote: We use an off-policy training strategy, with a constant learning rate of 1e-6 and a mini-batch size of 16 for math RL, and a constant learning rate of 5e-7 with a mini-batch size of 32 for coding RL. For rollout, we sample 8 responses for each prompt. It is worth mentioning that we use the pass rate of test cases as a reward for code RL.
bears_on: code RL hyperparameters

claim: At 32B, Qwen2.5-32B-Zero (large-scale RL from the base) scored 40.2 LiveCodeBench pass@1, against 57.2 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (SFT on DeepSeek-R1 samples) and 41.9 for QwQ-32B-Preview.

Qwen2.5-32B-Zero came from large-scale RL on Qwen2.5-32B-Base with math, code and STEM data for over 10K steps; it matched QwQ-32B-Preview, and the distilled 32B model was significantly better on all benchmarks.
quote: we conduct large-scale RL training on Qwen2.5-32B-Base using math, code, and STEM data, training for over 10K steps, resulting in Qwen2.5-32B-Zero, as described in B.4.1. The experimental results, shown in Table 16, demonstrate that the 32B base model, after large-scale RL training, achieves performance on par with QwQ-32B-Preview. However, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, which is distilled from DeepSeek-R1, performs significantly better than Qwen2.5-32B-Zero across all benchmarks.

claim: The authors conclude that distilling more powerful models into smaller ones yields excellent results, whereas smaller models relying on large-scale RL require enormous computational power and may not even achieve the performance of distillation.
quote: First, distilling more powerful models into smaller ones yields excellent results, whereas smaller models relying on the large-scale RL mentioned in this paper require enormous computational power and may not even achieve the performance of distillation.

claim: R1-Distill models are open Qwen and Llama models fine-tuned on a curated set of 800,000 samples generated with DeepSeek-R1, i.e. sequence-level distillation.
quote: Specifically, we fine-tune open-source foundation models such as Qwen (Qwen, 2024b) and LLaMA (AI@Meta, 2024; Touvron et al., 2023) using a curated dataset comprising 800,000 samples generated with DeepSeek-R1.

claim: DeepSeek-R1 does not apply neural reward models, outcome- or process-based, to reasoning tasks, because it observed they are susceptible to reward hacking during large-scale RL.
quote: Notably, we abstain from applying neural reward models-whether outcome-based or process-based-to reasoning tasks. This decision is predicated on our observation that neural reward models are susceptible to reward hacking during large-scale reinforcement learning.

claim: Listed among unsuccessful attempts: a model-based PRM inevitably leads to reward hacking and its benefit was limited relative to its overhead in large-scale RL, though PRMs remained useful for reranking top-N responses or guided search.
quote: Third, once a model-based PRM is introduced, it inevitably leads to reward hacking (Gao et al., 2022), and retraining the reward model needs additional training resources and it complicates the whole training pipeline. In conclusion, while PRM demonstrates a good ability to rerank the top-N responses generated by the model or assist in guided search (Snell et al., 2024), its advantages are limited compared to the additional computational overhead it introduces during the large-scale reinforcement learning process in our experiments.

claim: The R1-Distill models received SFT only, with no RL stage, although the authors say RL could substantially boost them; RL after distillation was left to others.
quote: For distilled models, we apply only SFT and do not include an RL stage, even though incorporating RL could substantially boost model performance. Our primary goal here is to demonstrate the effectiveness of the distillation technique, leaving the exploration of the RL stage to the broader research community.
bears_on: RL after distillation

claim: Pure RL from a 7B dense and a 16B MoE base failed to give meaningful AIME improvements; as responses grew longer these models fell into repetition and could not use long CoT.
quote: During the initial phase of our development, we experimented with smaller-scale models, specifically a 7B dense model and a 16B Mixtureof-Experts (MoE) model, as the foundational architectures for RL training. However, these configurations consistently failed to yield meaningful improvements when evaluated on the AIME benchmark, which we employed as the primary validation set. We observed that as response lengths increased, these smaller models exhibited a tendency toward repetition and were unable to effectively leverage long chains of thought (CoT) to improve reasoning accuracy.
bears_on: pure RL from a small base model

claim: In tension with that, Qwen2-Math-7B-Zero, trained with about 10,000 policy-gradient steps, significantly outperformed Qwen2-Math-7B-Instruct and GPT-4o on the AIME results of Table 17.
quote: We trained Qwen2-Math-7B-Zero with approximately 10,000 policy gradient update steps. As shown in Table 17, Qwen2-Math-7B-Zero significantly outperformed the non-reasoning models like Qwen2-Math-7B-Instruct and GPT-4o.
bears_on: pure RL from a small base model

claim: Distillation recipe: 2-3 epochs on the 800k samples, cosine decay to one-tenth of the initial learning rate, 32,768-token context, batch size 64; the 1.5B student starts from Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B at initial learning rate 1 × 10-4.
quote: For distillation, we fine-tune the corresponding base model for 2-3 epochs using the 800k data described in Section B.3.3. The base model and initial learning rate are listed in Table 6. We employ a cosine decay learning rate scheduler that gradually decreases the learning rate to one-tenth of its initial value. The maximum context length is 32,768 tokens, and the batch size is 64. Table 6 | DeepSeek-R1 Distilled Models, their corresponding Base Models, and Initial Learning Rates. | Distilled Model | Base Model | Initial Learning Rate | |-------------------------------|------------------------|-------------------------| | DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B | Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B | 1 × 10 -4 |
bears_on: distillation hyperparameters for a 1.5B student

claim: For 5151 Codeforces and 2504 AtCoder problems without public tests, DeepSeek-V2.5 wrote Python test generators; tests that made correct submissions fail were dropped, and subsets that caught incorrect submissions were kept.
quote: For code data, we collect a large set of competitive programming problems. In detail, We have compiled an extensive collection of competitive programming problems from multiple online judge (OJ) platforms, specifically 5151 problems from Codeforces and 2504 problems from AtCoder. Since the original test cases are not publicly available from these platforms, we developed a methodology to create reliable test cases for each problem. Our approach involves using DeepSeek-V2.5 to generate candidate test cases, followed by a rigorous validation process. Specifically, we prompted DeepSeek-V2.5 to write Python programs that generate test cases tailored to each problem's requirements as shown in Listing 2. After obtaining numerous candidate test cases, we implemented a two-phase filtering procedure. First, we used correct submissions to eliminate invalid test cases that produced incorrect outputs. Then, we strategically selected subsets of test cases that successfully identified flaws in incorrect submissions.
bears_on: building test suites when none exist

claim: R1's code RL data held 17k algorithm problems plus 8k bug-fixing problems from real GitHub issues, each with an issue, the buggy source and unit tests that partially or completely fail.
quote: Coding dataset includes 17k algorithm competition questions, along with 8k bug fixing problems. The algorithm competition questions are similar to problems found on platforms like Codeforces or LeetCode. Each problem typically includes a detailed problem description, constraints, and multiple input-output examples. The task is to write a complete function or program that can solve the problem correctly and efficiently, passing a comprehensive set of hidden test cases that assess both correctness and performance. These problems test algorithmic skills, including dynamic programming, graph theory, string manipulation, and data structure usage. The bug-fixing problems are extracted from real-world GitHub issues. Each task provides an issue description, a buggy version of the source code, and a set of unit tests that partially or completely fail.
bears_on: repair tasks in the RL mix

claim: On Qwen3-8B, starting from the same off-policy distilled checkpoint (LiveCodeBench v5 42.0), reinforcement learning reached 52.9 on LiveCodeBench v5 at 17,920 GPU hours, while on-policy distillation reached 60.3 at 1,800 GPU hours.

Qwen3's distillation-versus-RL comparison started both arms from the same off-policy distilled 8B checkpoint, used only math and code queries, and found distillation significantly better at approximately 1/10 of the GPU hours.
quote: both starting from the same off-policy distilled 8B checkpoint. For simplicity, we focus solely on math and code-related queries in this comparison. The results, summarized in Table 21, show that distillation achieves significantly better performance than reinforcement learning while requiring approximately only 1/10 of the GPU hours.

claim: Qwen3's strong-to-weak distillation pipeline built five dense models (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B) and the Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE, so it covers the 0.6B-4B models and more.
quote: The Strong-to-Weak Distillation pipeline is specifically designed to optimize lightweight models, encompassing 5 dense models (Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B) and one MoE model (Qwen3-30B-A3B).

claim: In Qwen3's preliminary experiments, distilling teacher logits into small students replaced running the four-stage pipeline per small model, gave higher Pass@1 and Pass@64, and needed only 1/10 of the GPU hours of the four-stage method.
quote: This approach eliminates the necessity of performing an exhaustive four-stage training process individually for every small-scale model. It leads to better immediate performance, as indicated by higher Pass@1 scores, and also improves the model's ability of exploration, as reflected in improved Pass@64 results. In addition, it achieves these gains with much greater training efficiency, requiring only 1/10 of the GPU hours compared to the four-stage training method.

claim: In the Qwen3-8B comparison, on-policy distillation from teacher logits raised pass@64 on AIME'24 and AIME'25 over the starting checkpoint, while RL did not improve pass@64 at all, only pass@1.
quote: Furthermore, distillation from teacher logits enables the student model to expand its exploration space and enhance its reasoning potential, as evidenced by the improved pass@64 scores on the AIME'24 and AIME'25 benchmarks after distillation, compared to the initial checkpoint. In contrast, reinforcement learning does not lead to any improvement in pass@64 scores.
bears_on: pass@k evaluation of RL versus distillation

claim: In thinking mode, on LiveCodeBench v5 (2024.10-2025.02), Qwen3-1.7B scores 33.2 and Qwen3-0.6B 12.3, against 13.2 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 42.5 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (Table 19 column order).
quote: | Coding LiveCodeBench v5 | 13.2 | 42.5 | 12.3 | 33.2 |
bears_on: baseline code scores of sub-2B students

claim: In non-thinking mode, on LiveCodeBench v5, Qwen3-0.6B scores 3.6 and Qwen3-1.7B 11.6, against 5.3 for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, 9.2 for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, 1.8 for Gemma-3-1B-IT and 10.4 for Phi-4-mini (Table 20 column order).
quote: | Coding LiveCodeBench v5 | 1.8 | 10.4 | 5.3 | 9.2 | 3.6 | 11.6 |
bears_on: short-answer code scores of sub-2B students

claim: Qwen3's reasoning-RL pool was 3,995 query-verifier pairs chosen to be unused in cold start, learnable for the cold-start model, as challenging as possible and broad across sub-domains, trained with GRPO.
quote: The query-verifier pairs used in the Reasoning RL stage must satisfy the following four criteria: (1) They were not used during the cold-start phase. (2) They are learnable for the cold-start model. (3) They are as challenging as possible. (4) They cover a broad range of sub-domains. We ultimately collect a total of 3,995 query-verifier pairs, and employed GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to update the model parameters.
bears_on: RL task pool selection

claim: On Qwen3-32B, the thinking-mode-fusion SFT and general RL stages that followed reasoning RL lowered thinking-mode AIME'24 and LiveCodeBench; the authors attribute it to training on a broader range of general tasks.
quote: In contrast, for challenging tasks like AIME'24 and LiveCodeBench, the performance in thinking mode actually decreases after these two training stages. We conjecture this degradation is due to the model being trained on a broader range of general tasks, which may compromise its specialized capabilities in handling complex problems.
bears_on: training order and mixing general data after code RL

claim: Qwen3 kept the long-CoT cold-start SFT deliberately small, minimizing both samples and steps, so as not to limit the gains of the following RL stage.
quote: The objective at this stage is to instill foundational reasoning patterns in the model without overly emphasizing immediate reasoning performance. This approach ensures that the model's potential is not limited, allowing for greater flexibility and improvement during the subsequent reinforcement learning (RL) phase. To achieve this objective effectively, it is preferable to minimize both the number of training samples and the training steps during this preparatory phase.
bears_on: size of the SFT stage before RL

claim: Open-RS's AMC23 rise from 63% to 80% (and MATH-500 from 83% to 85%) came within 50-100 steps of Experiment 2, the easy-plus-hard data mix with a reduced length limit; after 150-200 steps performance declined, KL divergence became unstable and mixed-language output returned.
quote: Initial completion lengths drop to approximately 2800 tokens, and performance improves significantly: AMC23 rises from 63% to 80%, and MATH-500 from 83% to 85% within 50-100 steps (Figure 2). However, after 150-200 steps (approximately 4000 local steps), performance declines, and KL divergence becomes unstable (Figure 4), with mixedlanguage outputs reemerging.

claim: In Open-RS Experiment 1 (open-s1 data only), AMC23 rose from 63% to 70% and MATH-500 from 83% to 84% in the first 50-100 steps, then after 200 steps fell below 60% on AMC23 and to 80% on MATH-500.
quote: Performance on AMC23 improves from 63% to 70% and on MATH-500 from 83% to 84% within the first 50-100 steps (see Figure 2). However, after 200 steps, accuracy degrades significantly, dropping below 60% on AMC23 and to 80% on MATH-500.

claim: Open-RS's $42 is the estimated cost of 24 hours on 4x A40 GPUs for 7,000 samples with 6 outputs per step; the same table puts DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview at $3,629 and Still-3-1.5B-Preview at $2,268.
quote: Our approach, using 7000 samples with 6 outputs per step (42,000 total samples), costs approximately $42 on 4x A40 GPUs over 24 hours. In contrast, 7B models like Qwen2.5-7B-SimpleRL ($1633) and Eurus-2-7B-PRIME ($1088) and 1.5B models like DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview ($3629) and Still-3-1.5B-Preview ($2268) require significantly more resources and data (e.g., 40k × 16 samples for DeepScaleR).

claim: Open-RS capped completions at 4,096 tokens in Experiment 1 and 3,584 in Experiments 2 and 3, and the authors found that too short for the hardest problems, which were truncated.
quote: Second, the maximum completion length (4096 tokens in Experiment 1, reduced to 3584 in Experiments 2 and 3) proved insufficient for extremely hard problems in the opens1 dataset, forcing the model to truncate reasoning processes prematurely.

claim: GRPO on the multilingual DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B drifted into other languages after 150-200 steps even with an English-only instruction in the system prompt.
quote: Third, the multilingual nature of the base model, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, introduced unintended language drift after 150-200 steps, despite efforts to enforce English-only outputs via prompts in Experiment 3.
bears_on: GRPO output drift on long runs

claim: Mixing easier problems into the hard pool, with a shorter length limit, improved early GRPO performance and stabilized reasoning, but did not make long runs stable.
quote: Incorporating a mix of easy and hard problems under reduced length constraints enhances early performance and stabilizes reasoning behavior, though long-term stability remains elusive.
bears_on: task difficulty mix in the RL pool

claim: Replacing the accuracy reward with a cosine length-scaled reward stabilized lengths but capped the gain: AMC23 went from 63% to 72.5% and MATH-500 from 83% to 84.4% within 50 steps, below Experiment 2's peak.
quote: Performance on AMC23 and MATH-500 increases modestly compared to the baseline (63% to 72.5% and 83% to 84.4%, respectively) within 50 steps, though it lags behind Experiment 2's peak (Figure 2).
bears_on: cost of a length-shaping reward

quote: Finally, our evaluation focused exclusively on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, leaving the generalizability of our approach to other domains - such as scientific reasoning or coding - unexplored.
bears_on: transfer of small-model GRPO results to code

claim: AMC23 in Open-RS's evaluation is 40 problems, so one problem moves the score by 2.5 points (100/40).

bears_on: statistical weight of small-benchmark gains

For context comparing potential full training runs, the cost to train a Tina model for a complete epoch is $14 USD (training only). Including evaluation costs for such a full run would increase the total to approximately $31 USD.

claim: Under Tina's uniform re-evaluation (lighteval with vLLM, zero-shot pass@1), Open-RS2 scores 62.50 on AMC23, the same as its base DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-Qwen-1.5B (62.50), with an average of 41.60 against the base's 41.18; on this protocol Open-RS2 shows no AMC23 gain over its base.
bears_on: evaluation noise in small-model RL gains

claim: In Tina's LoRA-rank ablation (LIMR setup), ranks 8, 16 and 32 averaged between 47.89% and 48.92%, rank 16 best at 48.92% against 48.47% for rank 32, with slightly lower scores at ranks 4 and 64.
quote: Ranks 8, 16, and 32 all produced strong results, with average scores clustering between 47.89% and 48.92%. Notably, rank 16 achieved the peak performance (48.92%) in this comparison, slightly outperforming rank 32 (48.47%). Performance decreased slightly at the extremes (rank 4 and 64).
bears_on: LoRA rank for GRPO

claim: Tina-Open-RS2's benchmark average was 50.60 at step 450 (the reported best checkpoint) and 43.05 at step 500, a 7.55-point swing between consecutive 50-step checkpoints (50.60 - 43.05).
bears_on: checkpoint selection and evaluation noise

claim: Across most Tina runs the best checkpoint came just before or around a phase transition in the format metrics (format reward, completion length), which accuracy reward did not show.
quote: the best-performing checkpoint, yielding the highest reasoning accuracy on held-out evaluations, consistently occurs just prior to or around this observed phase transition point in the format metrics (indicated by the red vertical dashed line).
bears_on: early stopping signal for GRPO

claim: In Tina's RL-algorithm ablation, GRPO and Dr.GRPO peaked at similar averages (49.45% and 49.53%), but Dr.GRPO reached its best checkpoint at 17% of an epoch against 57% for GRPO.
quote: Both algorithms led to similar peak average performance levels (49.45% for GRPO vs. 49.53% for Dr.GRPO). However, Dr.GRPO reached its best checkpoint significantly earlier in the training process (17% of an epoch vs. 57% for GRPO).
bears_on: loss_type choice for GRPO

claim: Tina ran GRPO training and vLLM generation on the same two GPUs by capping vLLM's memory, trading wall-clock time for a smaller hardware footprint.
quote: To enable this, we co-located the RL training process and the vLLM on the same two GPUs by constraining vLLM's GPU memory usage. The training itself utilized data parallelism across both GPUs. While running inference and training concurrently on two GPUs might result in a longer wall-clock training time compared to a setup with dedicated inference GPUs, it significantly reduces the hardware requirement.
bears_on: single-node GRPO setup

claim: Students of 3B parameters or fewer do not consistently benefit from long chain-of-thought or from distillation from larger models, and do better on shorter, simpler chains.
quote: small models (≤3B parameters) do not consistently benefit from long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning or distillation from larger models. Instead, they perform better when fine-tuned on shorter, simpler reasoning chains that better align with their intrinsic learning capacity.

claim: The 4.7- and 3.1-point gaps are Table 1's average performance across the evaluation benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, AIME, AMC, OlympiadBench), not MATH alone: long versus short CoT averaged 14.8 vs 19.5 (-4.7) for Qwen2.5-0.5B, 27.0 vs 34.2 (-7.1) for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 40.3 vs 43.4 (-3.1) for Qwen2.5-3B.
quote:
Table 1: Comparison of the average performance between fine-tuning with long CoT (PLong) and short CoT (PShort). We find that small student models may struggle to learn from long CoT data.

| Student Model | PLong | PShort | ∆Long | Better? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-0.5B | 14.8 | 19.5 | -4.7 | Short |
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | 27.0 | 34.2 | -7.1 | Short |
| Qwen2.5-3B | 40.3 | 43.4 | -3.1 | Short |
wiki_says: On MATH, long CoT scored 4.7 points below short CoT for a 0.5B student and 3.1 below for a 3B.

claim: Mix-Long combines long and short CoT data in a 1:4 ratio, trained on the 7.5k MATH samples with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Llama3.2-3B-Instruct as students.
quote: We use Llama3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the student model and 7.5k samples in MATH dataset as the training set. We distill different teacher models to generate responses as the baseline. Our proposed Mix-Long combines long CoT data and normal CoT data in a 1:4 ratio

claim: For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Mix-Long scored 64.7 on MATH against 56.2 for long CoT alone and 61.0 for short CoT alone; its benchmark average was 45.9 against 40.3 and 43.4.

On MATH alone, long CoT trailed short CoT by 8.44 points for Qwen2.5-0.5B (23.0 vs 31.5), 10.7 for Qwen2.5-1.5B (41.6 vs 52.3) and 4.84 for Qwen2.5-3B (56.2 vs 61.0); the 1.5B student had the largest gap of all.
bears_on: long versus short CoT for 0.5B-1.5B students

claim: Responses of the Qwen2.5-3B student averaged 3384.7 tokens after long-CoT training, 575.7 after short-CoT training and 1248.9 after Mix-Long.
quote: Additionally, the average token lengths of responses generated by long CoT, short CoT, and Mix-Long are 3384.7, 575.7, and 1248.9, respectively.
bears_on: target answer length for distilled SFT data

claim: Averaged over the evaluation benchmarks, Qwen2.5-0.5B scored 16.9 when distilled from Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct against 20.4 from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-1.5B 32.2 against 33.0: the small teacher was the better teacher for the smallest students.
bears_on: teacher size for a 0.5B-1.5B student

claim: Prompting the 72B teacher to answer more simply for a small student did not close the gap: Qwen2.5-0.5B averaged 0.204 with the 3B teacher and 0.161 with the 72B teacher under the revised prompt.
bears_on: prompting a teacher for student-friendly output

claim: The math-expert Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B showed a much smaller long-CoT gap than the general Qwen2.5-1.5B and gained more from large-teacher CoT, and the authors conjecture that the gap stems mainly from the student's limited in-domain knowledge.
quote: Our findings show that the long CoT gap of the small math expert model is significantly smaller than that of general small models. Furthermore, the performance improvement of Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B when fined-tuned with large teacher CoT exceeds that of Qwen2.5-1.5B, suggesting that math expert models benefit more substantially from large teacher CoT. We conjecture that a key factor leading to the small model learnability gap is the limited in-domain knowledge of small student models.
bears_on: distilling a language the student has never seen

claim: The learnability-gap study covers math only; code generation was not evaluated, so the short-over-long result for small students is untested on code.
quote: we acknowledge that our research primarily focuses on this specific domain and does not evaluate other crucial skills such as instruction following, code generation, or multi-modal understanding.
bears_on: transfer of the short-CoT result to code

claim: Caching only the teacher's Top-K probabilities gives a biased estimate of the teacher distribution and leads to suboptimal student performance and calibration; the evidence is from offline-logit distillation in pre-training, with students from 300M to 3B.
quote: we prove that naive approaches for sparse knowledge distillation such as caching Top-K probabilities, while intuitive, provide biased estimates of teacher probability distribution to the student, resulting in suboptimal performance and calibration.

claim: With vanilla Top-K and fewer than 25 tokens, the 300M student's loss was worse than plain cross-entropy training without distillation; only near 300 tokens did it approach full distillation.
quote: If a small number of Top-K tokens (< 25) are used, the student loss is worse than just than using CE loss without any distillation - Only after 300 tokens does the model performance start reaching close to FullKD.
bears_on: distilling from 20 API top_logprobs

claim: Assigning the residual probability to the ground-truth token repairs much of Top-K's damage: with 20 tokens it covered 73% of the gap between cross-entropy and full distillation, with ECE 2.3%.
quote:
| Naive Fix: Remaining Probability to Ground Truth | Naive Fix: Remaining Probability to Ground Truth | Naive Fix: Remaining Probability to Ground Truth | Naive Fix: Remaining Probability to Ground Truth | Naive Fix: Remaining Probability to Ground Truth | Naive Fix: Remaining Probability to Ground Truth |
| Top-k 1 | 3.37 | 2.81 | -5 | 7.1 | 41.3 |
| Top-k 5 | 2.96 | 2.78 | 44 | 4.4 | 42.4 |
| Top-k 10 | 2.88 | 2.77 | 61 | 3.3 | 42.4 |
| Top-k 20 | 2.83 | 2.76 | 73 | 2.3 | 42.9 |
bears_on: using truncated teacher probabilities

claim: When the student trains on data unlike the teacher's pre-training data, the teacher must first be adapted on that data: distilling a 300M student from an unadapted LLaMA-3-8B gave only a small improvement over cross-entropy, and adapting the teacher for 50B tokens increased it significantly.
quote: Sreenivas et al. (2024) found that if the student is being trained on a data distribution different from the teacher's pre-training data, the teacher should first be adapted (finetuned) on this data by training for a short while. We also observe the same - when training a 300M student on Fineweb-edu data with the LLaMA-3-8B model as teacher, using the original teacher model directly yields only a small improvement over CE (Table 13). After teacher adaptation for 50B tokens, this increases significantly.
bears_on: distilling a language the teacher does not know

claim: In offline-logit pre-training distillation (300M students, 8B Llama-3 teacher, 10B tokens), vanilla forward KL outperformed reverse KL, forward-plus-reverse KL, MSE and L1.
quote: We also experiment with alternative loss/divergence functions, by training 300M students with 8B Llama-3 teacher for 10B tokens. Some prior works (Kim et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2024b; Gu et al., 2023; Ko et al., 2024) find alternative objectives such as Reverse KL Divergence, Mean Squared Error as superior, while other works (Sultan, 2023; Wen et al., 2023; Muralidharan et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2024) have observed the opposite. In Table 15, we observe that vanilla forward KLD outperforms other objectives.
bears_on: KL direction for logit distillation

claim: Random Sampling KD, which importance-samples tokens from the teacher distribution, matched full distillation's performance and calibration with only 12 tokens per position, for a 300M student and 3B teacher trained on 10B tokens.
quote: We train LLaMA-style 300M student models using a 3B teacher (hyper-parameters in Table 17) for 10B tokens, 1.5x more than Chinchillaoptimal (Hoffmann et al., 2022) number of tokens. Our proposed method achieves very similar performance and calibration compared to FullKD, while using only 12 tokens (Table 6).
bears_on: caching logits of a local teacher

claim: Cached teacher logits whose prefix context no longer matched the student's after the first document boundary hurt the student surprisingly much, especially when the teacher ran with shorter sequence lengths.
quote: This resulted in the prefix-context of tokens seen by the teacher and student not being aligned after the first document boundary. This had a surprisingly large effect on student model performance, particularly if smaller sequence lengths were used during teacher inference.
bears_on: caching logits for offline distillation

claim: rStar-Coder puts its Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B starting point at 6.5% on its own LiveCodeBench evaluation, not 6.1; rStar-Coder SFT takes it to 40.1%. The 6.1 does not appear in rStar-Coder, so pairing it with rStar-Coder's 40.1 mixes two evaluation setups.
quote: For instance, Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, originally at only 6.5% accuracy on LiveCodeBench, improved dramatically to 40.1% with rStar-Coder, even outperforming GPT-4o and R1-Distill-Qwen1.5B.
wiki_says: rStar-Coder's 1.5B reaches 40.1 on LiveCodeBench and 88.4 on HumanEval, against 6.1 and 70.7 for Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct.

claim: rStar-Coder-1.5B scores 88.4 on HumanEval, +17.7 over its base (so the base scores 70.7), and 40.1 on LiveCodeBench, +33.6 (base 6.5); HumanEval+ is 81.7 (+16.5), while MBPP and MBPP+ gain only +8.9 and +1.5 (74.1 and 60.8).

For synthetic problems with no oracle solution, rStar-Coder samples 16 long-reasoning solutions from QWQ-32B, runs each on a shared set of at least 50 test inputs, and accepts both the outputs and the solutions that produced them when a majority of solutions produce identical outputs across the whole input set.
quote: As illustrated in Fig. 4, for each problem, we first sample 16 long-reasoning candidate solutions using a frontier reasoning model (QWQ-32B [29]). We then sample a diverse set of at least 50 test inputs with varying complexities. Each candidate solution is executed on this shared set of test inputs to generate the corresponding outputs. If a majority of these candidate solutions produce identical sets of outputs across this entire set of test inputs, then both these consistent sets of outputs and the candidate solutions that generated them are considered correct.

claim: The 96.8% output-label accuracy, against 12.7% when GPT-4o generated input-output pairs directly, was measured on 64 expert-written seed problems that have oracle solutions (3,150 test inputs), labeling each input by majority vote over QWQ-32B solutions and comparing with the oracle's output; it is measured on seed problems, not on the synthetic problems the mechanism serves.
quote: To evaluate its effectiveness, we randomly sample 64 expert-written seed problems with oracle solutions and collect all their test inputs (3,150 in total). For each input, we label test outputs using mutual verification: long CoT solutions from QWQ-32B are executed to produce outputs, and majority voting is applied to determine the final label. These outputs are then compared against ground-truth outputs obtained by running the oracle solutions. As a baseline, we prompt GPT-4o to directly generate input-output pairs, following prior work [31, 12] (see Prompt in Appendix Fig. 10). As shown in Table 5 (Left), mutual verification achieves 96.8% accuracy, while the GPT-4o baseline yields only 12.7%

claim: For the 7B model, the full rStar-Coder dataset (580K examples) beat the 37.7K seed problems with 16 solutions each (603K examples): 57.3 against 54.7 on LiveCodeBench and 16.15 against 10.41 on USACO 2025.
quote: Table 6: Ablation on scaling dimensions for the 7B model shows that expanding problem diversity is more effective and efficient than only increasing the number of solutions per problem. | Dataset | Unique Problems | Data size | LiveCodeBench | USACO 2025 | |-----------------------------|-------------------|-------------|-----------------|--------------| | Seed Problems× 1 solutions | 37.7K | 37.7K | 40.8 | 0.52 | | Seed Problems× 8 solutions | 37.7K | 302K | 51.1 | 3.64 | | Seed Problems× 16 solutions | 37.7K | 603K | 54.7 | 10.41 | | rStar-Coder dataset | 480K | 580K | 57.3 | 16.15 |

claim: On the same 37.7K seed problems, raising solutions per problem from 1 to 8 to 16 took the 7B model from 40.8 to 51.1 to 54.7 on LiveCodeBench (USACO 0.52, 3.64, 10.41): repeated sampling alone gave 13.9 points, and moving to the diverse dataset added 2.6 more (57.3) at slightly smaller size. Both axes help; the table also lists 480K unique problems where the text says 418K.
quote: Table 6: Ablation on scaling dimensions for the 7B model shows that expanding problem diversity is more effective and efficient than only increasing the number of solutions per problem. | Dataset | Unique Problems | Data size | LiveCodeBench | USACO 2025 | |-----------------------------|-------------------|-------------|-----------------|--------------| | Seed Problems× 1 solutions | 37.7K | 37.7K | 40.8 | 0.52 | | Seed Problems× 8 solutions | 37.7K | 302K | 51.1 | 3.64 | | Seed Problems× 16 solutions | 37.7K | 603K | 54.7 | 10.41 | | rStar-Coder dataset | 480K | 580K | 57.3 | 16.15 |
bears_on: distinct problems vs many solutions per problem

claim: rStar-Coder's scores, its 1.5B model's included, come from long-reasoning SFT decoded at temperature 0.6 with up to 32k output tokens, pass@1 averaged over 16 samples per problem: here a 1.5B student did gain from long chain-of-thought data, at a large inference budget.
quote: For inference, we set temperature of 0.6, maximum output length to 32k tokens. To mitigate performance variance inherent in single-run evaluations, we sample 16 solutions per problem and report the average pass@1 accuracy for all benchmarks.
bears_on: short answers vs long traces for 1.5B students

claim: Of 1,565,632 synthesized problems, 380,560 passed mutual verification (about 24%); with 37,754 verified seed problems (of 57,215 collected) the dataset totals 418,314 problems.
bears_on: verified yield of LLM-synthesized problems

claim: rStar-Coder discards a synthetic problem when fewer than 60% of its solutions agree on the outputs, lowering the bar to 40% for problems derived from Codeforces problems rated above 1600 so that harder problems survive.
quote: Specifically, if fewer than 60% of solutions agree on the outputs, the problem is discarded. For problems synthesized based on Codeforces problems, we use the original cf_rating to identify hard problems (cf_rating > 1600) and adjust the threshold to 40% to include harder problems.
bears_on: acceptance threshold for agreement-labeled tests

claim: rStar-Coder also keeps unverified traces: for seed problems where QWQ-32B produces no correct solution, all its generated solutions go into the training data.
quote: For particularly challenging problems where QWQ-32B fails to produce a correct solution, we follow prior work [26, 2] and retain all generated solutions to include more diverse and potentially correct intermediate reasoning steps in the training data.
bears_on: filtering teacher output by correctness

claim: Generating test inputs through LLM-written generator and validator functions, instead of prompting GPT-4o for inputs, raised the downstream LiveCodeBench score from 42.9 to 44.6 (hard problems 10.6 to 12.6).
quote: | GPT-4o verification | 12.7%      | GPT-4o prompting            |                      42.9 |                   87.3 |                     54.1 |                   10.6 | | Dual verification   | 96.8%      | Three-step input generation |                      44.6 |                   87.7 |                     56.5 |                   12.6 |
bears_on: test-input generation for the verifier

claim: OpenThoughts' answer-filtering ablation (its Table 7 shows math data) found that filtering answers, by majority consensus, response length and other methods, did not improve on training on all samples.
quote: Table 7: Filtering answers did not improve over not filtering at all. Using verification techniques such as majority consensus filtering or response-length-based filtering did not improve upon training on all samples.

claim: The unfiltered baseline that no filter beat was not compute-controlled: it trained on all 63,200 answers while every filtered set was cut to 31,600, so 'did not improve over not filtering' compares half the data with all of it, not filtered with unfiltered data at equal size.
quote: To ensure that we can still obtain datasets of size 31,600 after filtering, we first generate 63,200 answers, apply each answer-filtering strategy, and then sample 31,600 question-answer pairs from the filtered dataset. Our ablations also include a baseline with no filtering, which is not compute-controlled, as it contains 63,200 questions.
wiki_says: The 2025 reasoning-distillation literature found that filtering teacher traces for correctness "did not improve over not filtering at all".

claim: At equal size on code data, LLM-judged correctness filters slightly beat random filtering: majority consensus averaged 41.3 and GPT verification 40.7 (code average 25.5) against 39.8 (code 25.1) for random filtering, while the twice-larger unfiltered set scored 42.2. The converted table fuses each value with its standard error, so '40.70.4' reads 40.7 with error 0.4.
quote: | No Filtering                        | 42.20.5   |                                                 |                                                         |                                                 | | Shortest Answers Selection          | 42.00.5   |                                                 |                                                         |                                                 | | Python Tag Based Selection          | 41.70.5   |                                                 |                                                         |                                                 | | Majority Consensus Selection        | 41.30.5   |                                                 |                                                         |                                                 | | Longest Answers Selection           | 41.00.4   |                                                 |                                                         |                                                 | | GPT Verification                    | 40.70.4   | 25.50.4                                         |                                                         | 44.21.0                                         | | Removing Non-English Answers        | 40.60.4   | 26.20.5                                         | 54.51.1                                                 | 41.60.6                                         | | Random Filtering                    | 39.80.4   | 25.10.5                                         | 52.21.1                                                 | 43.00.5                                         |
bears_on: whether correctness filtering helps at equal data size

claim: The one execution-based filter tested used LLM-generated unit tests, not ground-truth tests: keeping only the 16,000 code examples that passed them gave 36.0 on LiveCodeBench against 38.5 for an unfiltered random sample (CodeElo 9.4 vs 10.7, CodeForces 10.4 vs 13.54).
quote: Table 18: Effect of using LLM-Generated unit tests for code data verification. Downstream performance of models trained on 16,000 code examples: one set filtered to include only samples verified by LLM-generated unit tests, and the other unfiltered. No improvement is observed from verification-based filtering. | SFT Datasets - Datasets | Benchmarks - LiveCodeBench | Benchmarks - CodeElo | Benchmarks - CodeForces | |----------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------|---------------------------| | Verified via Unit Tests | 36.0 | 9.4 | 10.4 | | Unfiltered (Random Sample) | 38.5 | 10.7 | 13.54 |
bears_on: LLM-written tests vs a real verifier as the filter

claim: Verification of OpenThoughts-114K helped the 32B student (average 64.5 verified vs 62.1 unverified; code 45.8 vs 43.8) but hurt the 7B one (45.0 unverified vs 41.9 verified; code 24.2 vs 21.8): the value of filtering depended on student size.
quote: Table 15: Impact of Verification on original OpenThinker models. We see verification hurts at the 7Bmodel scale but helps at the 32Bmodel scale. | Models | Average | Code Avg | Math Avg | Science Avg | |--------------------------------------------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------| | OpenThinker-32B OpenThinker-32B-Unverified | 64.50.3 62.10.3 | 45.80.3 43.80.4 | 83.71.0 81.40.9 | 63.70.2 60.50.3 | | OpenThinker-7B-Unverified OpenThinker-7B   | 45.00.4 41.90.6 | 24.20.3 21.80.5 | 64.60.9 62.01.9 | 46.90.6 41.90.6 |
bears_on: correctness filtering vs student size

claim: The stronger model was not the better teacher: QwQ-32B traces beat DeepSeek-R1 traces by 1.9 points of average accuracy for code questions and 2.6 for math, although QwQ-32B scores lower than DeepSeek-R1 on the benchmarks.
quote: Across all domains, using QwQ-32B as a teacher model outperforms all other teacher models, yielding an average accuracy improvement of 1.9% and 2.6% over using DeepSeek-R1 as a teacher for code and math, respectively. This is despite the fact that QwQ-32B scores lower on average when compared to DeepSeek-R1.
bears_on: choosing the teacher

claim: Shortening traces hurt the OpenThoughts student: with mean trace length 11593 tokens the benchmark average was 51.4 (LiveCodeBench 40.7); stripping self-reflection (mean 328 tokens) cut it to 26.3, -49.1% relative (LiveCodeBench 19.2); dropping traces over 2048 tokens gave 34.2, -33.3% (LiveCodeBench 26.9).
bears_on: short answers vs long traces

claim: For OpenThoughts' code data, many teacher answers per question matched many questions: one answer per question without deduplication scored only 0.7 points below exact deduplication with 16 answers per question, and the paper calls the combinations similar.
quote: For code and science data, various combinations of deduplication and multiple answer generation yield similar results. For example, the baseline of no deduplication with 1× answer per question performs 0.7 points worse on average than exact deduplication with 16× answers per question for the code domain.
bears_on: distinct problems vs many solutions per problem

claim: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on 151,251 solutions labeled incorrect scored 52.3 on LiveCodeBench against 47.0 for 151,251 labeled correct (CodeContests 15.53 vs 15.34); the unfiltered 445,618 scored highest, 54.1 (CodeContests 16.59).
quote: Table 3: Evaluation results of finetuning Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on execution filtered subsample of OPENCODEREASONING, pertaining to CodeContest training dataset. | Filtering | Dataset Size | LiveCodeBench | CodeContests | |---------------------|----------------|-----------------|----------------| | No Filtering | 445,618 | 54.1 | 16.59 | | Correct Solutions | 151,251 | 47.0 | 15.34 | | Incorrect Solutions | 151,251 | 52.3 | 15.53 |

claim: OpenCodeReasoning attributes the advantage of incorrect solutions to their covering harder questions than the correct ones.
quote: Investigating further, we identified that incorrect solutions span questions that are more challenging than the ones associated with the correct solutions.

claim: OpenCodeReasoning is pure sequence-level distillation: its models use SFT only and reach 61.8% on LiveCodeBench and 24.6% on CodeContests (best model), above RL-trained alternatives.
quote: Our distilled models use only SFT to achieve 61.8% on LiveCodeBench and 24.6% on CodeContests, surpassing alternatives trained with reinforcement learning.

claim: OpenCodeReasoning trained only 7B, 14B and 32B Qwen2.5 students (the incorrect-solution ablation at 14B); none of its results is tested at the student size this project targets.
quote: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5 base and instruct LLMs (7B, 14B, and 32B) with OPENCODEREASONING significantly outperformed R1-Distill-Qwen and other open-weight SFTonly models.
bears_on: student size

claim: LiveCodeBench kept rising up to 736k samples with no plateau, and the largest gains came from adding unique, varied and difficult questions.
quote: It is to be noted that the scaling curve in Figure 3 does not plateau despite the use of 736k samples, and it remains to be seen when the model's improvement will saturate and yield diminishing returns. The most significant gains in benchmark scores were observed by simply increasing the number of unique, varied, and difficult questions.
bears_on: data scale and problem diversity

claim: Adding 356k C++ traces to the Python set had no positive effect on the Python benchmarks but significantly improved the C++ benchmark (IOI): the second language's data helped that language only.
quote: Consequently, we explored the inclusion of 356k C++ samples, generated by R1, in conjunction with OPENCODEREASONING. In addition to LiveCodeBench and CodeContest, we evaluated on the IOI benchmark (Penedo et al., 2025b), which requires C++ solutions. The results are presented in Table 4. It is evident that the inclusion of C++ solutions has no positive impact on Python benchmark performance, but does significantly improve the accuracy on the C++ benchmark.
bears_on: mixing a second language's data

claim: Hard problems often exhausted a 16k-token reasoning budget, yet raising it to 32k gave no substantial gain on them, and long traces sometimes fell into reasoning loops that consumed all available tokens without producing a solution.
quote: During evaluation, we observed that a significantly larger token budget is required for hard problems, as models often did not complete their reasoning phase within 16k tokens. However, extending this budget to 32k tokens did not translate to improved accuracy. In fact, no substantial performance gains were observed on the hard problems. Our findings corroborate Wang et al. (2025) that suggests LLMs tend to be incorrect with more tokens, possibly due to increased backtracking in incorrect solutions (more analysis in the next section). Finally, as a consequence of long reasoning traces, models sometimes enter an unrecoverable reasoning loop, consuming all available tokens while repeating reasoning steps instead of producing a solution.
bears_on: long traces and generation budget

claim: The correct/incorrect labels behind the filtering ablation came from at most 50 tests per problem, out of an average of 192.7 generated tests, to save compute.
quote: Given an average of 192.7 generated tests per problem and a 445k sample dataset, we limited tests to 50 to reduce computational cost.
bears_on: how the incorrect-trace result was labeled

claim: Bridge-Coder compares fine-tunes of DeepSeek-Coder-Base on M-HumanEval and M-MBPP in R, D, Bash and Racket: DG is the base fine-tuned on directly generated target-language data, BC the base fine-tuned with the Bridge-Coder pipeline.
quote: Table 2: Comparison of different models across M-HumanEval and M-MBPP (R, D, Bash, Racket). All models are based on DeepSeek-Coder-Base. DeepSeek-Coder-DG is obtained by fine-tuning DeepSeek-Coder-Base using data generated through direct generation, while DeepSeek-Coder-BC is derived from our Bridge-Coder framework.

claim: The 14.78-21.73-point M-HumanEval gains are DeepSeek-Coder-BC over the untuned DeepSeek-Coder-Base, from the whole pipeline (bridge-generated data plus two-stage training). Fine-tuning the same base on directly generated data (DG) already gains 7.03-12.75; the bridge's own share, BC minus DG, is 5.73 (Bash) to 11.55 (R) points: R 49.11-37.56 = 11.55, D 35.51-27.76 = 7.75, Bash 42.99-37.26 = 5.73, Racket 41.57-30.95 = 10.62, average 42.30-33.38 = 8.92.
wiki_says: Putting a commented Python solution in the teacher's prompt raised low-resource HumanEval scores by 14.8-21.7 points.

claim: On M-MBPP the pipeline gains 7.16-12.68 points over the untuned base (10.81 on average), but over direct-generation fine-tuning only 1.57 (Bash: 35.83-34.26) to 9.61 (Racket: 43.57-33.96), 5.50 on average (43.36-37.86).
bears_on: size of the bridge effect

claim: Training first with the bridge solution in the student's input and then without it (bridged alignment) averaged 42.31 on R and D, against 37.54 training only without the bridge, 38.40 only with it, and 35.38 training on the bridge and target solutions as separate examples.
quote: Table 3: Comparison of training methods. | TrainingMethods | R | D | Avg | |--------------------|-------|-------|-------| | Separate Alignment | 46.89 | 23.87 | 35.38 | | Direct Alignment | 42.63 | 32.45 | 37.54 | | Assist Alignment | 42.93 | 33.87 | 38.40 | | Bridged Alignment | 49.11 | 35.51 | 42.31 |
bears_on: SFT format: Python reference in the input as a curriculum

claim: General-purpose models made better data generators than code-specific ones for both bridge synthesis and transfer: General/General averaged 32.85 on R and D, Code/Code 28.08.
quote: Table 4: Comparison of code-specific models (Code) and general-purpose models (General) in different combinations of Code-Bridge Synthesis and Guided Code Transfer. Bold indicates the best result, and underline indicates the second-best result. | Synthesis | Transfer | R | D | Avg | |-------------|------------|-------|-------|-------| | Code | Code | 29.56 | 26.61 | 28.08 | | Code | General | 32.22 | 27.50 | 29.86 | | General | General | 37.53 | 28.16 | 32.85 | | General | Code | 34.23 | 25.90 | 30.07 |
bears_on: teacher choice for a new language

claim: Python was the best bridge language: 47.61 on R and 33.87 on D, against 44.29 and 30.62 for C++ and 46.47 and 31.93 for Java.
quote: Table 6: Further Analysis of different Programming Languages used in Bridge-Coder. | Code-Bridge HRPL | R | D | |--------------------|-------|-------| | Python | 47.61 | 33.87 | | C++ | 44.29 | 30.62 | | JAVA | 46.47 | 31.93 |
bears_on: which language to put in the teacher prompt

claim: As the assist in training, code with comments (NL + PL) averaged 40.11 on R and D, code alone 37.61, comments alone 35.81.
quote: Table 5: Comparison of different assist formats in the phase of Assist Alignment. | Assist Format | R | D | Avg | |-----------------|-------|-------|-------| | PL | 42.64 | 32.57 | 37.61 | | NL | 40.89 | 30.72 | 35.81 | | NL + PL | 44.71 | 35.51 | 40.11 |
bears_on: commented reference vs bare code

claim: Instruction tuning on Python-heavy data (the Magicoder models) left the base model worse on D and Bash, so generic code SFT can cost a low-resource target language.
quote: For instance, Magicoder-DS and Magicoder-S-DS even perform worse than their baseline model DeepSeek-CoderBase [Guo et al., 2024] in D and Bash.
bears_on: Python-heavy SFT and the target language

claim: SelfCodeAlign beat GPT-4o distillation at equal data size on the same instructions, not at equal budget: GPT-4o wrote each response at temperature 0, while self-alignment sampled several responses and kept those passing their tests, which the authors describe as more post-validation compute.
quote: Additionally, SelfCodeAlign outperforms direct distillation, where we use the same set of SelfCodeAlign instructions but rely on GPT-4o [49] to generate each response at temperature 0. This suggests that weaker models, combined with more post-validation compute, can produce higher-quality responses.
wiki_says: A model's own sandbox-verified outputs beat direct GPT-4o distillation at equal budget.

claim: With CodeQwen1.5-7B as the base and 74k examples each, pass@1 (HumanEval+, per the text) was 67.1 for SelfCodeAlign, 65.9 for direct GPT-4o distillation, 61.6 for OSS-Instruct and 59.1 for Evol-Instruct (both GPT-3.5-Turbo): a 1.2-point margin over GPT-4o on one benchmark.
quote: Table 11: SelfCodeAlign versus distillation using CodeQwen1.5-7B as the base model. | Method | Dataset size | Teacher model | Execution filtering | Pass@1 | |---------------------|----------------|-----------------|-----------------------|----------| | Evol-Instruct | 74k | GPT-3.5-Turbo | | 59.1 | | OSS-Instruct | 74k | GPT-3.5-Turbo | | 61.6 | | Direct distillation | 74k | GPT-4o | | 65.9 | | SelfCodeAlign | 74k | CodeQwen1.5-7B | | 67.1 |

claim: Self-generated data beats a teacher's only when the teacher is not much stronger. StarCoder2-3B, the smallest model tested, scored 35.4 on its own data and 34.1 on Llama-3-8B's, but 42.1 on DeepSeek-Coder-33B's: a weak student with a clearly stronger teacher available learns more from the teacher.
quote: However, when the teacher model is clearly stronger, the base model learns better by distilling the teacher's knowledge. For example, StarCoder2-3B achieves higher pass@1 trained on its own data (35.4) compared to Llama-3-8B data (34.1), but when tuned with stronger models, StarCoder2-3B further improves (e.g., 42.1 with DeepSeek-Coder-33B data).
wiki_says: A quantized Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with the spec in context can serve as a local teacher, and the student itself can run SelfCodeAlign-style rounds of generate, verify and retrain.

claim: Unlike OpenThoughts and OpenCodeReasoning, SelfCodeAlign found execution filtering mattered: at 15.6k examples, responses passing their self-written tests scored 65.2 pass@1 on HumanEval+, random responses 61.6 (also 61.6 at 27.7k), failing ones 57.9; only 24.1% of raw responses passed.
quote: Table 9: Pass@1 on HumanEval+ with different response selection strategies. | Selection strategy | Data size | Execution pass rate | Pass@1 | |---------------------------|-------------|-----------------------|----------| | Random selection (all) | 27.7k | 24.1% | 61.6 | | Random selection (subset) | 15.6k | 24.2% | 61.6 | | Failures only | 15.6k | 0% | 57.9 | | Passes only | 15.6k | 100.0% | 65.2 |
bears_on: execution filtering of self-generated data

claim: The model writes its own tests, so a passing response may only pass wrong tests; the authors leave test validity open and suggest the discarded failing responses could feed a reinforcement-learning loop.
quote: Second, we gather several negative samples during response generation, which are currently filtered out. These negatives could be used in a reinforcement-learning loop to steer the model away from incorrect responses [31, 53]. Furthermore, the good responses are labeled by test execution, while the generated unit tests might be erroneous, calling for research to study and improve the generation of valid test cases.
bears_on: self-written tests as the verifier

claim: On 4 A100s, one pass from 37k seeds took 6h of generation and 16min of fine-tuning for StarCoder2-3B (12k examples kept) and 7h and 30min for CodeQwen1.5-7B (16k kept): generation, not training, dominates the cost.
quote: Table 12: End-to-end data generation time cost on 4×A100 | Base model | Seed data | Produced data | Generation cost | Finetuning cost | |--------------------|-------------|-----------------|-------------------|-------------------| | Llama-3-8B | 37k | 11k | 7h | 20min | | CodeQwen1.5-7B | 37k | 16k | 7h | 30min | | StarCoder2-15B | 37k | 15k | 12h | 2.5h | | StarCoder2-3B | 37k | 12k | 6h | 16min |
bears_on: local-GPU cost of self-generated data

claim: Generating tasks from concepts extracted from filtered seed functions, rather than directly from the seed, raised pass@1 on HumanEval+ from 59.8 to 65.2; random snippets as seeds with concept extraction gave 64.0.
quote: Table 10: Pass@1 on HumanEval+ using different seeds and pipelines. | Source of seeds | Pipeline | Pass@1 | |--------------------|-----------------------------|----------| | Filtered functions | Seed→ instruction | 59.8 | | Random snippets | Seed→concepts → instruction | 64.0 | | Filtered functions | Seed→concepts → instruction | 65.2 |
bears_on: task generation for a new language

claim: MojoBench's continued-pretraining corpus is 6,583,948 tokens (6.58M) after the last of its six filters, an English-language filter with a fastText confidence threshold of 0.4.
quote: F6 Applies language filtering using fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017), retaining English text with a confidence threshold of 0.4, yielding the final corpus, MC*, with 6,583,948 tokens.

claim: On HumanEval-Mojo pass@1, CodeGemma went from 5.1% to 36.7% after continued pretraining on the Mojo corpus and to 66.4% after SFT.
quote: | Candidates    | HumanEval-Mojo pass@1   | |---------------|-------------------------| | CodeGemma     | 5.1%                    | | CodeLLaMA     | 4.7%                    | | Mistral       | 1.3%                    | | CodeGemma-pt  | 36.7%                   | | CodeLLaMA-pt  | 34.4%                   | | Mistral-pt    | 23.1%                   | | CodeGemma-ft  | 66.4%                   | | CodeLLaMA-ft  | 54.2%                   | | Mistral-ft    | 26.9%                   |

claim: The 3,200 SFT pairs are 800 expert-selected Mojo code samples, each with four prompts (GPT-4o paraphrases refined by experts): 800 distinct solutions, not 3,200.
quote: Expert programmers review these, ultimately selecting 800 highquality samples, discarding any that are buggy or too lengthy. For prompt generation, we apply an AI-in-theloop approach using GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) via the OpenAI API, producing three paraphrases per prompt. This results in 3,200 prompt-code pairs, with iterative expert refinement yielding four distinct prompts per snippet.

claim: In the ablation grid, SFT alone on 3,200 pairs reached 42.3, above pretraining alone on 6M tokens (36.7), and both together 66.4; the grid is not monotonic (with 1500 pairs, 46.7 at 5M tokens but 44.5 at 6M; with 3000 pairs, 56.7 at 3M but 55.1 at 4M).
bears_on: continued pretraining vs SFT for a new language

claim: Off-the-shelf models writing Mojo usually got the algorithm right and the syntax wrong.
quote: When prompted to write code in Mojo, the models often get the algorithm right for the tasks but the syntax wrong. This is likely due to their exposure to lots of PLs but just not Mojo.
bears_on: failure modes in an unseen language

claim: The base model mattered: after pretraining and SFT the code models reached 66.4% (CodeGemma) and 54.2% (CodeLLaMA), while the general Mistral went from 1.3% to 23.1% to only 26.9%.
quote: | Candidates    | HumanEval-Mojo pass@1   | |---------------|-------------------------| | CodeGemma     | 5.1%                    | | CodeLLaMA     | 4.7%                    | | Mistral       | 1.3%                    | | CodeGemma-pt  | 36.7%                   | | CodeLLaMA-pt  | 34.4%                   | | Mistral-pt    | 23.1%                   | | CodeGemma-ft  | 66.4%                   | | CodeLLaMA-ft  | 54.2%                   | | Mistral-ft    | 26.9%                   |
bears_on: choosing the base model

claim: Continued pretraining took about 32 hours on 8 A100 GPUs with 40 GB each; SFT took about 9 hours on a single 40 GB A100.
quote: Pretraining For the pretraining phase, we utilize a cluster of 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 40 GB memory, provided by Lambda Labs 9 . This configuration yields a total of 320 GB GPU memory, complemented by 512 GB system memory and 2 TB disk space. The pretraining process spans approximately 32 hours on this highperformance cluster. Finetuning The finetuning stage is conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with 40 GB memory, accessed through Google Colab 10 . This setup is augmented with 80 GB system memory and 256 GB disk space. The finetuning process requires approximately 9 hours to complete on this configuration.
bears_on: compute budget

claim: Mojo-Coder's SFT used LoRA at rank 64.
quote: where FE and FM are English-only and multilingual finetuning functions, respectively. The LoRA rank r = 64 balances parameter efficiency and model capacity.
bears_on: LoRA rank for language-adaptation SFT

claim: All Mojo-Coder models are about 7B; the authors argue the small datasets suit smaller models, but nothing below 7B was trained, so the recipe is untested at this project's student size.
quote: Furthermore, our models are confined to the ∼7B parameter range, a decision influenced by two primary factors. First, the relatively modest size of our datasets aligns better with smaller models, as larger models might overfit on limited data.
bears_on: transfer of the recipe to small students

claim: AceCoder's rule-based RL reward was binary: 1.0 when every test case of the question passes, 0 otherwise (the paper likens it to Tulu3's and DeepSeek-R1's verifiable reward).
quote: During training, we set the pass rate to be a binary reward, which is 1.0 when all test cases pass, otherwise 0. This is similar to the verifiable reward used in Tulu3 (Lambert et al., 2024a) and DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025).

claim: RL from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Base with the binary rule reward (Reinforce++, not GRPO) raised HumanEval-Plus from 53.0 to 78.0 (+25.0 points) and the average over its nine benchmark columns from 44.4 to 52.3 (+7.9); LiveCodeBench V4 moved 28.7 to 28.5 (-0.2). The learned-RM reward reached 75.6 on HumanEval-Plus and 49.1 on average.

The base-model RL run took 80 optimization steps (48 H100 GPU hours); the introduction calls the HumanEval-plus gain '25%' and the MBPP-plus gain '6%', which Table 4 shows are absolute points, not relative percent.
quote: we also perform RL training directly from the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-base model and saw a surprising 25% improvement on HumanEval-plus and 6% improvement on MBPP-plus (Liu et al., 2023) with merely 80 optimization steps (48 H100 GPU hours)

claim: RM-based RL did not lose to the rule reward on every starting model. From Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the AceCode-RM reward averaged 51.5 against 50.9 for the binary rule (baseline 49.6); the rule won only from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Base (52.3 vs 49.1) and, narrowly, from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (55.9 vs 55.3). RM-based RL still beat the untrained baseline on average in all three.
