wiki_says: Learned reward models trained on the same test data underperformed the rule-based reward in RL (summary table: 'AceCoder RMs lost to rules | hacked'; opening: 'learned reward models lose to rule-based checks').

claim: The reward-hacking explanation is the authors' hypothesis ('potential reward hacking'), stated for the RL run from the base model, where RM-based RL gave worse results than the rule reward; no hacked outputs are shown.
quote: However, we do find that using reward models for RL tuning can lead to worse results. We attribute this to the potential reward hacking during the tuning process.

claim: AceCoder filtered GPT-4o-mini-imagined tests with one program from a stronger model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct): every test that program failed was removed, then every question left with fewer than 5 tests was dropped as likely ambiguous. The filter is a single model solution, not a reference solution or a majority vote.
quote: we facilitated a stronger coder model Qwen2.5Coder-32B-Instruct (Hui et al., 2024a) as a proxy to perform quality control. Specifically, we prompt it for each xr to generate a program y′ and then run these programs over the test cases to approximate their quality. We removed all test cases ti where the generated solution program y′ could not pass. Furthermore, we removed questions with fewer than 5 tests after filtering, as these questions might be overly ambiguous.

claim: After filtering, a human audit of 40 questions with 5 sampled tests each found 3 of 200 tests invalid (3/200 = 1.5%).
quote: we conducted a human case study by randomly selecting 40 questions, each with 5 randomly sampled test cases, resulting in 200 manually annotated test cases. Encouragingly, only 3 out of these 200 test cases were found invalid upon review
bears_on: residual error rate of model-filtered synthetic tests

claim: AceCoder's RL kept only the hardest 25% of questions (lower average pass rate, higher variance) so groups have diverse outcomes; rollout batch 256, 8 programs per question, training batch 128, learning rate 5e-7, 1 episode, 6 hours on 8 H100s.
quote: We train our model on a subsampled hard version of ACECODE-87K, where we keep the 25% of the questions with lower average pass rates and higher variance. This is to ensure the question is hard and that the sampled programs are diverse enough. For the training hyperparameters, we set the rollout batch size to 256, and 8 programs are sampled per question. The training batch size is 128 with a learning rate of 5e-7. All the models are trained for 1 episode and finished in 6 hours on 8 x H100 GPUs.
bears_on: task-pool selection and RL budget

claim: From the already strong Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, binary-rule RL moved the average only from 55.2 to 55.9 and lowered HumanEval-Plus from 86.0 to 84.8 (RM reward: 55.3 and 84.1); the limitations section attributes the small gain to the model's strong starting ability and reward noise.
bears_on: RL gains shrink on an already strong checkpoint

claim: The authors concede that filtered synthetic tests can come from a wrong reference or be too simple to catch edge cases, so passing all tests does not guarantee correctness and the RL signal is noisy.
quote: These errors may stem from an incorrect reference solution or test cases that are too simple, failing to capture challenging edge cases. Consequently, passing all test cases does not necessarily guarantee a program's correctness, leading to noise in the reward model training and reinforcement learning (RL) tuning signals.
bears_on: verifier weakness in synthetic test suites

claim: Of 124,006 seed questions with 18.26 imagined tests on average, filtering kept 87,149 questions (87,149/124,006, about 70%) with 15.87 tests on average, from which 307,509 preference pairs were built.
quote: | # Examples | 36,256 | 37,750 | 50,000 | 124,006 | | # Avg Test Cases | 19.33 | 17.21 | 18.27 | 18.26 | | After Filtering | After Filtering | After Filtering | After Filtering | After Filtering | | # Examples | 26,920 | 25,862 | 34,367 | 87,149 | | # Avg Test Cases | 15.14 | 16.33 | 16.08 | 15.87 | | # Pairs | 89,089 | 91,636 | 126,784 | 307,509 |
bears_on: yield of an LLM test-synthesis pipeline

claim: Every run in the pass-rate study trained for 768 gradient-update steps with 64 problems per batch and N=16 rollouts per problem, strictly on-policy.
quote: We train for 768 gradient-update steps in all experiments. Training employs a batch size of 64 problems, with N=16 rollouts per problem.

claim: RLOO was run only on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (binary 41.0% pass@1 and 58.8% pass@16 vs pass-rate 40.8% and 57.1%); Qwen3-4B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct were trained with GRPO only, so the study has four model-algorithm configurations, not three models times two algorithms.
quote: We replicate the experiments using RLOO. As shown in Figure 1, pass-rate reward again converges to a level nearly identical to the binary baseline. At convergence, the binary reward achieves 41.0% pass@1 and 58.8% pass@16, while the pass-rate reward yields 40.8% and 57.1%, respectively (Table 1).
wiki_says: A controlled 2026 study ran GRPO and RLOO on three base models for 768 steps.

claim: The 0.6-2.0 range is the pass@4 to pass@16 gap of one configuration, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with GRPO (averaged over LiveCodeBench and LeetCodeDataset): -0.6, -1.2 and -2.0 at pass@4, 8 and 16 (pass@16 55.6 vs 57.6). At pass@1 that configuration's pass-rate reward finished 0.3 above binary (40.9 vs 40.6).
wiki_says: Pass-rate rewards learned faster at first but ended 0.6-2.0 points below binary at convergence (for example pass@16 of 55.6 against 57.6); summary table: 'pass-rate study -0.6 to -2.0'.

claim: On Qwen3-4B with GRPO the pass-rate deficit exceeded the survey's range at every k: pass@1 44.2 vs 46.4 for binary (-2.2) and pass@16 56.8 vs 59.1 (-2.3), with -3.0 at pass@1 on LeetCodeDataset alone.
wiki_says: Pass-rate rewards ended 0.6-2.0 points below binary at convergence.

claim: The faster early learning of pass-rate reward appeared under GRPO and was muted under RLOO; the authors' plausible explanation is that GRPO's per-group std normalization amplifies partial-pass advantages when full-pass samples are scarce.
quote: As a secondary observation, the early-stage acceleration seen under GRPO is muted under RLOO. A plausible explanation is that GRPO's variance normalization (Equation (6)) can amplify partial-pass advantages when full-pass samples are scarce, whereas RLOO lacks this scaling (Equation (8)).
wiki_says: Pass-rate rewards learned faster at first (stated without an algorithm condition; the opening says raw fraction-of-tests credit 'learns faster at first but finishes lower').

claim: Pass-rate reward can reinforce shortcut solutions (brute-force heuristics, overfitting to the test suite) that reach high pass rates while penalizing near-correct solutions that need minor fixes.
quote: In particular, pass-rate rewards can reinforce solutions that exploit shortcuts (e.g., brute-force heuristics or overfitting to the provided test suite) to achieve high pass rates, while penalizing near-correct solutions that require minor fixes to pass all tests.

claim: In groups with no full-pass sample, a probe of the GRPO update under pass-rate reward moved the log-probability of a verified full-pass reference only negligibly.
quote: Even though pass-rate provides non-binary rewards in this regime, the induced group-level update produces only a negligible change in the log-probability of the full-pass reference solution.

claim: The 57.4% (225 of 392 tasks) counts tasks that contain both a harmful sample with positive advantage and a helpful sample with negative advantage, as labeled by a DeepSeek-R1 judge, on 392 tasks drawn from an early GRPO pass-rate checkpoint whose groups had no full-pass sample and for which DeepSeek-R1 found a full-pass reference.
quote: We also quantify a pattern that directly reflects policy gradient updates. Specifically, we check whether a task contains (i) a harmful sample with positive advantage and (ii) a helpful sample with negative advantage. This is exactly the "push-pull" scenario where optimization increases the likelihood of a harmful mode while decreasing that of a helpful mode. We observe this advantage-sign conflict in 225/392 tasks (57.4%)
wiki_says: In 57.4% of tasks, harmful samples received positive advantage, because partially passing samples in the same group pull gradients in conflicting directions.

claim: Across four judge prompts and two judge models (DeepSeek-R1, GPT-5.4), the conflict rate ranged from 21.5% to 57.5% and the reversal rate from 28.8% to 37.4%; the headline conflict figure comes from the most permissive configuration (DeepSeek-R1 with the baseline prompt).
quote: The reversal signal stays in the 28.8%-37.4% range across every prompt variant and judge model, comparable to the paper baseline of 36.5%. The conflict signal becomes more conservative under stricter rubrics and under GPT-5.4, but remains clearly positive (between 21.5% and 57.5%) in every configuration.
bears_on: how robust the gradient-conflict evidence is

claim: A two-stage schedule (pass-rate reward for the first 256 of 768 steps, then binary) reached 40.6% pass@1 and 57.8% pass@16, and a MiMo-style difficulty-reweighted pass rate 40.4% and 55.3%, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with GRPO; neither offered a significant advantage over binary.
quote: Specifically, we train with passrate reward for the first 256 of 768 steps and switch to binary reward for the remaining training. As illustrated in Figure 1, both variants exhibit learning dynamics similar to standard pass-rate reward and fail to consistently surpass the binary baseline. For the DeepSeekR1-Distill-Qwen-7B + GRPO configuration, reweighted pass-rate achieves 40.4% pass@1 and 55.3% pass@16, while two-stage training reaches 40.6% pass@1 and 57.8% pass@16.
bears_on: phasing partial credit out after a warm-up

claim: Pass-rate reward was genuinely dense: among groups with any reward variance, 77.5% had three or more distinct values and only 22.5% had two, so lack of density does not explain its failure.
quote: only 22.5% of effective groups have two distinct reward values, while the remaining 77.5% contain three or more distinct pass-rate values
bears_on: whether denser rewards fix sparse groups

claim: On the held-out test set binary and pass-rate runs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, GRPO) disagreed on only 23 tasks; binary solved 231 against 224, with 15 tasks solved only by binary and 8 only by pass-rate, so pass-rate reward did not unlock new problems.
quote: Among the 23 disagreement cases, binary solves slightly more tasks overall (231 vs. 224), with 15 tasks solved only by binary and 8 tasks solved only by pass-rate.
bears_on: whether partial credit unlocks unsolved tasks

claim: The study used a constant learning rate of 1e-6, no KL term, no entropy control and temperature 1.0 for training and evaluation, with one gradient update per rollout batch.
quote: We set a constant learning rate of 1e-6 throughout training and apply neither KL regularization nor entropy control. We use a temperature of 1.0 for both training and evaluation
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters for code RL

claim: Code ran in a firejail sandbox with a per-problem timeout set from the canonical solution's runtime times a multiplier of 3, clamped to 10-30 s.
quote: where tcanon is the canonical solution's execution time, S=3 is a time limit multiplier, Tmin=10s, and Tmax=30s.
bears_on: sandbox timeout policy

claim: The 60-70% share of zero-advantage groups under binary GRPO, and VeRPO's below-25%, were measured in the multi-turn setting (up to several attempts with execution feedback), with Qwen3-8B trained on a TACO subset; VeRPO stays below 25% 'for most of training', not throughout.
quote: To better understand the performance gains of VeRPO, we analyze how often rollout groups provide non-degenerate optimization signals in the multi-turn setting. We employ the degenerate group ratio: the fraction of rollout groups with identical rewards, which yield zero relative advantages and thus no policy-gradient signal under group-relative optimization. Fig. 1 (Left) shows that outcomedriven GRPO maintains a high degenerate group ratio, typically between 60% and 70%, indicating that binary outcome rewards discard substantial information from partial execution outcomes. In contrast, VeRPO keeps this ratio below 25% for most of training
wiki_says: 60-70% of groups gave every sample the same reward in a TACO setup with Qwen3-8B; VeRPO cut groups lacking any reward variance from 60-70% to under 25%.

claim: In multi-turn training and evaluation with Qwen3-8B, VeRPO beat binary-reward GRPO by 2.57 on LiveCodeBench v6 (33.07 - 30.50) and by 8.83 on CodeElo Codeforces (40.44 - 31.61).

The +2.57 and +8.83 gains are multi-turn (train and evaluate with execution-feedback retries). In the single-turn setting, the one a one-shot writer would use, VeRPO's average gain over binary GRPO across six benchmarks was +1.26 (and +2.18 over AceCoder-RM rewards).
quote: In the ST→ST setting, VeRPO achieves the best performance across all benchmarks, obtaining an average improvement of +1.26 and +2.18 over the outcome-driven GRPO and the RM-based AceCoder, respectively.
wiki_says: The result was +2.57 LiveCodeBench v6 and +8.83 CodeElo over binary GRPO (no setting stated; summary table: 'VeRPO +2.57 LiveCodeBench v6').

claim: Raw pass rate (PS) and difficulty-weighted credit (Diff) underperformed binary GRPO only when used alone, without the outcome term, and not on every benchmark: alone, PS fell on LiveCodeBench v6 (29.64 vs 30.50) and CodeElo (29.41 vs 31.61) but Diff beat GRPO on CodeElo (35.23 vs 31.61). Combined with the binary outcome advantage, raw pass rate beat GRPO on all five benchmarks (LCB 32.00, CodeElo 35.75).
wiki_says: In the same paper, raw and naively difficulty-weighted partial credit both underperformed the outcome-only baseline.

claim: VeRPO weights each test by exp(-alpha * rho_j), rho_j being the test's empirical pass rate in the group, divided by a kernel density estimate of tests at that pass rate plus a small delta, with alpha = 2; the uncalibrated exp(-alpha * rho_j) variant is the paper's 'Diff' baseline.
quote: Diff uses the uncalibrated difficulty-aware weight wj = exp(-αρj), while VeRPO uses the densitycalibrated weight w′j = exp(-αρj)/( ˆN(ρj) + δ). We set α = 2 for both Diff and VeRPO

claim: VeRPO adds a binary trajectory-level outcome reward (complete test suite passes) to the density-calibrated partial-success reward, to anchor optimization to full correctness.
quote: To anchor optimization to end-to-end functional correctness, VeRPO further incorporates a binary trajectory-level outcome reward

claim: VeRPO's extra computation is 0.10 s per iteration, under 0.02% of total training time, with no extra GPU memory since no reward model or critic is added.
quote: Computing Aturn adds only 0.10s per iteration, accounting for less than 0.02% of total training time, while rollout and policy updates dominate the cost.

claim: On the smaller Qwen3-4B backbone VeRPO also beat binary GRPO: average 55.86 vs 52.33 pass@1, LiveCodeBench v6 36.34 vs 30.05, CodeElo 32.50 vs 29.64 (the appendix does not say whether single- or multi-turn).
quote: Table 7: Additional main results with Qwen3-4B. All values are pass@1 scores. | Method | HumanEval Plus | BigCodeBench Full | LCB V6 | Codeforces CodeElo | Avg | |---| | Qwen3-4B | 83.91 | 49.76 | 20.46 | 25.57 | 44.93 | | GRPO | 90.32 | 59.30 | 30.05 | 29.64 | 52.33 | | VeRPO | 92.84 | 61.76 | 36.34 | 32.50 | 55.86 |
bears_on: calibrated partial credit at smaller model scale

claim: Using AceCodeRM-7B as a dense turn-level reward, multi-turn RL collapsed after about 190 training steps, while binary GRPO and VeRPO stayed stable.
quote: the RM-based AceCoder fails to exhibit a distinct upward trend and succumbs to catastrophic collapse after approximately 190 training steps.
bears_on: learned reward models in RL

claim: Test suites are dominated by easy tests: for 53% of TACO problems under Qwen3-8B, over 90% of the tests already had pass rate above 0.8 before training, and intermediate tests drift toward easy as training proceeds.
quote: for 53% of TACO problems with Qwen3-8B, over 90% of their respective test cases are already easy (ρj > 0.8)
bears_on: test-suite composition and partial credit

claim: VeRPO's runs used 32 problems times 10 responses per rollout batch, 16384-token responses at temperature 1.0, a learning rate of 1 × 10-6, DAPO-style clipping 0.2/0.28 and no KL penalty.
quote: We utilize a rollout batch size of 32 code problems, with 10 responses sampled per problem. We set the maximum response length to 16384, with sampling parameters temperature = 1.0, top-p = 1.0 and top-k = -1.0. The policy learning rate is fixed at 1 × 10-6 . We set clipping parameters ϵlow = 0.2 and ϵhigh = 0.28. All RL methods omit the KL divergence penalty to foster exploration.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters for code RL

claim: In VeRPO's ablation, GRPO-style standard-deviation normalization of advantages consistently underperformed a fixed normalization factor (an unbiased leave-one-out-style estimator), though by less than removing either advantage term.
quote: Finally, replacing the fixed normalization with standard-deviation normalization consistently underperforms VeRPO, but the gap is smaller than those caused by removing either advantage term.
bears_on: advantage normalization choice

claim: CodeRL grades a sampled program by four unit-test outcomes, compile error, runtime error, failed test and passed test, and trains a critic to predict which outcome a program gets.
quote: For each program, the model is trained to predict one of four possible test outcomes: {CompileError,RuntimeError, FailedTest,PassedTest}.

claim: CodeRL used its graded returns relative to a greedy-decoding baseline. On APPS with CodeT5-770M, dropping the baseline (model B) gave the worst pass@1 (1.36 overall), a single sequence-level return with no critic (model A) 1.62, and baseline plus critic (model D) 2.20.
bears_on: relative versus absolute graded rewards

claim: Fine-tuning with the RL loss alone hit vanishing gradients and degraded the models; CodeRL mixed cross-entropy and RL losses with equal weights after a supervised warm start.
quote: Firstly, when we experiment with using only Lrl, we note the problem of vanishing gradients during finetuning, which was similarly observed by Ranzato et al. [2016], Bahdanau et al. [2016]. Therefore, the final models actually deteriorate and lead to performance drops.
bears_on: keeping a supervised term during RL

claim: After CodeRL training, compile errors became rarer, but the share of programs with runtime errors rose: graded credit moved failures from the compile stage to the runtime stage rather than removing them.
quote: Secondly, we note that the percentages of having compiling errors decrease in CodeRL-generated programs, with more effects on interview and competition-level problems. As compiling errors are less likely to occur with CodeRL programs, these programs are still suffered from runtime errors. This leads to a higher probability that a CodeRL program contains runtime errors.
bears_on: compile credit shifting the failure mode

claim: Programs passing the visible example tests often failed the hidden tests; the authors call the example tests less comprehensive and a source of false positives.
quote: This observation suggests that example tests are not as comprehensive as hidden tests and hence, limit the positive impacts of our CodeRL generation procedure due to false positives.
bears_on: visible versus hidden tests in the reward

claim: Over 90% of the compile errors left after CodeRL training were syntax mistakes, with few indentation or tab errors.
quote: The majority of mistakes are syntactical problems, assuming more than 90% of compiling errors.
bears_on: what compile-stage failures look like

claim: CodeRL's inference-time repair model conditions on the problem, the failing program, the test-outcome type and the error subtype taken from compiler traces, and is trained on the RL run's own failed samples paired with the ground truth.
quote: We also include additional signals received from the unit test results, include the type of test outcomes (as defined in the return definitions in Eq. (4) to (7), and error subtypes (e.g. syntax errors, out-of-index
bears_on: repair training on structured diagnostics

claim: Arctic-Text2SQL-R1's GRPO reward uses only final execution correctness and basic syntax validity (executable SQL), unlike Reasoning-SQL, SQL-R1 and Think2SQL, which add n-gram, LLM, schema, length, format or precision/recall terms.
quote: Instead, we define a reward function focused solely on (1) final execution correctness and (2) basic syntax validity

claim: The paper (v2) never says 'more intricate rewards'. Its reward ablation is one sentence: various reward designs gave no significant improvement, and finer-grained designs induced 'lazy' behaviors that chased short-term reward. No reward-ablation table is reported, and the syntax-validity credit itself is never ablated.
quote: Other Observations. We explored variations in rollout count (16, 24, 32), human- or LLM-generated prompts, and various reward designs. None produced significant improvement, and, notably, more fine-grained reward designs induced "lazy" behaviors, where models pursued local optima for short-term rewards rather than global correctness.
wiki_says: Arctic-Text2SQL found that 1 for a correct result, 0.1 for valid executable SQL and 0 otherwise beat "more intricate rewards".

claim: The head-to-head with Reasoning-SQL (BIRD-dev +2.28, Spider-test +5.77, Spider-DK +2.07) changes data filtering and reward design together, so it does not isolate the simple reward's effect.
quote: Under these controlled settings, the two methods differ primarily in training data filtering (Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 uses simple empty-return-based removal, Reasoning-SQL uses LLM filtering) and reward design (our simple execution/syntax signal vs. a complex mixture). As shown in Table 9, Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 outperforms Reasoning-SQL by clear margins on BIRD-dev (+2.28), Spider-test (+5.77), and Spider-DK (+2.07).
bears_on: strength of the simple-reward evidence

claim: QwQ-32B, a reasoning model not tuned for SQL, started over 10 points behind Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and RL could not close the gap; stronger SFT starting points (OmniSQL) consistently gave better RL results.
quote: QwQ-32B is optimized for math and reasoning tasks, e.g., math, but not SQL, and its initial accuracy trailed the Qwen-2.5-Coder-instructed version by over 10 points, a gap RL fine-tuning could not close.
bears_on: SFT before RL and choice of starting checkpoint

claim: Adding unfiltered synthetic tasks lowered performance; keeping only tasks where at least one of ten samples (temperature 1.0) from the best trained model was correct made the synthetic set help.
quote: However, naively adding GretelSynth-NonFiltered to training reduced performance (the first section of Table 4). To remedy this, we employed a model-based filtering-using our best Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Inst-trained model, we retained only queries where at least one of the ten generations (tempearture=1.0) was correct.
bears_on: filtering an RL task pool to solvable tasks

claim: Reference queries that return empty results give spurious rewards; removing them and anything running over five seconds dropped about 1,400 BIRD and 1,700 SPIDER samples and sped up convergence.
quote: We exclude these and filter out samples with execution times exceeding five seconds, markedly reducing overall training time. This straightforward filtering step removed about 1,400 samples from BIRD and 1,700 from SPIDER
bears_on: cleaning reference answers before RL

claim: Arctic's GRPO settings: temperature 0.8, batch 256 with 16 rollouts each, update batch 128 per step, KL penalty 0.001, clip 0.2.
quote: RL-specific settings include a generation temperature of 0.8, a total batch size of 256 (16 rollouts each), an update batch size of 128 per GRPO step, KL penalty β = 0.001, and clip ratio ϵ = 0.2
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters

claim: In VeriReason's ablation, Qwen2.5-1.5B scored 25.6 (base), 38.6 (after SFT) and 44.7 (after SFT then GRPO) on VerilogEval-Machine pass@1; the survey's three numbers are pass@1 on the Machine split. The same stages gave 40.8, 46.3 and 49.1 on Machine pass@5, and 8.2, 17.8 and 23.5 on VerilogEval-Human pass@1.
quote:
| Model | Training Stage | VerilogEval-Machine - pass@1 | VerilogEval-Machine - pass@5 | VerilogEval-Human - pass@1 | VerilogEval-Human - pass@5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | Base + SFT + GRPO | 25.6 38.6 44.7 | 40.8 46.3 49.1 | 8.2 17.8 23.5 | 17.9 23.9 26.7 |

claim: VeriReason's filtered training set holds 1149 hard and 743 easy samples, 1892 in all (1149 + 743), the survey's 1.9K.
quote: Based on the reward, we split the dataset into simple and hard portions for the next training steps. We end up with 1149 samples in the hard level and 743 samples in the easy level.

claim: VeriReason's reward combines testbench functional correctness, syntactic correctness by successful parsing, and an AST score in [0, 1] measuring structural similarity to the reference implementation; the reward's constants sit in an equation the converted text does not carry.
quote: Functional correctness is determined by running the generated code through testbenches and comparing outputs with the expected behavior. Syntactic correctness is verified by successful parsing of the Verilog code. The ASTscore(o) measures structural similarity between the generated code's Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and reference implementations, with values ranging from 0 to 1.

claim: VeriReason keeps only problems whose mean reward over the base model's samples lies between 0.3 and 1.8 and whose reward spread exceeds 0.1, dropping problems that are always failed or always near-perfect: a band filter on reward.
quote: αmin = 0.3 is the minimum acceptable mean reward, αmax = 1.8 is the maximum acceptable mean reward, β = 0.1 is the minimum acceptable reward variance.
bears_on: task pool filtering before GRPO

claim: VeriReason's GRPO settings: temperature 0.5, total batch 16 with 8 rollouts each, update batch 2 per step with gradient accumulation 8, a constant learning rate of 1.0e-6, and repetition penalty 1.3.
quote: RL-specific settings include a generation temperature of 0.5, a total batch size of 16 (8 rollouts each), an update batch size of 2 per GRPO step with a gradient accumulation of 8, a lowered learning rate of 1.0e-6 with constant scheduler type, and repetition penalty of 1.3.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters at 1.5B

claim: The abstract's 83.1% headline is the 7B model's pass@5 on VerilogEval-Machine, not pass@1 and not the 1.5B model.
quote: We observe that VeriReason-Qwen2.5-7B achieves state-of-the-art performance on Machine pass@5 (83.1%), outperforming even GPT-4-Turbo on this metric
bears_on: reading headline numbers: pass@1 versus pass@5

claim: For Qwen2.5-1.5B, GRPO after SFT added 6.1 points of VerilogEval-Machine pass@1 (38.6 to 44.7) but only 2.8 points of pass@5 (46.3 to 49.1), so most of the RL gain is in first-attempt accuracy.
quote:
| Model | Training Stage | VerilogEval-Machine - pass@1 | VerilogEval-Machine - pass@5 | VerilogEval-Human - pass@1 | VerilogEval-Human - pass@5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | Base + SFT + GRPO | 25.6 38.6 44.7 | 40.8 46.3 49.1 |
bears_on: what GRPO adds after SFT at 1.5B

claim: VeriReason states that GRPO yields substantial gains with as few as 20 annotated examples, but no table or experiment in the paper reports that run.
quote: we demonstrate that even with as few as 20 annotated examples from the VeriReason dataset, GRPO yields substantial performance gains
bears_on: minimum RL data for a new language

claim: VeriReason reports significant overhead: many testbench evaluations per training iteration, and reasoning steps that make generation 2.5-3 times slower at inference.
quote: the approach incurs significant computational overhead during both training (requiring numerous testbench evaluations per iteration) and inference (where reasoning steps increase generation time by 2.5-3×)
bears_on: cost of reasoning-style RL for a small coder

claim: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct's CodeContests 1@3 solve rate went from 8.9 to 17.2 on the valid set but from 10.5 to 16.0 on the test set: the doubling holds on the valid set, which also served for checkpoint selection, while the test set gain is about 1.5 times (16.0 / 10.5).
quote:
| Llama 3.1 8B Instruct | Ours | 1@3 | 8.9 | 10.5 |
| + RLEF | Ours | 1@3 | 17.2 | 16.0 |
wiki_says: RLEF roughly doubled Llama 3.1 8B on CodeContests, from 8.9% to 17.2%.

claim: RLEF adds a small penalty for invalid code, introduced because generating invalid code in non-final responses was a failure mode in initial experiments.
quote: In initial experiments we found that a possible failure mode concerns the generation of invalid code in non-final responses, which we address by providing a small penalty for invalid responses.

claim: RLEF shows public-test feedback inside the dialog and gives the episode reward on whether all public and private tests pass.
quote: At the end of an episode, a scalar reward is provided corresponding to whether all public and private tests are passing.

claim: RLEF drops the invalid-code penalty for single-turn training, because there the reward for an incorrect solution already covers invalid code; the penalty only matters for non-final turns.
quote: We use the same training loop for single generations, albeit without the penalty for invalid code (Section 2.2) as this is subsumed by the reward signal for incorrect solutions.
bears_on: invalid-output penalty in a single-turn repair reward

claim: RLEF scores on held-out private tests because a model shown fixed test inputs and outputs in its feedback can learn to copy the expected outputs into later answers.
quote: held-out tests guard against shortcuts during the optimization procedure in which an LLM can copy expected test outputs in subsequent answers, based on execution feedback.
bears_on: reward hacking when feedback reveals expected outputs

claim: Before RLEF, the Instruct models made only minimal edits between turns and often resubmitted the same code despite feedback pointing out errors.
quote: This underscores a shortcoming of the Instruct models without RLEF in that they perform only minimal code edits; indeed, we observe that they frequently output the same code solution despite inline feedback pointing out errors.
bears_on: untrained models in multi-turn repair

claim: A dedicated repair model trained by SFT on the single-turn RL model's failed generations, paired with that model, reached 14.8 (valid) and 12.6 (test) 1@3, above the single-turn model alone (10.2 and 10.9) but below joint multi-turn RLEF (17.2 and 16.0).
quote: Together, the single-turn and repair model obtain 1@3 solve rates of 14.8 on the validation set and 12.6 on the test set; an improvement over the single-turn model alone (10.2 and 10.9) but significantly below the corresponding multi-turn model (17.2 and 16.0).
bears_on: separate repair model versus joint multi-turn RL

claim: SFT of the Instruct models on successful multi-turn trajectories mined from the larger model improved the validation set only, with no test set gain, and RLEF scored significantly higher than SFT.
quote: Supervised fine-tuning improves Instruct model performance on the validation set only; we do not see improvements on the test set.
bears_on: SFT on mined repair trajectories versus RL

claim: An RLEF run took about 20 wall-clock hours on H100 GPUs, using 288 GPUs for the 8B model (128 training, 160 inference) and 2304 for the 70B model.
quote: We train our models on NVidia H100 GPUs; a training run takes approx. 20 wall time hours. With the above parameters we use 288 (128 for traning, 160 for inference) and 2304 (1024 for training, 1280 for inference) GPUs for 8B and 70B models, respectively.
bears_on: compute budget of multi-turn PPO

claim: muCode treats multi-turn code generation as a one-step recoverable MDP: the correct code can be recovered from any intermediate code state in a single turn.
quote: Our key insight is that code generation is a one-step recoverable MDP, where the correct code can be recovered from any intermediate code state in a single turn.

claim: One-step recoverability is argued from the definition (the correctness of the code depends only on the prompt, not on the interaction history), not measured. muCode uses it to replace multi-turn RL with imitation learning: expert iteration in which a learned verifier plus the oracle relabels each turn with the best solution found for that prompt. The paper does not test whether single-step repair training captures most of the multi-turn skill.
quote: this reduces the problem from reinforcement learning, which requires exploration and credit assignment, to imitation learning, where the model simply learns to mimic correct code
wiki_says: muCode showed that code generation is one-step recoverable, so training single-step repair conditioned on feedback captures most of the skill.

claim: With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, muCode raised greedy multi-turn accuracy from 53.8 to 59.0 on MBPP and from 64.5 to 70.5 on HumanEval; rejection fine-tuning reached 57.0 and 66.6.
quote:
Table 4. Comparison of our method µCODE with baselines across MBPP, HumanEval using the Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct model.

| Method | N | MBPP | HE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instruct | 1 | 53.8 | 64.5 |
| +BoN | 5 | 60.9 | 70.3 |
| RFT | 1 | 57.0 | 66.6 |
| +BoN | 5 | 58.0 | 71.3 |
| µCODE | 1 | 59.0 | 70.5 |
bears_on: multi-turn repair gains at 1.5B

claim: Multi-turn rejection fine-tuning fell below the untrained Instruct model, which the authors attribute to training on sub-trajectories whose non-terminal steps contain incorrect code.
quote: Interestingly, the performance of RFT drops when compared to the base Instruct model for the multi-turn setting which can be attributed to the fact that finetuning dataset consists of sub-trajectories with incorrect code solution at non-terminal steps.
bears_on: building SFT data from repair trajectories

claim: To pick among candidates at each turn, public test outcomes beat the learned verifier alone; the best rule ranks by public tests and breaks ties with the learned verifier.
quote: Interestingly, the hierarchical approach (PT+LV) that uses the learned verifier to break ties on the outcomes of public tests performs best across methods and datasets.
bears_on: exact checks versus learned verifiers

claim: With the example tests removed from the MBPP prompt, first-turn accuracy dropped by up to 13% for all methods, and muCode gained 15.9% from turn 1 to turn 6 using execution feedback, recovering its MBPP level.
quote: We observe that the performance at first turn drops for all methods by upto 13%. With the execution feedback at each turn, µCODE improves the code solutions leading to gains of 15.9% from turn 1 to turn 6 and matches its performance on the MBPP dataset.
bears_on: value of execution feedback when the prompt underspecifies

claim: muCode trains on MBPP's 374 training problems, in Python only, and its authors caution that the findings may not generalize to other programming languages.
quote: Additionally, we train models on MBPP, whose training set has only 374 examples. However, we hypothesize that more training examples will lead to better performance. Finally, our datasets are only in Python, and our findings might not generalize to other programming languages.
bears_on: transfer to a new language

claim: The 93% is measured for one model, few-shot prompted pre-trained Qwen2.5-1.5B, and only over cases where its second response is incorrect: there it changed the code minimally (edit distance ratio at most 0.05) 93% of the time, against 32% for Gemini.
quote: This is further supported by Figure 2, where Qwen2.5-1.5B shows minimal changes (edit distance ≤ 0.05) in 93% of cases when the second response is incorrect, compared to only 32% for Gemini.
wiki_says: CoCoS found that untrained 1B-scale models make second attempts that are 93% near-identical to the first.

claim: On MBPP, Qwen2.5-1.5B trained with CoCoS scored 45.0% on its first attempt and 54.2% on its second (incorrect-to-correct 11.0%, correct-to-incorrect 1.8%). 45.0% and 54.2% are the trained model's two turns; the starting Boost model scored 9.0% and 10.2%.
quote:
Table 3: Main results of Qwen2.5-1.5B on the MBPP dataset. The highest accuracy values are highlighted in bold. CoCoS has the highest selective correction rate, correcting incorrect responses without changing correct ones. It also demonstrates strong generalization, achieving high correction success rates even on unseen data.

| Method | Accuracy@t1 | Accuracy@t2 | ∆i→c (t1, t2) | ∆c→i (t1, t2)↓ | ∆Acc (t1, t2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Boost model | 9.0% | 10.2% | 1.2% | 0.0% | 1.2% |
| Turn-SFT | 44.2% | 44.4% | 1.4% | 1.2% | 0.2% |
| Self-Corrector | 43.8% | 48.8% | 11.2% | 6.2% | 5.0% |
| ReVISE | 34.6% | 41.2% | 11.3% | 4.9% | 6.4% |
| Turn-RL | 46.4% | 48.6% | 4.0% | 1.8% | 2.2% |
| COCOS | 45.0% | 54.2% | 11.0% | 1.8% | 9.2% |

claim: CoCoS gives the model no external feedback, neither compiler or test outcomes nor another model's critique, only a fixed revision instruction between turns, so its results measure intrinsic self-correction rather than diagnostic-conditioned repair.
quote: Since we do not consider external feedback (e.g., compiler outcomes, other LMs' feedback), p1:t-1 is fixed for each turn.
bears_on: whether CoCoS evidence transfers to diagnostic-conditioned repair

claim: Trained with a binary all-pass reward, Qwen2.5-1.5B reached 51.2 at turn 2 on MBPP, against 54.2 with the pass-ratio progressive reward, both starting from 45.0 at turn 1; passing tests lost between turns fell from 3.4 to 1.9.
quote:
Table 5: Comparison of progressive vs. binary reward schemes. Qwen2.5-1.5B models are trained under each reward setting and evaluated on MBPP.

| Dataset - Binary / Progressive | Accuracy@t1 - Binary / Progressive | Accuracy@t2 - Binary / Progressive | ∆i→c unit - Binary / Progressive | ∆c→i unit ↓ - Binary / Progressive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MBPP | 45.0 / 45.0 | 51.2 / 54.2 | 10.5 / 11.9 | 3.4 / 1.9 |
bears_on: partial-credit test reward for repair

claim: Rewarding only the improvement r2 - r1 (discount 0) led the model to deliberately lower its first-attempt reward; rewarding only the second response (discount 1) ignored the first turn.
quote: When γ = 0, training focuses on maximizing the reward difference r2 -r1, often by deliberately decreasing r1. When γ = 1, the reward depends only on the second response, disregarding the first turn.
bears_on: reward hacking in improvement-based repair rewards

claim: SCoRe-style training of the small Llama model collapsed to zero reward with first-turn KL regularization and also eventually without it, which the authors attribute to binary rewards on small models.
quote: In the case of Llama, applying KL-regularization leads to a rapid convergence of the reward to zero, similar to what was observed with Qwen. Even without KL regularization, the Llama model eventually collapses. We speculate that this shows a limitation of training SLMs with binary rewards.
bears_on: sparse binary rewards in multi-turn RL for small models

claim: The untrained small Llama model left its response unchanged in 99% of the cases measured (second response incorrect).
quote: Remarkably, the Llama model exhibits an extreme tendency to make no changes to its responses, with a no-edit rate of 99%.
bears_on: untrained small models in multi-turn repair

claim: Used as its own verifier, Qwen2.5-1.5B judged code correctness with 42% accuracy against test outcomes, near random, while the strong teacher model reached 70%.
quote: The Qwen verifier achieves an accuracy of 42%, which is close to random performance in distinguishing correct and incorrect responses. This indicates that small-scale Qwen fails to provide effective feedback, thereby harming rather than improving the initial response. In contrast, the teacher verifier reaches a higher verification accuracy of 70%.
bears_on: small models as their own judges

claim: The 15.1 is absolute points of a seven-benchmark average (five math, two coding) for a Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Base model after SFT: Eurus-2-7B-SFT averages 28.8 and Eurus-2-7B-PRIME 43.9 at step 592 (43.9 - 28.8 = 15.1 points; 43.9 / 28.8 = 1.52, about 52% relative). Outcome-only RLOO already reaches 36.9 at 240 steps, against 41.0 for PRIME at the same step. On the coding benchmarks, LeetCode went from 21.7 to 33.3 and LiveCodeBench from 17.8 to 28.6.
wiki_says: PRIME improved its 7B model by 15.1% on average over the SFT starting point.

claim: PRIME updates a process reward model online using only policy rollouts and outcome labels, through implicit process rewards that give a dense per-token signal.
quote: we propose PRIME (Process Reinforcement through IMplicit rEwards), which enables online PRM updates using only policy rollouts and outcome labels through implicit process rewards.

claim: At 240 steps, implicit process rewards added 4.1 average points to RLOO (36.9 to 41.0), 1.8 to REINFORCE (36.0 to 37.8) and 1.7 to GRPO (36.1 to 37.8); with GRPO, LiveCodeBench fell from 25.8 to 23.9.
bears_on: dense learned reward on top of GRPO

claim: A process reward model that is not updated online loses accuracy during RL as the policy's distribution shifts, so a learned reward needs continual retraining on policy rollouts.
quote: The offline PRM, though starting with high accuracy, gradually drops during RL training procedure due to distribution shift.
bears_on: learned rewards and reward hacking

claim: PRIME reached RLOO's training reward in 40% of the steps, which the authors estimate as 2 times more efficient in wall-clock time despite the extra reward-model update per step.
quote: PRIME only takes 40% of the training steps to achieve the same training rewards as RLOO. This means PRIME would still be 2× more efficient than RLOO when estimated by training time.
bears_on: cost of a learned dense reward

claim: RL straight from the base model (no SFT) converged faster than from the SFT model but saturated early, at about 50 steps, which the authors tie to falling response diversity.
quote: we find it quickly saturated at a very early stage (about 50 steps), which hinders further improvement like in DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025)
bears_on: SFT before RL versus RL from base

claim: On a 1.5B distilled reasoning model, PRIME's first-stage training raised the math test average by 3.1 points.
quote: On testsets, as shown in Table 7, PRIME consistently improves the performance of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B by 3.1 points.
bears_on: PRIME at 1.5B

claim: SWE-RL's rule-based reward is -1 when the response is incorrectly formatted and otherwise the difflib.SequenceMatcher similarity, between 0 and 1, of the predicted patch to the oracle patch; it compares patch text and runs nothing.
quote: If the response is incorrectly formatted, the reward will be -1; otherwise, the reward is a similarity score (between 0 and 1) of the predicted and the oracle patch calculated by Python's difflib.SequenceMatcher

claim: SWE-RL's malformed-output penalty is -1 against a positive reward bounded between 0 and 1, so the penalty is as large as the whole positive range, not a small one; the paper reports no ablation of its size.
quote: If the response is incorrectly formatted, the reward will be -1; otherwise, the reward is a similarity score (between 0 and 1) of the predicted and the oracle patch
wiki_says: The invalid-output penalties that work are small and fixed: RLEF used -0.2 ... and SWE-RL -1 for malformed output.

claim: SWE-RL applied to Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct gives Llama3-SWE-RL-70B, which solves 41.0% of SWE-bench Verified with the Agentless Mini pipeline scaffold.
quote: Applying SWE-RL to Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), our model Llama3-SWE-RL-70B solves 41.0% of the issues in SWE-bench Verified (OpenAI, 2024), a human-verified subset of SWE-bench, with Agentless Mini

claim: As the abstract states it, RL on issue solving alone improved results on five out-of-domain task categories (function coding, library use, code reasoning, mathematics, general language understanding), while the SFT baseline degraded performance on average.
quote: it shows improved results on five out-of-domain tasks, namely, function coding, library use, code reasoning, mathematics, and general language understanding, whereas a supervisedfinetuning baseline even leads to performance degradation on average

claim: Table 3 is not uniform: the RL model improved HumanEval+ (76.2 to 79.9) and CRUXEval-I (60.5 to 71.6) but only matched the base model on BigCodeBench-Hard (28.4 and 29.1, unchanged), so library use did not improve; the SFT model fell on HumanEval+ (73.2) and BigCodeBench-Hard (25.7, 24.3) but rose on CRUXEval-I (68.4). SFT regressed on average, not on every task.
quote: | HumanEval+ | 76.2 | 73.2 | 79.9 | | Library use | | | | | BigCodeBench-Hard (I) | 28.4 | 25.7 | 28.4 | | BigCodeBench-Hard (C) | 29.1 | 24.3 | 29.1 | | Code reasoning | | | | | CRUXEval-I | 60.5 | 68.4 | 71.6 |
wiki_says: RL also improved five out-of-domain tasks, while an SFT baseline regressed.

claim: The SWE-RL authors list as a limitation that the reward compares sequence similarity to the oracle patch rather than semantic equivalence, which may keep the policy from exploring functionally equivalent alternative fixes.
quote: our reward implementation compares the sequence similarity between the predicted and oracle patch rather than their semantic equivalence. This may prevent the policy LLM from exploring alternative, functional equivalent solutions.

claim: The 41.0% headline samples 500 patches per problem at temperature 1.0 and reranks them by executing the top 30 generated reproduction tests; it measures a large sample-and-rerank pipeline, not single-sample repair.
quote: In the main evaluation (§3.2), we generate 500 patches for each problem using a 1.0 temperature, and use the top 30 reproduction tests for execution and reranking.
bears_on: inference budget behind SWE-RL's headline number

claim: In the repair-only setting (oracle files given, one greedy edit), base Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct produced a correctly formatted edit only 12.2% of the time and scored 5.4; the SFT model reached 96.2% format and 29.6; the RL model 95.6% format and 34.8. SFT fixes the format; RL adds 5.2 points of repair (34.8 - 29.6) on top.
quote: | Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct | Greedy decoding | 12.2% | 5.4 | | Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct | Majority voting | 44.6% | 16.6 | | Llama3-SWE-SFT-70B | Greedy decoding | 96.2% | 29.6 | | Llama3-SWE-RL-70B | Greedy decoding | 95.6% | 34.8 |
bears_on: format competence before RL; RL gain over SFT on repair

claim: A discrete exact-match reward (1 if the patch equals the oracle, else 0) trained under the same setup reached 29.0 repair (oracle) against 34.8 for the continuous similarity reward, at similar format accuracy (94.2% vs 95.6%).
quote: | Discrete | 94.2% | 29.0 | | Continuous | 95.6% | 34.8 |
bears_on: dense similarity vs exact-match reward for repair

claim: Training ran 1,600 steps at 16k context with 16 rollouts for each of 32 problems per batch (global batch 512), on 512 H100 GPUs for about 32 wall-clock hours.
quote: using SWE-RL for 1,600 steps with a 16k context window. We use a global batch size of 512, sampling 16 rollouts from each of the 32 problems in every batch. For every global step, a single optimization step is performed using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2017). We train our models on 512 NVIDIA H100 GPUs; a training run takes approximately 32 wall-time hours.
bears_on: compute scale of the published SWE RL result

claim: When the context held only the files the PR modified, the model learned to edit every file it was shown and could not handle noisy files; SWE-RL therefore adds relevant but unmodified files to each prompt.
quote: In our earlier experiments, we noticed that this approach let LLMs learn a bias: the model consistently generated edits for every code file presented and was unable to handle noisy files presented in the context.
bears_on: distractor context in repair training data

claim: SoRFT's localization reward (file, function and line subtasks) is 0 if the extracted localization is empty or contains any target not present in the problem description, otherwise the F-beta score against the ground-truth answer: one absent target zeroes the whole reward, not just that target.
quote: For the localization subtask (line 1-7), we first extract the localization result Oloc from the response. If the localization result is empty or contains a target not present in the problem description, the reward is set to 0; otherwise, the reward is calculated as the Fβ score between Oloc and the ground-truth answer A.

claim: SoRFT also scores code edits by F-beta against the ground-truth edit, with reward 0 when the edit is empty or its search target does not appear in the input. Like the localization rule, it zeroes the whole sample; the survey's SoRFT-style guide table instead drops an off-file location and scores the rest.
quote: For the code editing subtask (line 8-15), we first extract the modification target Osearch and the modification code Oedit from the response. If the modification code is empty or the modification target does not appear in the problem description, the reward is 0; otherwise, the reward is calculated as the Fβ score between Oedit and the ground-truth answer A.
bears_on: repair and guide reward for hallucinated targets

claim: SoRFT weights recall over precision: beta must exceed 1 and is set to 3.
quote: Since recall has a greater influence on the final outcome across different subtasks, β should be a value greater than 1. In our experiments, we set β = 3 to prioritize recall while maintaining a reasonable trade-off with precision.
bears_on: precision/recall weighting in a localization reward

claim: Replacing F-beta with a hit score (1.0 if the answer contains at least one ground-truth element, else 0.0) caused reward hacking: the model wrote fewer thoughts and listed more answers to raise the chance of a hit.
quote: Specifically, if the response contains at least one element from the ground-truth answer, the reward score is set to 1.0; otherwise, it is set to 0.0. As shown in Figure 3a, using the hit score leads to reward hacking, where the model tends to generate fewer thoughts and more answers to increase the likelihood of including a ground-truth element.
bears_on: list-padding hack in localization rewards

claim: On SWE-bench Verified, most of SoRFT's gain comes from the rejection-sampled SFT stage: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct went 7.6 to 18.0 resolved with SFT and to 21.4 with SFT plus RL (applied 55.6, 85.2, 95.6); the 32B model went 25.6 to 28.8 to 30.8.
quote: | Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct | 7.6 | 55.6 | | + SFT | 18.0 | 85.2 | | + SFT + RL (Our SoRFT-Qwen-7B) | 21.4 | 95.6 | | Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct | 25.6 | 84.4 | | + SFT | 28.8 | 90.6 | | + SFT + RL (Our SoRFT-Qwen-32B) | 30.8 | 95.8 |
bears_on: training order and size of the RL increment

claim: SoRFT's authors note that comparing a response to a single ground truth can mark valid alternative resolutions as failures, and suggest unit-test execution as the fairer measure.
quote: The correct resolution to an issue is often not unique. Relying solely on rule-based rewards by comparing the LLM's response to a single ground truth may incorrectly classify valid solutions as failures.
bears_on: reference-match rewards vs executed tests

claim: Raising SFT data from 60k to 90k samples slightly raised resolved rate but lowered the applied rate, and still fell short of SFT plus RL.
quote: Increasing the training data for SFT from 60k to 90k samples slightly improved the %resolved but decreased the %Applied, indicating that excessive SFT might impair the model's generalization ability.
bears_on: diminishing returns of more SFT data

claim: HardTestGen's Type 3 hacking inputs come from generator programs: the LLM lists candidate (likely wrong or inefficient) programs, then writes one input-generation function per candidate aimed at making it fail, each called 10 times.
quote: Therefore, we first prompt an LLM to list several candidate programs for the problem in natural language. Then, we prompt it to generate mH input generation functions, each attempting to cause one candidate program to fail. Each function is called nH = 10 times, generating mH × nH inputs.

claim: On AtCoder problems, judging Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct programs, TACO's tests (with the official test cases removed) reach 69.97 average precision and 72.53 recall; HardTests reach 85.64 precision and 94.77 recall.
On AtCoder problems of difficulty level 4+ (Luogu labels), for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct programs, TACO's tests reach 21.67 precision and 68.42 recall, HardTests 60.00 precision and 94.74 recall.
quote: For example, for the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model on AtCoder problems with difficulty level 4+, TACO achieves a precision of 21.67 and a recall of 68.42, whereas HARDTESTS achieves a precision of 60.00 and a recall of 94.74.

claim: GRPO on Qwen3-4B with the same problems and setup but different tests (binary all-pass reward): on LiveCodeBench-105, pass@1 fell from 38.48 to 36.95 with TACO's tests and rose to 39.42 with HardTests; pass@5 fell 52.04 to 51.01 with TACO, while pass@10 rose under both (57.14 with TACO, 64.76 with HardTests, from 56.19).

All downstream results are on LiveCodeBench-105, a 105-problem C++ stdin subset, so one problem is about 0.95 pass@1 points (100 / 105) and the TACO pass@1 drop in the RL claim is under two problems (2 x 0.95 = 1.9 points); the paper reports no repeated runs.
quote: we build an evaluation pipeline for evaluating C++ programs for LiveCodeBench and select a 105-problem subset where all problems have test cases of
bears_on: strength of the weak-tests-hurt-RL evidence

claim: In teacher distillation (DeepSeek-R1 trajectories into Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct), all 46.6k unfiltered trajectories gave 32.86 pass@1 against 25.24 for the 13k that HardTests judged correct; the filtered set also has fewer questions, so this is quantity against correctness, not a controlled correctness ablation.
bears_on: test-filtering teacher data vs keeping volume

claim: Self-distilling Qwen3-4B on 5k of its own trajectories lowered pass@1 in every variant (38.48 base; 34.00 incorrect-only, 32.75 random, 36.00 verified-correct), while the verified-correct set raised pass@5 (52.04 to 55.15) and pass@10 (56.19 to 60.00).
bears_on: self-distillation and rejection sampling on own outputs

claim: Tests made only of small inputs the LLM writes directly (Type 1) judged AtCoder programs from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with 55.48 average precision at 95.90 recall, and 10.40 precision at the hardest level: LLM-written inputs catch little without generator and hacking inputs.
bears_on: LLM-written tests for synthetic tasks

claim: Among incorrect programs, 30.0% of the LLM-written ones fail by time limit against 14.9% of human-written ones, so tests without large inputs pass more LLM programs wrongly.
quote: among incorrect human-written programs, 14.9% are due to TLE (Time Limit Exceeded), whereas among the incorrect programs written by the three LLMs, 30.0% are due to TLE
bears_on: large inputs and time limits in the grader

claim: HardTests' RL runs used learning rate 5e-7, global batch 32 with 32 samples per rollout, no KL term, on 8 H100 GPUs.
quote: initial learning rate 5e-7. We use a global batch size of 32 and generate 32 samples per rollout. All our experiments are run on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. We do not use KL divergence in our RL loss.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters for code RL

claim: Two configurations of the math-verify library (plain-expression and LaTeX extraction) disagree on 49.9% of certified-equivalent math answer pairs, counted over pairs both returned a verdict on; the pairs are synthetic meaning-preserving rewrites, not model outputs.
quote: Pairwise disagreement on certified-equivalent pairs, computed only over pairs where both verifiers returned a verdict. V1 = mv-expr, V2 = mv-latex, V3 = strip-string, V4 = sympy-cascade. Two configurations of the same library (V1, V2) disagree on 49.9% of cases.

claim: On identical inputs, the four verifiers accept between 53.8% and 95.2% of certified-equivalent answers, a 41.3-point spread.
quote: Acceptance of certified-equivalent variants ranges from 53.8% to 95.2% across the four implementations on identical inputs, a spread of 41.3 points.
bears_on: reporting the verifier configuration

claim: Whitespace and punctuation handling cause 93.0% of in-contract failures for math-verify's LaTeX configuration and 74.1% for the plain-expression one; a trailing period or newline dominates the error budget.
quote: Whitespace and punctuation handling accounts for 93.0% of in-contract failures for the default LaTeX configuration and 74.1% for the plain-expression configuration. A trailing period or a newline, which no reasonable specification treats as semantically meaningful, dominates the error budget.
bears_on: output normalization in a test grader

claim: A relative tolerance of 10^-4 is scale-invariant, so the reference cascade accepts off-by-one wrong answers from a gold of 10,000 upward (10,001 differs by 0.01%); its aggregate off-by-one false-positive rate is 16.0% (n = 1,287).
quote: V4 steps deterministically at 104 : a relative tolerance of 10-4 is scale-invariant, so 10,001 differs from 10,000 by 0.01% and is accepted. Aggregate rate 16.0% (95% CI [14.1, 18.1], n = 1,287).
bears_on: numeric tolerance in the grader

claim: The SymPy cascade returns a verdict on only 87.3% of inputs but is correct on 100% of those it judges; its whole residual is parse failure, which an aggregate rate conflates with rejection.
quote: sympy-cascade returns a verdict on 87.3% of inputs and is correct on 100% of those it judges: its entire residual is parse failure, not equivalence error.
bears_on: separating grader crashes from failed tests

claim: The audit is verifier-level only: it runs no training and does not measure the effect on RLVR outcomes.
quote: No training runs. We do not measure downstream RLVR effect; Zhang (2026) examine hardened versus leaky rewards in code RLVR and find bounded effects.
bears_on: whether verifier disagreement changes training

claim: KodCode labels difficulty by the success rate of GPT-4o's (solution, test) self-verification across 10 attempts per question: easy above 2/3, medium 1/3 to 2/3, hard below 1/3, fail if every attempt fails. The rate measures the generator, not the model being trained.
quote: We analyze the difficulty distribution across KODCODE subsets by examining the success rate of (sol, test) pairs in self-verification across n = 10 attempts per question, as shown in Figure 5. We categorize questions into four difficulty levels: easy (pass rate >2/3), medium (1/3 to 2/3), hard (<1/3), and fail (all failures).

claim: KodCode checks contamination against the benchmarks it evaluates on (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench V5) by embedding cosine similarity, counting a question contaminated above 0.95 similarity to its nearest benchmark question.
quote: We evaluate potential contamination between KODCODE and existing evaluation benchmarks, including HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2024), and LiveCodeBench (V5) (Jain et al., 2024). For each question in KODCODE , we identify the most similar benchmark question using cosine similarity of embeddings, considering a question contaminated if the similarity exceeds 0.95.

claim: Only 94 of 447K questions were flagged, mostly between the simple Prefill subset and HumanEval/MBPP questions: a pool of HumanEval/MBPP-level problems is where overlap with those benchmarks concentrates.
quote: First, the contamination rate is minimal, with only 94 potentially contaminated questions out of 447K. Second, most overlaps occur between the Prefill subset and simple Python questions from HumanEval/MBPP.
bears_on: decontaminating translated HumanEval/MBPP-level tasks

claim: Self-verification kept 80 MBPP solutions (88.9%) and 190 LiveCodeBench-V5 solutions (49.9%); of those kept, 78 of 80 (97.5%, after manual review) and 189 (99.47%) passed the human tests. It is precise, but it drops about half of the harder problems.
quote: After applying our Self-Verification approach, 80 solutions (88.9%) pass self-verification for MBPP, while 190 solutions (49.9%) pass self-verification for LiveCodeBench-V5. We then evaluate these retained solutions against the ground-truth unit tests. We note that due to inherent ambiguity in MBPP questions, some solutions that follow correct logic fail assertions because of mismatched input formats or numerical precision differences. After manual review of these edge cases, 78 out of 80 solutions pass all ground-truth unit tests, achieving a 97.5% pass rate for MBPP. For LiveCodeBench-V5, 189 solutions (99.47%) successfully pass all tests.
bears_on: precision and yield of generate-then-verify data

claim: KodCode keeps a question-solution-test triplet only if the solution passes its generated tests and those tests reach 100% branch coverage of the solution (pytest-cov).
quote: Additionally, we perform branch coverage analysis using the PYTEST-COV framework to ensure the diversity of test cases. Only questionsolution-test triplets that pass self-verification and achieve 100% branch coverage are retained.
bears_on: test validation for generated tasks

claim: With 10K SFT samples each, the hard-labelled subset beat a random subset on BigCodeBench-I Hard (31.8% vs 27.7%, +4.1) and Full (50.6% vs 49.9%, +0.7).
quote: KODCODE-SFTHard-10K outperforms KODCODE-SFT-10K on BigCodeBench-I Hard (31.8% vs. 27.7%, +4.1%) and BigCodeBench-I Full (50.6% vs. 49.9%, +0.7%)
bears_on: selecting hard items for distillation data

claim: KodCode's RL runs GRPO for 256 steps on 9.5K training samples, actor learning rate 5e-7, 16 rollouts per question, batch 256, max response 4096 tokens, KL coefficient 0.001, binary all-tests-pass reward.
quote: using 9.5K randomly selected samples from KODCODEas the training set, and 0.5K as the validation set. We refer to this dataset as KODCODE -RL-10K. We perform GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) for 256 steps with actor learning rate of 5 × 10-7 , 16 rollouts per question, a batch size of 256, max response length of 4096, and apply KL coefficient of 0.001. We assign binary rewards for RL: 1 if the model's solution passes all unit tests, and 0 otherwise.
bears_on: GRPO hyperparameters for code RL

claim: GRPO on KodCode-RL-10K lifted Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct's average from 52.32 to 53.99 at step 256 (+1.67 = 53.99 - 52.32), while LiveCodeBench Medium fell 23.0 to 19.9 and Hard 4.4 to 3.3.
bears_on: size of RL gains on synthetic verified tasks

claim: SWE-smith's bug-strategy ablation sampled 1000 instances per strategy, generated Claude 3.7 Sonnet expert trajectories, and fine-tuned one Qwen 2.5 7B Coder Instruct student per strategy with training points capped at 507 (the smallest successful-trajectory count of any strategy), evaluated on SWE-bench Verified. The paper's own heading for the result is that LM Rewrite and Procedural bugs are comparable to PR mirrors.
quote:
We use Claude 3.7 Sonnet as the expert for fine-tuning Qwen 2.5 7B Coder Instruct, and report the performance on SWE-bench Verified.

LM Rewrite and Procedural bugs are comparable to PR mirrors. We randomly sample 1000 instances per bug generation strategy (LM Modify, LM Rewrite, Procedural Modifications, PR Mirrors). Per instance, we generate issue text with an LM and run expert trajectory generation. We then fine-tune a student model per strategy, capping training points to the minimum number of successful trajectories from any strategy (507) for fair comparison.

claim: In that matched ablation the per-strategy students resolved, on SWE-bench Verified: PR Mirror 9.2% (±1.7), LM Rewrite 8.8% (±1.7), Procedural 8.6% (±1.8), LM Modify 5.7% (±1.5). The successful expert trajectories available per strategy were 557, 507, 745 and 802.

SWE-smith does not conclude that realism decides training value: PR mirrors were best, as expected for a SWE-bench evaluation, but procedural AST mutations and LM rewrites trained competitive models (within the error bars of PR mirrors); only LM Modify bugs fell off steeply.
quote: Trajectories generated from PR mirrors are empirically the most effective training data - this is expected, since they are most reflective of SWEbench. What's noteworthy is that trajectories from Procedural Modification and LM Rewrite instances lead to competitive models. There is a steep drop-off with LM Modify bugs.
wiki_says: For repair tasks, how realistic a bug is decides its training value. SWE-smith compared bug-generation strategies with matched data (table of 9.2 / 8.8 / 8.6 / 5.7).

claim: Four SFT sets of 500 trajectories each, at difficulty scores 2, 4, 6 and 8 (easy/medium/hard scored 1/5/9), trained students to 12.4%, 10.8%, 13.6% and 12.2% on SWE-bench Verified: no strong correlation between training-task difficulty and downstream performance.
quote: Next, from all successful trajectories, we create four fine-tuning datasets of 500 trajectories each corresponding to difficulty scores of 2, 4, 6, and 8. As mentioned in Section 2.2, the corresponding scores for easy/medium/hard are 1/5/9. Therefore, the SFT dataset for score 2 is made up of trajectories corresponding to 375 easy and 125 medium instances, and so on. Somewhat surprisingly, we do not observe strong correlation between increased difficulty and downstream performance. For the student models trained on the 2/4/6/8 difficulty SFT datasets, we get pass@1 scores of 12.4%, 10.8%, 13.6%, and 12.2% on SWE-bench Verified.

claim: The paper's sentence is 'Task difficulty correlates with solvability but not with effectiveness as training data.' The string the survey puts in quotation marks, 'does not correlate with effectiveness as training data', does not occur in the paper; the substance holds but the quotation is not verbatim.
quote: Task difficulty correlates with solvability but not with effectiveness as training data.
wiki_says: It also found that difficulty "does not correlate with effectiveness as training data"

claim: Combining bugs had a 96.9% yield (share of candidates that break at least one test), producing 10,092 instances at 0.00¢ per candidate, with a median of 15 fail-to-pass tests and 11 edited lines.

The near-total yield of combined bugs is an artifact of the input: only bug patches already validated as breaking at least one test are combined, so the yield says nothing about the value of combined bugs, and SWE-smith runs no training ablation of combined bugs on their own.
quote: Finally, combining bug patches has an extremely high yield rate - this is to be expected because we only attempt to combine bug patches that have been validated as usable task instances breaking 1+ tests.
wiki_says: combining several bugs into one task kept 96.9% of candidates

claim: Average cost to generate one candidate and its yield: Procedural 0.00¢ (40.2%), LM Modify 0.38¢ (56.0%), LM Rewrite 3.93¢ (35.0%), PR Mirror 5.53¢ (33.8%). Procedural AST mutation is free and trained nearly as well as PR mirrors in the matched ablation, while a new language has no PR history to mirror at all.
bears_on: cheapest bug source for a new language

claim: Fine-tuning on Python-only SWE-smith trajectories did not carry over to other languages: on 300 SWE-bench Multilingual tasks SWE-agent-LM-32B resolved 8.4% against 6.5% for its base Qwen 2.5 Coder Instruct (Claude 3.7 Sonnet 43%), and its edits drifted toward Python syntax in files that were not Python.
quote: Out of 300 task instances, we found that Claude 3.7 Sonnet achieved a 43% Pass@1 resolve rate, which is significantly better than SWE-agent-LM-32B (8.4%) and Qwen 2.5 Coder Instruct (6.5%). SWE-agent-LM-32B does not demonstrate a significant improvement over the baseline model. Through several spot checks of different trajectories, we came to a working hypothesis that while the rejection sampling fine-tuning process had improved its ability to carry out multi-turn interactions in this task setting, there were instances where code edits reflected syntax closer to Python despite code and files viewed in previous steps clearly not being written in Python.
bears_on: Python drift in a Python-like language

claim: Putting a fail-to-pass test in the problem statement gave more successful expert trajectories but taught the student to skip reproducing the bug: on 500 SWE-bench Verified instances it attempted reproduction in 127 runs against 379 for the student trained on LM-written issues, a 66% decrease, which accounts for its lower resolve rate.
quote: While providing a Fail-to-Pass test case leads to more successful expert trajectories, leaking the evaluation criteria causes the model to skip over writing a reproduction script, which accounts for the performance drop. Of 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, the student model trained on LM-generated issues attempts to reproduce the bug for 379 of the runs. The model trained on test-based issues only does so for 127 cases, a 66% decrease.
bears_on: what a training prompt should reveal

claim: Trajectories of tasks solved repeatedly across runs degraded the student, so SWE-smith caps any task instance at 3 trajectories in the training set.
quote: we also observe that "easier" trajectories - task instances that are repeatedly solved across multiple runs - degrade model performance. Therefore, we limit the number of times any SWE-smith task instance is represented in the training set to 3 trajectories.
bears_on: deduplicating distillation data

claim: Asking an LM to inject bugs with an open-ended prompt produced mostly trivial variable-assignment swaps, rated easy, and low diversity; this is the strategy that trained worst.
quote: LMModify are consistently rated to be easy - from several manual spot checks, we notice that while the prompt for LMModify provides several examples of types of bugs and does not name specific issues to create, the large majority of bugs created by this strategy are simple variable assignment mistakes (e.g. a=a; b=b is changed to a=b; b=a). An openended prompt like ours does not actually yield high diversity in terms of mistakes created.
bears_on: LLM-generated mutants for training

claim: SWE-smith's own authors say its seeded tasks are not fit for evaluation: the fail-to-pass tests are visible in the repository and there are no hidden tests, so seeded bugs train but should not be the test set.
quote: Finally, SWE-smith does not yield instances appropriate for evaluation. The SWE-smith pipeline as presented does not produce hidden tests, a crucial difference that makes SWE-bench more suitable for evaluation.
bears_on: evaluating on seeded bugs

claim: On Qwen3-32B (base 25.00), continuing SFT from BASEMIX (49.87 Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified) on equal-size trajectory sets reached 51.93 with FEATADD bugs (introduced by an agent while adding a feature), 50.73 with R2E-GYM, 50.53 with SWE-SMITH, and 49.87 with BUGINSTRUCT (bugs introduced on purpose), i.e. no gain from deliberate bugs.

The SFT advantage is shown only for the larger model. On Qwen3-14B, SFT on FEATADD after BASEMIX lowered Pass@1 from 41.13 to 40.40; FEATADD helped at 14B only through RL (42.20) or the full data mixture (45.27), and deliberate bugs (BUGINSTRUCT) were not tested at 14B. The paper's prose nevertheless says the smaller model shows the same trend.
wiki_says: Bugs that agents introduce by accident while adding features train better than deliberate perturbations

claim: Qwen3-32B students trained on GPT-5 and GPT-4o trajectories, which carry almost no assistant text beside the tool calls, reached only 31.40% and 21.57% on SWE-bench Verified, although GPT-5 solves more of the training bugs than the Claude teacher whose reasoning-rich trajectories trained BASEMIX; the authors conclude the teacher's reasoning text is essential for distillation.
quote: We trained a Qwen3-32B student model on the successful trajectories collected using the GPT models as backbone (similar setting as BASEMIX). The student models trained on GPT-5 and GPT-4o trajectories result in a success rate of 31.40% and 21.57% on SWE-Bench Verified, respectively. This suggests the assistant content (a summary of the teacher's reasoning) is essential in distilling code repairing skills from teacher models into student models
bears_on: format of distillation traces

claim: RL on FEATADD did not beat SFT on FEATADD for any hard subset of SWE-bench Verified; the authors attribute it to GRPO needing partially solvable problems, since too-hard problems give zero advantage.
quote: Moreover, training with RL does not improve over training with SFT on FEATADD for any subset. This could be because we use the GRPO algorithm that requires a problem to be partially solvable to make progress - if problems are too difficult, the advantage will be zero for those problems.
bears_on: task difficulty for GRPO

claim: Their agentic RL run, 25 steps of 64 bugs with 8 rollouts per bug, took 8 nodes of 8 H100s for 50 hours, far beyond a single consumer GPU.
quote: To train reinforcement learning for 25 steps with 64 bugs per step and 8 rollouts per bug, we require 8 nodes of 8 × H100s for 50 hours.
bears_on: cost of agentic RL

claim: FEATADD bugs look large partly because of padding: about half of the files they edit are newly created and half of the edited lines are documentation.
quote: FEATADD bugs involve many more lines and files edited that SWE-SMITH or BUGINSTRUCT. However, about half of the files edited are new files and half of the lines edited are documentation.
bears_on: what makes agent-made bugs complex

claim: On real PyPIBugs single-token bugs, RealiT (pre-trained on mutants, fine-tuned on real fixes) localized 44.23% against 23.02% (Transformer), 23.82% (GNN) and 23.62% (GREAT) for other architectures trained only on mutants, nearly doubling them (44.23 / 23.82 = 1.86); joint localization and repair 39.00% against 18.24-19.03%.

Against its own mutants-only ablation (same architecture, pre-trained on mutants, not fine-tuned), fine-tuning on real fixes raised real-bug localization from 30.92% to 44.23%: 13.31 points, about 1.43x. The near-doubling compares RealiT with other architectures trained on fewer mutants, so it mixes the effect of real fixes with architecture and mutant count.
wiki_says: Pretraining a bug detector on mutants and then fine-tuning on real fixes roughly doubled localization accuracy over mutants alone

claim: Order matters as the survey says: real fixes alone, without mutant pre-training, localized only 16.07% of real bugs (joint 12.67%), worse than mutants alone (30.92%, joint 25.10%); RealiT pre-trains on mutants and then fine-tunes on real fixes. Real-only training did have the lowest false-positive rate on bug-free code, 19.32%.
quote:
| RealiT - without pre-training on mutants       |  19.32 |                          12.67 |                         16.07 |                           40.38 |              2.37 |             8.58 |              31.34 |
| RealiT - without fine-tuning on real bug fixes |  33.41 |                          25.10 |                         30.92 |                           65.53 |             77.41 |            84.49 |              90.18 |

claim: RealiT does give a count: fine-tuning on subsamples of its real fixes, performance rose with every increase, and even around 1000 real fixes (less than 5% of its dataset) already improved localization and repair. What it does not say is how many close the gap entirely, and it measures single-token bugs only.
quote: We can observe a clear trend that more real bug fixes lead to an improved performance across all RealiT variants. This holds true even for small fine-tuning datasets of around 1000 (less than 5% of the original dataset size) bug fixes.
wiki_says: The number of real failures needed to close the gap between seeded and real bugs is unknown. RealiT shows the effect but gives no count

claim: Matching the gain from scaling mutants from 5x to 100x per snippet took fine-tuning on at least 10% of the real-fix dataset, 3314 bugs; mutants are the cheaper lever until they saturate.
quote: For example, to achieve the same performance gain obtained from scaling the number of mutants generated from 5x to 100x, we have to fine-tune on at least 10% of our real bug fix dataset (3314 bugs).
bears_on: real failures versus more mutants

claim: More mutants per snippet helped up to 100x (average 85 unique mutants per snippet, so many are oversampled) and hurt beyond 100x.
quote: First of all, in contrast to common believe [12], we observe that increasing the number of mutants up to 100x generated mutants per code snippet leads to a performance improvement for both localization and repair 7 . This is surprising as the number of unique mutants per code snippet is limited (with an average of 85 unique mutants per code snippet) and, henceforth, buggy programs with more mutant candidates are oversampled. Still, we found that increasing the limit of mutants beyond 100x (and thereby oversampling code snippets in our dataset that provide up to 200k unique mutants) actually decreases the localization and repair performance.
bears_on: how many mutants per program

claim: Fine-tuning on real fixes lowered RealiT's scores on held-out mutants while raising them on real bugs; the authors find no correlation between mutant-benchmark and real-bug performance, so gains measured on seeded bugs are hard to interpret.
quote: As there is clearly no correlation between the real world performance and the performance on mutants when the model is fine-tuned on real bug fixes, performance gains on mutants independent from real world performance become difficult to interpret.
bears_on: evaluating on seeded bugs

claim: Placing mutants where real bugs occurred (apply the real fix, then re-inject a mutation) did not substitute for real fixes; its small gain looked like a scaling effect, not an effect of realistic context.
quote: Still, we find that a model trained on real bug fixes clearly outperforms a model trained on postfix mutants when evaluated on real bug fixes. Since the performance of detecting mutants does not decrease when training on postfix mutants (similar to scaling the number of mutants generated), we actually conclude that the performance gain is likely a scaling effect and can not necessarily be attributed to the mutation context.
bears_on: realistic seeding versus real failures

claim: RealiT is a 6-layer Transformer encoder (hidden size 512, 8 heads) that points at one token and picks its replacement, on single-token bugs; it is not a generative LLM, so its gains are a weak guide for fine-tuning a decoder that writes whole repairs.
quote: RealiT. We follow the same architectural design for RealiT. As an encoding model, we employ a 6-layer Transformer encoder [8], a hidden size of 512, an intermediate size of 2048 and 8 attention heads.
