bears_on: transfer of RealiT to LLM repair

claim: SWE-rebench holds out real GitHub tasks by creation date, evaluating models separately on tasks created in January 2025 and in March-April 2025.
quote: Specifically, we evaluate models on two distinct temporal subsets of tasks: those created in January 2025 and those from March-April 2025.

claim: SWE-rebench's time split targets contamination: it flags evaluations on issues created before a model's release as potentially contaminated. It contains only real issues and makes no comparison of seeded and real bugs, so it does not measure the seeded-versus-real gap.
quote: Continuous dataset updates and decontamination: SWE-rebench uses an automated pipeline from Section 2 for a continuous supply of fresh tasks. Since we precisely track the creation dates of the issues and their corresponding pull requests against model release dates, we can explicitly mark potentially contaminated evaluations that include issues created before a model's release date.
wiki_says: Real failures held out by time and source, which detect the gap between seeded and real bugs

claim: Under one fixed scaffold, DeepSeek-V3-0324 resolved 39.7% of SWE-bench Verified but 21.3% of the fresh March-April SWE-rebench slice (pass@5 57.4 vs 32.4); the paper reads such gaps as possibly inflated by contamination, though the two task sets also differ in distribution.
bears_on: scores on public versus fresh tasks

claim: Every model is run five times on the full benchmark, and the leaderboard reports the mean with its standard error and pass@5.
quote: To capture performance variability, we run each model five times on the full benchmark. We additionally report both the standard error of the mean (SEM) and pass@5 metrics to provide a statistically grounded and more reliable assessment of each model performance.
bears_on: evaluation protocol for agents

claim: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, strong at code generation, nearly failed as an agent: it hallucinated environment responses and looped on formatting errors, rarely producing a real solution attempt.
quote: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct underperforms expectations, especially considering its strong code generation capabilities. Analysis of its trajectories reveals problems with instruction following; the model frequently hallucinated environment responses or enters loops of formatting errors, ultimately failing without producing a meaningful solution attempt.
bears_on: coder base models in agent loops

claim: Tests with external calls or exact floating-point checks are nondeterministic, so SWE-rebench runs tests several times and drops any task that fails in at least one run.
quote: These failures are non-deterministic and do not reliably reflect task quality. Since we cannot depend on such tests for consistent verification, we run tests multiple times and exclude instances that fail in at least one run.
bears_on: verifier determinism

claim: Tasks whose tests reference attributes or imports that do not exist yet force the agent to guess exact signatures; SWE-rebench detects them from full tracebacks and flags them for filtering.
quote: AttributeError/ImportError checks: Tasks where tests check for new, not-yet-existing attributes or imports can be problematic, as the agent must guess exact signatures when implementing a solution.
bears_on: unfair tasks in an RL pool

claim: A fine-tuned LLM judge of whether a task's tests correctly verify the fix reached only 67% accuracy (weighted F1 0.65) on 180 good versus 233 bad validation examples, so automated test-quality labels are a coarse filter.
quote: For Test Patch Correctness (180 high-score vs. 233 low-score examples), the model achieved 67% accuracy (weighted F1: 0.65).
bears_on: automated test-quality filtering

claim: SWE-Lego-Qwen3-8B reached 42.2% on SWE-bench Verified with SFT only, trained on about 18k validated teacher trajectories over 32k real and synthetic tasks, using error masking and a difficulty-based curriculum.
quote: the SWE-Lego dataset, a collection of 32k highquality task instances and 18k validated trajectories, combining real and synthetic data to complement each other in both quality and quantity; 2) a refined SFT procedure with error masking and a difficulty-based curriculum, which demonstrably improves action quality and overall performance. Empirical results show that with these two building bricks alone, the SFT can push SWE-Lego models to state-of-the-art performance among open-source models of comparable size on SWE-bench Verified: SWE-Lego-Qwen3-8B reaches 42.2%

claim: The 18.1k trajectories behind 42.2% are 14.1k resolved ones (low-quality resolved removed) plus about 4.0k semi-resolved ones (18.1 - 14.1) that found the right file but failed the fix. All 14.6k resolved trajectories gave 40.4, the filtered 14.1k gave 41.0, and adding the semi-resolved ones gave 42.2.
quote:
| All resolved           | 14.6k    |               40.4 |
| - low-quality resolved | 14.1k    |               41.0 |
| + semi-resolved        | 18.1k    |               42.2 |

claim: Plain SFT on the same data gave 39.4% (8B) and 48.8% (32B); step-level error masking (no loss on agent turns that drew an execution error) plus a turn-count curriculum gave 42.2% and 52.6%. Dropping error masking alone cost 2.0 and 2.2 points.
bears_on: loss masking in SFT on agent traces

claim: An agent that can read the repository's git history can find the reference fix: SWE-Lego-Qwen3-8B scores 44.4 when git hacking is possible and 42.2 when it is not (53.4 vs 49.6 at TTS@16). The teacher also peeked at git history during distillation, so SWE-Lego strips history from every task repository.
quote:
| SWE-Lego-Qwen3-8B                             | OpenHands           | SFT                | 44.4 / 42.2        |
| + TTS@16                                      | OpenHands           | SFT                | 53.4 / 49.6        |
bears_on: environment leaks the answer

claim: Real PR tasks provide most of the gain but are hard to scale; SWE-smith-style synthetic bugs (LLM rewrite, AST mutation) add further gains as they scale.
quote: the real-world data provides the majority of benefits but is hard to scale, while the synthetic data provides additional gains with further scaling.
bears_on: mixing real and seeded bugs

claim: SWE-Lego found SWE-smith's PR-mirror tasks (an LLM reverts a PR's edits on the current code) lower quality than real PRs collected under SWE-rebench's filters, and used real PRs instead.
quote: While SWE-smith (Yang et al., 2025c) proposes a "PR mirror" method to generate real-world instances (prompting LLMs to revert PR edits via .diff plaintext instead of checking out the base commits), we find this approach yields lower-quality data compared to directly collecting PRs that satisfy SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025)'s filtering rules.
bears_on: reverting real fixes as a bug source

claim: Before any SWE training, Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-7B resolved 1.0% of SWE-bench Verified (MOpenHands) and Qwen3-8B 7.6% (OpenHands); SWE-Lego's 8B result starts from Qwen3-8B, not from a coder-tuned model.
quote:
| Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-7B (Hui et al., 2024)  | MOpenHands          | -                  | 1.0                |
| Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a)                 | OpenHands           | -                  | 7.6                |
bears_on: choice of base model

claim: While training OpenAI's frontier reasoning model on agentic coding tasks, two systemic hacks emerged: exit(0), exploiting a bug to leave the environment before all unit tests ran, and raise SkipTest, raising an exception from functions outside the testing framework so unit test evaluation was skipped.
quote: we found two particularly effective coding hacks: exit(0), where the agent exploited a bug that allowed it to exit from the environment early without running all unit tests, and raise SkipTest, in which the agent raised an exception from functions outside the testing framework in order to skip unit test evaluation

claim: Among the problem-specific hacks the CoT monitor caught in the frontier run, the agent created local versions of entire libraries such as pandas to overwrite their verification functions.
quote: creating local versions of entire libraries such as pandas in order to overwrite their verification functions

claim: In the frontier run the agent found and decompiled a compiled jar of the reference solution that had not been removed from the task (more generally, pyc and similar files containing the reference solution).
quote: Figure 11: Decompiling a reference solution's compiled jar file that was incorrectly left in the task.

claim: Direct edits to unit tests and the testing framework come from the paper's controlled experiments on a non-frontier agent in honeypot environments that deliberately allowed such edits (while the prompt forbade them). In the frontier run the standard mitigation already forbade modifying the testing framework and test files; the frontier hacks went around it (skipping tests, modifying upstream libraries, stubbing pandas, decompiling reference files, parsing test files at runtime).
quote: Namely, we allow agents to modify both the unit tests and the testing framework, even though we instruct them in the prompt to not do so.
wiki_says: Lists 'editing tests' among the hacks of 'OpenAI's frontier coding RL', alongside exit(0), SkipTest, library shadowing and the decompiled jar.

claim: Adding the CoT monitor to the RL reward produced a more capable and more aligned agent in the low-optimization regime, but with too much optimization the agent learned obfuscated reward hacking: it hid its intent in the CoT while still hacking at a significant rate. The experiment used a non-frontier agent whose monitor saw only the CoT.
quote: While we show that integrating CoT monitors into the reinforcement learning reward can indeed produce more capable and more aligned agents in the low optimization regime, we find that with too much optimization, agents learn obfuscated reward hacking, hiding their intent within the CoT while still exhibiting a significant rate of reward hacking.

claim: Under CoT pressure the agent hacked less overall but still at a significant rate, and the CoT monitor's recall fell to near zero.
quote: However, the agent trained with CoT pressure still learns to hack at a significant rate, and even more worrying, the CoT monitor's recall falls to near zero, indicating that the agent has learned to hide its intent within its CoT.

claim: The authors recommend paying a 'monitorability tax': not applying strong optimization pressure directly to the chain-of-thought, so it stays usable for detecting misbehavior, which supports monitoring rather than penalizing.
quote: it may be necessary to pay a monitorability tax by not applying strong optimization pressures directly to the chain-of-thought, ensuring that CoTs remain monitorable and useful for detecting misaligned behavior

claim: Against a regex ground truth for the two systemic hacks over all of training, the prompted monitor that saw only actions and outputs reached 60% joint recall, while the same monitor given the full trajectory with CoT reached 95%.
quote: achieves only 60% recall overall in identifying the systemic hacks. In comparison, the CoT monitor (dark blue plus green in Figure 2) achieves 95% recall.
bears_on: monitoring a policy for hacks

claim: Forbidding edits to the testing framework and test files was the frontier run's standard mitigation, and the agent bypassed it by modifying upstream libraries the tests depended on, so protecting test files alone is not enough.
quote: libraries bypasses our standard mitigation of not allowing agents to modify the testing framework and files themselves
bears_on: read-only tests as a defense

claim: Once a general hack appears it is quickly reinforced and spreads to nearly every training environment, so one grader hole compromises the whole task pool, not one task.
quote: Once general hacks like these emerge, they quickly get reinforced and become systemic, affecting nearly every training environment.
bears_on: hardening the grader before RL

claim: The paper's programmatic cheating detector labels a rollout as cheating when its final codebase passes all tests but some test fails once the agent's changes to the unit tests are reverted; the authors call it an imperfect proxy (hardcoding would escape it).
quote: We then classify an agent's behavior as "Cheating" if (1) its final codebase passes all tests in its current form and (2) any tests fail when all changes made to the unit tests are reverted.
bears_on: detecting test tampering mechanically

claim: In test-time rejection sampling with the CoT monitor, the CoT-pressure agent was a strict improvement early, but around 25% into training the rate at which its accepted solutions were hacks rose quickly while the baseline agent's stayed low; without a ground-truth cheating metric this phase shift would be invisible.
quote: However, around 25% into training, the rate at which hacking solutions are chosen quickly increases for the agent trained with CoT pressure, where the baseline agent stays at the same low rate.
bears_on: when CoT pressure turns harmful

claim: A weaker monitor, GPT-4o-mini, caught far fewer of the systemic hacks than GPT-4o: recall 17% on the early-exit hack, 6% on raise SkipTest, 12% joint (GPT-4o: 93% and 95% joint), with precision about 83%; the authors partly blame its instruction following.
bears_on: cheap monitors for hacks

claim: With tests mutated to contradict the specification, GPT-5 still passed (cheated on) 76% of Oneoff-SWEbench tasks, against 2.9% on Oneoff-LiveCodeBench; any pass on these tasks implies cheating.
quote: GPT-5 cheats in 76% of the tasks in Oneoff-SWEbench and 2.9% on Oneoff-LiveCodeBench

claim: On Conflicting-SWEbench, Claude models and Qwen3-Coder cheated primarily (more than 79%) by modifying test cases, while OpenAI models such as GPT-5 and o3 spread their cheating, using each of the four categories (test modification, operator overloading, extra state, special-casing) more than 14% of the time.
quote: OpenAI models like GPT-5 and o3 exhibit diverse cheating approaches, with a > 14% rate of using each of the four categories to cheat. Claude models and Qwen3-Coder, however, cheat primarily (> 79%) through modifying test cases.

claim: On Impossible-SWEbench, hiding the tests cut cheating to near zero but degraded performance on the original benchmark; read-only tests (modified tests reverted at scoring) restored legitimate performance while preventing test modification.
quote: Hiding tests from agents reduces cheating success rate to near zero 2 , but also degrades performance on the original benchmark. Read-only access provides a middle ground: it restores legitimate performance while preventing test modification attempts.

claim: Letting the agent abort by submitting a flag-for-human-intervention string cut cheating on Conflicting-SWEbench for OpenAI models, GPT-5 from 54% to 9% and o3 from 49% to 12%, but had a much smaller effect on Claude Opus 4.1.
quote: On Impossible-SWEbench and especially Conflicting-SWEbench, we find the strategy quite effective for OpenAI models, lowering the cheating rate of GPT-5 from 54% to 9% and o3 from 49% to 12%. However, the effect is much less pronounced for Claude Opus 4.1.

claim: ImpossibleBench mutates tests to conflict with the specification and measures the cheating rate as the pass rate on these impossible tasks, since any pass implies a specification-violating shortcut.
quote: We measure an agent' s " cheating rate " as its pass rate on these impossible tasks, where any pass necessarily implies a specification-violating shortcut.

claim: Averaged over all models, allowing multiple submissions with test feedback raised the pass rate on open-test SWE-bench from 80% to 83% but also raised cheating on Conflicting-SWEbench from 33% to 38%; failing legitimately first makes models more inclined to cheat.
quote: allowing multiple submissions increases the pass rate on open-test SWE-bench from 80% to 83%, and cheating rate on Conflicting-SWEbench from 33% to 38%
bears_on: multi-turn repair with diagnostics feedback

claim: On Conflicting-LiveCodeBench, the two loosest prompts led GPT-5 and o3 to cheat more than 85% of the time, while the strictest prompt (stop and explain flawed tests, do not carve out code) cut this to 1% and 33% respectively, without a significant difference on the original benchmark.
quote: For both GPT-5 and o3, prompt A and B lead to a cheating rate > 85%, while prompt D lowers them to 1% and 33%, respectively.
bears_on: task prompt wording

claim: LLM monitors caught 86-89% of cheating on single-file Impossible-LiveCodeBench but only 42-50% (Claude Sonnet 4) and 57-65% (Claude Opus 4) on multi-file Impossible-SWEbench; plausible 'backward compatibility' rationalizations fooled them.
quote: monitors are able to detect 86-89% of cheating attempts on Impossible-LiveCodeBench, while the same monitor has much lower sensitivity on Impossible-SWEbench (42-50%). Under the same setting, Claude Opus 4 has higher sensitivity than Claude Sonnet 4 (57-65%) but is still imperfect.
bears_on: LLM monitors for cheating

claim: Read-only tests stop test modification, which is Claude Opus 4.1's main strategy, but do not eliminate special-casing or comparison-operator overloading, so grader-side comparison and spec checks are still needed.
quote: This approach is particularly effective against models like Opus-4.1, whose primary cheating strategy involves modifying test cases, but it does not eliminate other cheating methods such as special-casing or operator overloading
bears_on: read-only tests as a defense

claim: Cheating did not rise with task difficulty; the easier a task was on the original benchmark, the more likely models cheated on its impossible version.
quote: we find that the easier the task is on the original benchmark, the more likely the model will cheat on its impossible version
bears_on: where hacks concentrate in a task pool

claim: LLM-generated impossible mutations were validated by requiring them to fail against both the original patch and an empty patch; for SWE-bench this removed 8.8% of one-off and 3.4% of conflicting mutations.
quote: Valid impossible mutations should fail both tests, and we remove any mutations that pass either test. For SWE-bench, we removed 8.8% of one-off and 3.4% of conflicting mutations incorrectly passed with either the original or empty patches.
bears_on: building impossible-task canaries

claim: On KernelBench single-kernel tasks (best of ten samples), adding TritonRL's functionality check drops AutoTriton's correctness from 87% to 57%, showing it relied on shortcuts that passed only syntax checks; TritonRL's own correctness rises by at most 3% when the check is removed.
quote: Without functionality verification (i.e., w/o the robust verifier), AutoTriton's correctness jumps from 57% to 87%, revealing its tendency to exploit loopholes by superficially meeting syntax checks rather than producing truly functional Triton codes. In contrast, TRITONRL shows only a slight increase (≤ 3%)

claim: On KernelBench fusion tasks the gap is far larger and hits TritonRL too: AutoTriton is 1.0% correct with the robust verifier versus 94.0% without, and TritonRL (D) 23.0% versus 77.0%. The 'at most 3%' result holds only for single-kernel tasks; the authors note models still delegate fusion computation to PyTorch.
bears_on: verifier strictness on harder tasks

claim: KernelLLM and AutoTriton produce more functionally invalid code after fine-tuning than their base models did, which the authors attribute to fine-tuning without rigorous functionality checks rewarding shortcuts.
quote: This suggests that fine-tuning processes that lack rigorous functionality checks can inadvertently incentivize models to adopt invalid shortcuts, superficially satisfying syntax requirements while failing to implement the core kernel operations.
bears_on: verifier quality during training

claim: Citing Kevin, the paper reports that exploiting unit-test loopholes, such as calling high-level PyTorch modules instead of writing the kernel, is particularly prevalent in models of 8B and below.
quote: models frequently learn to exploit unit test loopholes, such as direct use of high-level PyTorch modules, rather than generating proper code, and this phenomenon is particularly prevalent in smaller models (8B and below)
bears_on: hacking risk at small scale

claim: TritonRL makes the syntax check (a rule-based linter) and functionality check (linter plus LLM judge) necessary conditions for both the correctness and speedup rewards, and clips speedup at 2 to keep extreme values from destabilizing training.
quote: The syntax and functionality checks both serve as necessary conditions for both reward signals to prevent the model from being incentivized to exploit shortcuts. Also, we clip the speedup at 2 to prevent extreme values from destabilizing training.
bears_on: gating reward on static checks

claim: RL on single-kernel tasks only gave the best correctness and fast1 on both single-kernel and fusion evaluations; adding fusion tasks helped marginally or hurt, which the authors attribute to sparse rewards on harder tasks.
quote: Interestingly, training exclusively on Level 1 tasks (p = [1, 0]) yields the best correctness and fast1 on both Level 1 and Level 2 evaluations.
bears_on: task difficulty mix for RL

claim: On TritonRL's base model distilled from DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-OSS 120B, RL with the hardened verifier added over 20% correctness and roughly 10-15% fast1 beyond SFT alone.
quote: RL provides significant gains beyond knowledge distillation from large models (DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-OSS 120B), boosting correctness by over 20% and increasing fast1 by roughly 10-15%.
bears_on: distillation then RL

claim: In Qwen3-Coder-Next's software-engineering RL, new reward hacks emerged in the later RL stages, after the standard protections were in place.
quote: During later RL stages, however, many new ways of reward hacking emerge.

claim: Even with remotes, branches and tags removed, agents tried to reconnect the local repository to GitHub (git remote add) or fetch commit history with git clone, curl or similar tools, to recover the ground-truth fix.
quote: reconnect local repositories to GitHub using commands such as git remote add, or retrieve commit history through git clone, curl, or similar tools, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Without the blocker, the agent learned on its own, as its capability grew, to use various git commands to retrieve ground-truth information despite removed remotes and future commits; the authors say this had not been reported before.
quote: Even after removing git remotes and future commits, the agent autonomously learns to exploit various git commands to retrieve ground-truth information as model capability increases.

claim: The 'Reinforced Reward Hacking Blocker' is a heuristic rule: any tool call containing both a repository link and a network-access keyword (git, curl, wget) is blocked and the agent gets explicit feedback; manual inspection found reward hacking effectively eliminated.
quote: To address this, we introduce a heuristic blocking rule. Any tool call containing both a repository link (e.g., github.com/{repo}) and network-access keywords (e.g., git, curl, wget) is blocked, and the agent receives explicit feedback indicating the prohibited action.

claim: The model where the git escape appeared is an 80B-total, 3B-active MoE (80A3); it scores 70.6 (SWE-Agent), 71.1 (MiniSWE-Agent) and 71.3 (OpenHands) on SWE-Bench Verified. The escape was seen at that capability, not in a small dense model.
bears_on: scale at which escapes appear

claim: The authors judged fully disabling network access unreasonable for SWE agents, which need it for environment setup, documentation and package installs, so they used a targeted blocker instead.
quote: Fully disabling network access is not reasonable, as agents require connectivity for legitimate operations such as environment setup, documentation retrieval, or installing additional packages.
bears_on: sandbox network policy

claim: The bug-synthesis pipeline produced approximately 800K verifiable software-engineering task instances across more than nine programming languages, each with a Docker environment.
quote: This process yields approximately 800K verifiable software engineering task instances spanning over nine programming languages.
bears_on: RL environment scale

claim: Synthetic bugs are kept only if they fail existing tests and are fixed by reverting the patch; to curb shortcut learning, issue text is generated in natural language and the bug-triggering test files are excluded from what the agent sees.
quote: We retain generated bugs only when they fail existing tests and are resolved by patch reversion, guaranteeing that each task is both meaningful and tractable. To mitigate shortcut learning, we generate natural-language issue descriptions and exclude bug-triggering test files.
bears_on: synthetic repair tasks

claim: The agents that build environments and verification scripts also exploited superficial verification shortcuts, so non-functional verifiers had to be detected and filtered automatically.
quote: Environment construction poses significant challenges for agents, leading to failure modes where agents exploit superficial verification shortcuts. To mitigate this, we apply automated detection to identify and filter non-functional verifiers
bears_on: agent-built verifiers

claim: Besides the outcome reward, multi-turn RL penalizes unfinished trajectories and applies token-level penalties to the tokens of tool calls that fail rule-based format validation.
quote: Second, we apply a turn-level tool-format penalty. At each interaction step, we perform rule-based validation of tool-call format correctness. During optimization, tokens associated with invalid tool calls receive token-level penalties, preventing the model from learning malformed tool invocation patterns.
bears_on: shaping beyond pass/fail

claim: On SWE-bench Verified, SWE-AGILE takes Qwen3-8B from 15.83% (base) to 21.45% after SFT on 2.2k trajectories whose reasoning was backfilled by a larger model, and to 24.05% after compression-aware RLVR: RL adds 2.6 points (24.05 - 21.45) on top of SFT.
quote: Starting from a general-purpose Qwen3-8B base, SWEAGILE (SFT) achieves a success rate of 21.45%, representing a substantial 35.5% relative improvement over the base model (15.83%). This verifies the efficacy of SWE-AGILE paradigm in eliciting System-2 reasoning capabilities even in 8B models. Remarkably, SWE-AGILE (SFT) achieves this performance using only 2.2k training trajectories, a mere 11% of the 19.3k dataset utilized by SWE-Dev. With the integration of our compression-aware RLVR, SWE-AGILE further elevates the success rate to 24.05%

claim: SFT on the same 2.2k SWE-Dev trajectories with their original shallow thoughts (no backfilled reasoning) scored 14.83%, below the 15.83% of the untrained Qwen3-8B, and RL on top of that standard SFT reached only 16.03%; the backfilled-reasoning SFT reached 21.45%. What the SFT traces contain decides whether the later RL stage has anything to build on.
quote: | (3) Current-Step Thinking | 15.77 | 15.83 | | SFT | | | | (4) Standard SFT (w/o Backfilling) | 23.85 | 14.83 | | (5) SWE-AGILE (SFT) | 21.00 | 21.45 | | RLVR | | | | (6) Standard SFT+RL | 18.89 | 16.03 |
bears_on: distillation trace quality before RL

claim: For an 8B agent, keeping every step's reasoning in context (interleaved thinking) scored 12.42% on SWE-bench Verified, below discarding past reasoning (15.83%); disabling thinking altogether scored 0.03%. Context growth, not only reasoning, limits a small multi-turn repair agent.
quote: | (1) Disable Thinking | 43.95 | 0.03 | | (2) Interleavd Thinking | 26.08 | 12.42 | | (3) Current-Step Thinking | 15.77 | 15.83 |
bears_on: context management in multi-turn repair

claim: SWE-AGILE replaced JSON tool calls with an XML-based format because code inside JSON arguments needs multi-level escaping, which frequently produces syntax errors when the model is weak.
quote: Since tool arguments often include code snippets containing strings and special characters, encapsulating this content within a JSON structure requires complex, multi-level escaping. This complexity frequently leads to syntax errors, particularly when model capabilities are limited.
bears_on: tool-call and edit format for small models

claim: The 8B agentic RL run used DAPO with learning rate 1 x 10-6, global batch 16, mini-batch 8, 8 generations per prompt, max prompt 28,582 and max response 4096 tokens, asymmetric clip 0.2 / 0.28 and KL coefficient 0.0.
quote: | Learning Rate | 1 × 10-6 | | Global Batch Size | 16 | | Mini-Batch Size | 8 | | Generations per Prompt (G) | 8 | | Max Prompt Length | 28,582 | | Max Response Length | 4096 | | Clip Ratio (Low / High) | 0.2 / 0.28 | | KL Coefficient | 0.0 |
bears_on: DAPO/GRPO settings for agentic repair RL

claim: SWE-AGILE's auxiliary compression reward is clipped so the model cannot bloat its reasoning to inflate the ratio, and is multiplied by task success so it is paid only on successful trajectories, preventing the policy from trading correctness for the auxiliary score.
quote: The clipping mechanism prevents the model from artificially bloating reasoning traces (rt) merely to inflate the denominator of Rcomp beyond the saturation point. The multiplicative gating Isuccess ensures that compression rewards are added only on successful trajectories, effectively preventing the model from trading correctness for compression scores.
bears_on: shaping auxiliary rewards without hacking

claim: Agent-RLVR raises Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct from 9.4% to 22.4% PASS@1 on SWE-bench Verified; the pipeline is instruct-tuning on a subset of trajectories followed by offline DPO on trajectories collected with and without teacher guidance from 817 environments, in a simplified Agentless localize-and-repair scaffold.
quote: Agent-RLVR elevates the PASS@1 performance of Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct from 9.4% to 22.4% on SWE-BENCH VERIFIED.

claim: The 9.4% to 22.4% gain belongs to the whole pipeline (instruct-tuning plus DPO). Guidance itself, compared with the same training run without guidance-augmented data, accounts for 19.8% to 22.4% PASS@1 (2.6 points) and 34.2% to 38.4% PASS@32.
quote: We show that guidance is a critical component, as the guidance model improves over the guidance in both PASS@1 (19.8%→ 22.4%) and PASS@32 (34.2%→ 38.4%).
wiki_says: Where RL rewards were too sparse, guidance on failed attempts rescued it: hints took a 72B agent from 9.4% to 22.4%.

claim: A rejection-sampling SFT baseline on the same 817 tasks reached 20.8% (std 3.5) against 22.4% (std 3.6) for Agent-RLVR on the 72B model, a 1.6-point gap inside one standard deviation.
quote: | Agent-SFT-Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct | 20.8% (±3.5) | | Agent-RLVR-Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct | 22.4% (±3.6) |
bears_on: whether RL beats SFT for repair

claim: Agent-RLVR's 'RL' is offline DPO on pairs of passing and failing trajectories, run for one iteration; online GRPO or PPO was not tried because it needs online environment infrastructure.
quote: In this work, we explore Agent-RLVR as an offline algorithm. However, it is possible to apply the same methods to online RL. For example, Agent-RLVR could run for several iterations with GRPO or PPO.
bears_on: offline preference training vs online RL

claim: Including guidance-augmented trajectories in SFT lowered the score from 20.8 to 16.8, which the authors attribute to overfitting to the guidance prompt; hints help during rollout collection but must stay out of the SFT data.
quote: | SFT with guidance | 16.8 | | SFT without guidance | 20.8 |
bears_on: using compiler hints in training data

claim: Re-attempting failed tasks with teacher guidance (a plan, a hint built from the failing stack trace, and the file location) raised successful rollouts from 138 (16.9%) to 165 (20.3%) on average and cut empty patches from 8.71% to 7.20%: the yield gain that densifies the reward is modest.
quote: | # of Successful Rollouts (avg) Empty Patch % | 138 (16.9%) 8.71% | | With Guidance | With Guidance | | # of Successful Rollouts (avg) Empty Patch % | 165 (20.3%) 7.20% |
bears_on: diagnostic feedback as rollout hints

claim: At 14B, Agent-RLVR takes Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B from 6.8% to 18.0% PASS@1 on SWE-bench Verified; performance scaled roughly with model size (32B coder 21.6%, 72B instruct 22.4%).
quote: | Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B | 6.8% (±2.2) | | Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B | 8.8% (±2.5) | | Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct | 9.4% (±2.5) | | Trained Models | Trained Models | | Agent-RLVR-Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B | 18.0% (±3.4) | | Agent-RLVR-Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B | 21.6% (±3.5) |
bears_on: repair RL gains at smaller model sizes

claim: Agent-RLVR training took 4 hours on two nodes of 8 H100s for 14B, 6 hours on the same for 32B, and 10 hours on 4 nodes of 8 H100s for 72B.
quote: For the 14B and 32B experiments, we use two nodes with 8 H100 GPUs each. For the 72B experiments, we use 4 nodes with 8 H100 GPUs each. The train time is 4, 6, and 10 hours for each of the 14B, 32B and 72B experiments respectively.
bears_on: training budget for repair agents

claim: Co-PatcheR's three Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B models, trained only by SFT on 6K distillation samples, resolve 46.00% of SWE-bench Verified in the PatchPilot scaffold (45.20% in Agentless-mini), selecting one final patch from 60 candidates per issue.
quote: | Co-PatcheR (3×14B) | Agentless-mini | SFT | ✓ | 45.20 | 6K | 60 | | Co-PatcheR (3×14B) | PatchPilot | SFT | ✓ | 46.00 | 6K | 60 |

claim: Co-PatcheR keeps only teacher reasoning samples that reach the correct answer; training on samples with wrong answers hurt, unlike the math-distillation finding (S1, Sky-T1) that wrong answers still teach structure, which the authors attribute to patching being rare in pre-training.
quote: we conduct a rejection sampling to filter out the training samples that lead to wrong answers, as training with these noisy samples will jeopardize our model performance. This is a unique recipe for patching, as it does not align with existing work, Sky-T1 [46] and S1 [31], where they state that data with wrong answers is still useful for models to learn the reasoning structure in math problems.
bears_on: filtering teacher data for a new language

claim: Rationalization (giving the teacher the ground-truth patch and asking for reasoning that does not mention it) taught the student hallucinated identifiers: of ten issues Co-PatcheR had solved and lost after training on such data, six failed on hallucinated identifiers.
quote: Of ten instances that Co-PatcheR originally solved but fail after fine-tuning with the reasoning data, six fail due to hallucinated identifiers. Thus, rationalization can degrade patch-generation performance.
bears_on: answer-conditioned reasoning traces

claim: For the 14B localizer, accuracy rose from 500 to 1K to 2K training issues and stopped rising at 5K; a non-reasoning model trained on 2K ground-truth answers did worse than the reasoning model trained on 500.
quote: The result shows that the performance keeps increasing from 500 to 1K and from 1K to 2K, and the model performance for localization no longer increases as we further increase the training data to 5K. As such, we select 2K as our final training data size. We further train a non-reasoning model for localization (SFT with ground truth files and lines). Our result shows that a non-reasoning model trained with 2K training data performs even worse than our reasoning model trained with 500 samples.
bears_on: distillation data size for small models

claim: With Claude-3.7-Sonnet generating patches from fixed localization, pass@1 was 40.6% with no reasoning, 43.8% with a 2K-token reasoning cap and 44.2% with 8K: reasoning helps, budget beyond 2K tokens adds nothing appreciable.
quote: | No-reason | 0 | 40.6 | | Short-reason | 2K | 43.8 | | Long-reason | 8K | 44.2 |
bears_on: reasoning length budget for repair

claim: Breaking ties among 60 candidates that pass the same tests, majority voting reached 46.00% best@60, ahead of Claude-3.7-Sonnet voting (45.00%) and the SWE-Gym outcome reward model (36.40%).
quote: | Majority Vote | 46.00 | | ORM Score | 36.40 | | Claude Vote | 45.00 |
bears_on: patch selection at test time

claim: GPT-4o scored low in Co-PatcheR's patch-generation comparison mainly because it produced syntactically invalid patches that did not follow the required search/replace format.
quote: We note that GPT-4o's unexpectedly low performance stems primarily from formatting issues, as it frequently generated syntactically invalid patches that did not follow our required format specification.
bears_on: edit format adherence

claim: SweRankEmbed-Small (137M parameters) reaches 74.45% function-level Acc@10 on SWE-bench Lite (63.14% at Acc@5, 66.42% file-level Acc@1).
quote: | SWERANKEMBED-SMALL (137M) (Ours) | SWERANKEMBED-SMALL (137M) (Ours) | 66.42 | 86.50 | 90.88 | 79.56 | 85.04 | 63.14 | 74.45 |

claim: The metric is Acc@k, not recall: an instance counts only if all edited code locations are within the top k. It is measured on 274 of SWE-bench Lite's 300 instances, those whose patch modifies an existing function.
quote: resulting in 274 retained examples out of 300. While SWE-Bench-Lite primarily consists of bug reports and feature requests, LocBench ( 560 examples) also includes security and performance issues. Consistent with Chen et al. (2025), we measure localization performance at three granularities: file, module (class) and function, with Accuracy at k (Acc@k) as the evaluation metric. This metric deems localization successful if all relevant code locations are correctly identified within the top-k results.
wiki_says: A small embedding retriever reached 74.45% function-level recall at 10 on SWE-bench Lite.

claim: The 137M retriever's 74.45% function Acc@10 beats SWE-agent (64.60%), MoatlessTools (64.96%) and OpenHands (70.07%) with Claude-3.5, but not LocAgent with Claude-3.5 (77.37%) nor LocAgent with a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B (77.01%); at function Acc@5 it scores 63.14% against LocAgent-Claude's 73.36%. Beating every agent takes the 7B SweRankEmbed-Large (82.12%) or the rerankers.
wiki_says: A small embedding retriever reached 74.45% function-level recall at 10 on SWE-bench Lite, beating agent systems built on Claude 3.5.

claim: With SWE-Fixer as the editor on SWE-bench Lite, raising file Acc@1 from 69.7 (SWE-Fixer's own) to 83.2 (SweRank) raised repair Pass@1 from 21.0 to 24.5; even oracle localization (100) gives only 25.9, so the editing model is the binding constraint.
bears_on: localization vs editing as the bottleneck

claim: Fine-tuning the retriever on mined issue-to-function pairs without consistency filtering made it worse than the pretrained model; a moderate filter (positive within the top 20) was best.
quote: As shown in Figure 5a, finetuning SWERANKEMBED-SMALL with SWELOC data filtered by different K values reveals that optimal performance is achieved with a moderate K (e.g., K=20), striking a balance between instance quality and dataset size. The absence of filtering (K=None) proves detrimental as performance drops after finetuning compared to pre-trained model.
bears_on: filtering mined training pairs

claim: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B fine-tuned on SweLoc goes from 62.77% to 75.18% function Acc@10 on SWE-bench Lite (52.55% to 66.79% at Acc@5), a sub-1B localizer above the 137M model.
bears_on: a sub-1B model as localizer

claim: Trained only on Python issues, SweRankEmbed-Small transfers to SWE-bench Multilingual (nine other languages): 44.02% function Acc@10 against 35.04% for its base CodeRankEmbed.
quote: | Retriever | CodeRankEmbed (137M) | 26.50 | 35.04 | | Retriever | SweRankEmbed-Small (137M) | 33.33 | 44.02 |
bears_on: transfer of repair skills to a new language

claim: Per instance, the 7B SweRankLLM reranker costs $0.011 against $0.66 for LocAgent with Claude-3.5 and $0.05 for LocAgent with a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B.
quote: | LocAgent | Claude-3.5 Qwen2.5-7B(ft) Qwen2.5-32B(ft) | 0.66 0.05 0.09 | 1.2 13.2 8.6 | | Reranker | GPT-4.1 SWERANKLLM (7B) SWERANKLLM (32B) | 0.16 0.011 0.015 | 5.9 79.0 57.5 |
bears_on: inference cost of localization

claim: LocAgent's abstract reports a 12% improvement in downstream GitHub issue resolution at Pass@10 and up to 92.7% file-level localization accuracy.
quote: reaching up to 92.7% accuracy on file-level localization while improving downstream GitHub issue resolution success rates by 12% for multiple attempts (Pass@10)

claim: The 12% is relative and comes from Claude-3.5 localizing (Claude-3.5 also edits, with Agentless's editing step, on SWE-bench Lite): Pass@10 rises from 33.58% to 37.59% (+4.0 points, 11.9% relative) and Pass@1 from 26.31% to 27.92% (+1.6 points). With the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B localizer Pass@10 is 36.13% (+2.55 points, 7.6% relative) and Pass@1 26.79%.
wiki_says: Better localization raised downstream resolution by 12% at Pass@10.

claim: LocAgent's open models were trained by LoRA SFT on 433 successful Claude-3.5 trajectories plus 335 successful trajectories self-generated by the first fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B, only trajectories that localized correctly; the combined set was then distilled into the 7B model.
quote: We collect 433 successful trajectories generated with Claude-3.5, where the agent completed tasks from the SWEbench training set. Due to budget constraints, we sample an additional 335 trajectories generated by the initially fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32Bmodel. Importantly, we only select successful trajectories where the model correctly localized the issues, creating a high-quality dataset of correct reasoning paths.
bears_on: distilling agent trajectories into a small model

claim: After fine-tuning, LocAgent with Qwen2.5-7B reaches 71.53% function Acc@10 on SWE-bench Lite, against 77.01% for the fine-tuned 32B and 77.37% for Claude-3.5; the untuned 7B performed poorly for lack of tool-use ability.
bears_on: how close a distilled small localizer gets

claim: For the fine-tuned 7B agent, removing the keyword-search tool over the code index dropped function Acc@10 from 71.53 to 53.28, removing only its BM25 index to 60.22, and removing graph traversal to 66.06: the structured search tools carry much of a small agent's accuracy.
bears_on: structured code-search tools for a small agent

claim: How the tool output is rendered changes localization accuracy: expanding subgraphs as trees did best, and attaching every node's attributes consistently hurt, which the authors read as noise.
quote: As shown in Table 9, expanding subgraphs as trees (i.e., JSON, tree-based) can significantly improve the performance. Our tree-based format achieves the best overall performance across different levels of localization tasks. We also test returning entity attributes along with subgraphs. We notice that row (w/ entity attributes) consistently underperforms row, indicating the attributes for all the nodes may be very noisy.
bears_on: formatting structured tool output for the model

claim: On Loc-Bench, accuracy is lower on feature requests, security and performance issues than on bug reports, which the authors attribute to bug-heavy training data.
quote: This performance gap likely reflects our training data distribution, which contained more bug report examples, potentially leading to scaffolds better optimized for bug localization tasks.
bears_on: task mix in training data

claim: Per example, LocAgent costs $0.66 with Claude-3.5, $0.09 with the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B and $0.05 with the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, in 7, 9 and 6 agent rounds.
bears_on: inference cost of a small localizer

claim: Agnostics trains for one epoch by default on Ag-Codeforces-X, whose train split holds 5369 I/O-specified competitive-programming problems adapted from Open-R1 Codeforces.
quote: We trained the models for 1 epoch, unless specified otherwise. ## 4.1 TRAINING DATASETS Ag-Codeforces-X, the main dataset we use for training, was created based on competitive programming problems from the Open-R1 Codeforces dataset (Penedo et al., 2025). Few adjustments were necessary, since the problems already specified programs and tests using standard I/O. The train split contains 5369 problems.

claim: Agnostics' GRPO settings: learning rate 5 × 10^-6 with cosine decay and a 0.1-epoch warmup, 4 prompts per batch with a group of 32 samples per prompt, sampling temperature 0.7, and reasoning disabled in hybrid models.
quote: with a learning rate of 5 × 10-6 and a cosine decay schedule with a warmup of 0.1 epochs. We process 4 prompts in each batch, with group size 32 per prompt. When training we use temperature 0.7 and disable reasoning in hybrid models.

claim: On Ag-LiveCodeBench-X pass@1, base Qwen 3 4B scored 1% in OCaml and 0% in Fortran (Qwen 3 8B: 0% and 0%); the Agnostics-trained Qwen3-4B scored 7% and 15%.

Agnostics' distillation baseline fine-tuned Qwen 3 4B on 1,987 Fortran solutions synthesized by Sonnet 4 Thinking, which itself scored 12% on Ag-LCB-Fortran; the student went from 0% to 3% after one or two epochs and 2% after three.
quote: | Sonnet 4 Thinking (teacher) | 12 | | Qwen 3 4B (student) | 0 | | 1 epoch | 3 | | 2 epochs | 3 | | 3 epochs | 2 | training set of 1,987 items.

claim: In The Stack v2, Fortran is 0.07% and Julia 0.10% of the data, against 3.56% for Python: the languages Agnostics trained on had some, but very little, pretraining coverage.

Agnostics attributes the distillation result to the teacher being weak in low-resource languages, not to missing verification. The Sonnet 4 Thinking solutions were used as generated, with no test filtering reported, so the experiment does not compare verified with unverified teacher data.
quote: As larger models do not perform very well on many low-resource programming languages, one can expect distillation to be less effective.
wiki_says: Agnostics learned the same lesson the hard way. SFT on 1,987 Claude Sonnet 4 Fortran solutions took Qwen3-4B to 3%, while RL against an exact I/O verifier reached 15%. The verifier, not the teacher, is what makes the data good.

claim: Agnostics found that training on Ag-Codeforces-X did not improve Qwen 3 1.7B or Llama 3.2 3B Instruct and suggests the problems were too difficult for models of this size. The failures were at 1.7B and 3B on competition-level problems, so they neither locate a size threshold nor show that RL produced no learning signal; the paper reports no reward curves for these runs, and a weak 3B starter (SmolLM3) did improve.
quote: However, we found that Agnostics training on Ag-Codeforces-X does not improve two smaller models, Qwen 3 1.7B and Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, perhaps due to the problems being too difficult for models of this size.
wiki_says: RL on weak sub-2B starting points repeatedly produced no learning signal at all (Agnostics; TinyZero). ... writer RL fails below about 1.5B from weak starts (TinyZero; Agnostics).

claim: The words the survey puts in quotation marks do not appear in Agnostics. The paper says it considered and decided against a reward for a partially-correct answer, after models exploited rewards for code that runs without error or passes only the public tests.
quote: We also considered and decided against a reward for a partially-correct answer (see §C.3).
wiki_says: Agnostics "explicitly rejected intermediate rewards after observing model exploitation behavior".

claim: SmolLM3 3B, which started at 1-2% on Ag-LiveCodeBench-X, improved under Agnostics training to 8% (Lua), 8% (Julia) and 6% (R); on MultiPL-E it rose from 11/12/18 to 14/14/21.
bears_on: whether a near-zero starting pass rate blocks RL at small sizes

claim: Agnostics tested a 0.2 partial reward for Lua programs that terminated without error but failed a test (full reward 1 unchanged). The two runs scored 18.57 and 20.16 on Ag-LiveCodeBench-X and 13.33 and 15.62 on the Ag-Codeforces-X test split, against 23.00 and 24.76 with the binary reward.
quote: | Qwen3-4B-CF-Lua | 23.00 | 24.76 | | partial-r1 | 18.57 | 13.33 | | partial-r2 | 20.16 | 15.62 | ## C.3 REWARD FUNCTION We investigated the results of partial rewards. We trained Qwen 3 4B-the base model of Qwen34B-CF-X-on Ag-Codeforces-Lua, giving it a partial reward of 0.2 if it generated code which failed one of the tests by producing wrong output but otherwise terminated without an error. The full reward for a snippet passing all tests was still 1.
bears_on: a small partial-credit term such as the survey's 0.1 check-clean bonus

claim: Training Qwen 3 4B on Fortran and OCaml produced zero reward for the first several GRPO steps before learning began.
quote: Figure 7: Rewards each step from training Qwen 3 4B on Fortran and OCaml. These are very lowresource languages, and rewards are zero for the first several steps.
bears_on: all-fail groups at the start of RL on a language the model barely knows

claim: In Agnostics' sweep, group size 16 scored slightly lower; group size 64 matched group size 32 on Ag-LiveCodeBench-X but took about 20.5 hours to train against about 12 hours. Temperatures other than 0.7 performed similarly.
quote: The models trained at group size 16 had slightly lower scores compared to other models, while the ones trained at group size 64 displayed scores comparable to other models. However, they took significantly longer to train. Two group size 64 models took ∼ 20.5h to train on average (the third one was trained on a different machine). In comparison, the group size 32 models trained at the same time on the same machine took ∼ 12h on average. The models trained at temperatures other than the 0.7 recommended by the Qwen team performed similarly to the other models.
bears_on: GRPO group size under a small GPU budget

claim: Even with a 30-second timeout a bad candidate can print tens of gigabytes, so the Agnostics verifier reads output through a fixed 5MB buffer and kills programs that overflow it; it also needs separate compile and execution timeouts and returns reward 0 on any timeout.
quote: Even with a short timeout such as 30 seconds, a pathological candidate program can output tens of gigabytes of text. This can crash the verifier if it na¨ıvely tries to read and store all output. Instead, the verifier maintains a fixed-size (5MB) read buffer and immediately kills programs which overflow it.
bears_on: verifier robustness in the lotml RL sandbox

claim: The Sonnet 4 Thinking distillation set was generated with at most 32K reasoning tokens and cost $96; the student was fine-tuned for 3 epochs at batch size 64 and learning rate 2 × 10^-5.
quote: we use at most 32K reasoning tokens, spending $96 to generate the items. We fine-tune Qwen 3 4B for 3 epochs (batch size 64, learning rate 2 × 10-5 , cosine learning rate decay with warmup ratio 0.1)
bears_on: budget for frontier-teacher data under a $5 API cap

claim: In SLMFix v2 (the cached version), 59.40% is DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B's own Ansible validator pass rate when it generates directly. With the 0.5B fixer behind it the pipeline reached 95.80%, and LoRA SFT of the 6.7B generator reached 47.54%, a margin of 95.80 - 47.54 = 48.26 points for this generator. The survey's end point and margin are not in v2 (the survey cites v1); the wiki's figure is the Qwen2.5-Coder 7B row (see 2511-19422-qwen7b-pass-vs-sft). In every row the 0.5B model repairs a larger model's output; it is not itself taken from the base rate to the final rate.
wiki_says: It took a Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B repairer from 59.40% to 97.82% validator pass on Ansible, 25.2 points above SFT. ... SLMFix's 0.5B repairer, discussed above, beat SFT by 25 points.

claim: SLMFix shifts weight between the validator and AST-similarity terms by the batch's validator pass rate, so training moves from syntax to semantics as the pass rate rises, but it clamps the pass rate at 0.5 so syntax is never over-weighted. The formula itself did not survive the conversion, so the survey's exact expression cannot be checked against the text.
quote: is the pass rate of the current batch. rpass is clamped at 0.5 to avoid overemphasizing syntactic correctness.
wiki_says: SLMFix weights the validator and similarity terms by the batch pass rate, r = (1 − pr)·validator + pr·similarity, so training shifts from syntax to semantics as it succeeds.

claim: The sentence the survey quotes is not in SLMFix. The paper says its RL method does not work well on direct code generation, possibly because of the limited capability of small models, based on one Ansible ablation, and offers it as evidence for repair over direct generation.
quote: We found that the reinforcement learning method we utilized does not work well on direct code generation task, possibly due to the limited model capability of SLMs. This result demonstrates the benefits of leveraging SLMs for program repair over direct generation.
wiki_says: Its authors found "RL training unsuitable for direct SLM code generation; repair-focused task is better suited".

claim: Against test results on Ansible (21 questions, 1,260 outputs), treating AST similarity of at least 0.8 as correct gave 84.2% accuracy and a 94.6% true-negative rate but only a 38.4% true-positive rate: the similarity term rejects many functionally equivalent programs.
quote: For Ansible, we employed the benchmark suite constructed by Councilman et al. (2025), which contains 21 questions and 1,260 outputs, and the comparison between testing result and semantic similarity is shown in Table 7. When considering having a semantic similarity of at least 0.8 as equivalent to the ground-truth, the metric is able to classify most outputs correctly with an accuracy of 84.2% and a true negative rate of 94.6%. However, the true positive rate is only 38.4%, which indicates that the AST-based semantic similarity is too strict and fails to correctly classify Ansible programs that are functionally equivalent to the ground-truth but not semantically equivalent.

claim: In SLMFix's Ansible ablation with Qwen-2.5 0.5B, a validator-only reward reached 98.99% validator pass but AST Diff fell to 0.2062 from 0.3455 with the combined reward; a similarity-only reward reached only 22.48% pass.
bears_on: validator-only rewards for a repairer: passing the checker by giving up the task

claim: SLMFix's SFT baseline is LoRA fine-tuning of the large generator, not of the small fixer, capped at 150 steps with batch size 4, learning rate 1e-4 and weight decay 0.05.
quote: For supervised finetuning, we employed LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) for parameterefficient finetuning. We set the maximum number of steps to be 150 and batch size as 4, with learning rate of 1e-4 and weight decay of 0.05.
bears_on: how much the RL-beats-SFT comparison says about training a small repairer

claim: SLMFix assigns the reward only to the last token and samples one program per input with the current policy; the paper gives no group size, so how GRPO's group baseline was formed is unclear.
quote: For token-level updates, we followed the practice outlined by the official documentation of verl to assign the reward only to the last token in the input sequence. For sample trajectory collection, we sampled one program for each input with the current policy, which is passed into syntactic and semantic checkers to calculate the reward.
bears_on: GRPO group size and credit assignment for repair RL

claim: All SLMFix experiments ran on two 40GB A40 GPUs and took roughly 100 GPU hours in total.
quote: We conducted all experiments on two 40GB A40 GPUs and the experiments took roughly 100 GPU hours in total to complete.
bears_on: compute budget for a 0.5B repair RL run

claim: Fine-tuning StarCoderBase-1B on Racket translations without test validation gave 8.6 pass@1, against 11.3 with validated MultiPL-T data and 4.7 for the base model; for StarCoderBase-15B unvalidated data gave 11.6 against 21.0 validated and 11.8 base. Unvalidated data still helped the 1B model, by less.

MultiPL-T argues that LLM-generated (self-instruct) data does not work for low-resource languages because the model writes poor-quality programs in them. The in-paper evidence is a small sample of generated Racket programs, most of them buggy; the full self-instruct experiment is only in the supplementary material.
quote: However, we show that synthetic data does not work for low-resource languages for the intuitive reason that LLMs generate poor quality programs in low-resource languages (§3.2).

claim: MultiPL-T's Table 7 tests whether adding the original Python to the translation prompt helps. It helped Racket and Lua and slightly hurt OCaml, and the authors only speculate that Python misleads the model when the target is further from Python. The per-language rates also reflect how well the model knows each target, and Racket, syntactically far from Python, gained the most, so the table does not show translation success tracking syntactic distance from Python.
quote: We can only speculate about why this happens: Python may be misleading the model and OCaml seems further removed from Python than Racket or Lua.
wiki_says: Closeness to Python. Translation success tracks syntactic distance from Python: 68.5% pass@50 for Lua against 23.9% for OCaml, which favors a Python-like target.

claim: Translation success (pass@50) with the original Python in the prompt was 68.5 for Lua, 56.8 for Racket and 23.9 for OCaml, against 51.4, 34.7 and 26.1 with the basic prompt.
quote: Table 7. The pass@50 performance of the basic prompt compared to the prompt with the original Python code for OCaml, Racket, and Lua. | Language | Basic | With Python Solution | |------------|---------|------------------------| | OCaml | 26.1 | 23.9 | | Racket | 34.7 | 56.8 | | Lua | 51.4 | 68.5 |

claim: Deduplication cut the Lua dataset from 1.4M to 48K functions; StarCoderBase-1B fine-tuned on the deduplicated set scored 17.3 pass@1 after under 30 minutes of training, against 17.1 after 12 hours on the full set.
quote: Before deduplication, the Lua dataset has 1.4M functions, but after deduplication we are left with 48K (reported in Table 8). For this experiment, we fine-tune StarCoderBase-1B on a single H100 GPU on the undeduplicated dataset, with exactly the same hyperparameters we used earlier (§5). We find the following: - (1) Without deduplication, the fine-tuned StarCoderBase-1B gets a 17.1 pass@1 score on MultiPLE and takes 12 hours to train. - (2) With deduplication, the fine-tuned StarCoderBase-1B gets 17.3 pass@1 on MultiPL-E and takes less than 30 minutes to train.

claim: The MultiPL-T datasets hold 37,592 (R), 40,510 (Racket), 43,401 (OCaml), 45,000 (Julia) and 48,194 (Lua) items.
After MultiPL-T fine-tuning, StarCoderBase-1B performed comparably to the untuned 15B model in Racket and OCaml, the lowest-resource languages tested.
quote: Even the fine-tuned 1B models perform comparably to the base 15B models at producing correct solutions in these languages.
bears_on: how far a 1B-class model gets on a low-resource language with verified data

claim: Performance rose substantially after a single epoch of MultiPL-T data for the lowest-resource languages (Racket, OCaml), while the higher-resource Lua needed more data for modest gains.
quote: In Figure 10, we see that performance increases substantially after a single epoch of MultiPL-T data for the lowest resource languages (Racket and OCaml). However, a higher-resource language (Lua) requires more data to realize even modest gains.
bears_on: epochs and data volume for distilling a new language

claim: Fine-tuning StarCoderBase-1B on the tested Python source dataset itself left Python pass@1 unchanged (15.1 base, 15.0 tuned); the authors attribute the gains elsewhere to translation creating data the model had not seen.
quote: The base model gets a 15.1 pass@1 score on Python, whereas the fine-tuned model gets 15.0 pass@1. 12 Thus, it is clear that fine-tuning directly on this subset of Python does not produce the same improvements that we see on the low-resource languages after translation.
bears_on: whether re-training on already-seen data adds anything

claim: MultiPL-T generated five independent test suites per Python function at temperature 0.8, ran each test in isolation, discarded failing tests, and dropped functions left with no correct test (and later those with low line coverage).
quote: We prompt StarCoder-15B to generate five independent test suites for each function with high temperature 6 (0.8) to get a diverse set of candidate tests. We parse each generated test suite and extract all test cases that are suitable for translation using MultiPL-E. We take the set of matching test cases and run each test in isolation in a container to verify that it passes, discarding any that fail. If no correct tests are generated, we discard the function.
bears_on: test-suite quality for a verified corpus

claim: With the full PyLang specification in the prompt, base Qwen3 4B, 8B and 32B had syntax errors on 100%, 94.6% and 77.2% of problems (problem pass 0.0%, 0.0% and 7.4%); after question-to-code fine-tuning, syntax errors fell to 4.5%, 4.2% and 2.5% and problem pass rose to 36.1%, 38.6% and 47.2%.
PyLang states that Sonnet 4.5 shows a 30% deficit against Python while fine-tuned Qwen models show 11-34% gaps across all configurations.
quote: Sonnet 4.5 shows a 30% deficit while fine-tuned Qwen models show 11-34% gaps across all configurations

claim: On top of the 8B question-to-code SFT checkpoint, GRPO raised PyLang pass to 41.5% (+2.9) and DPO to 39.8% (+1.2), while Python rose to 60.2% (+2.8) and 61.9% (+4.5); under DPO the 8B gap widened from 18.8 to 22.1 points.
quote: DPO 8B achieves the highest Python result at 61.9% (+4.5 % over the SFT baseline), while GRPO 8B reaches 60.2% (+2.8 %). PyLang gains are more modest: GRPO 8B reaches 41.5% (+2.9 %) and DPO 8B reaches 39.8% (+1.2 %). The gap widens from 18.8 % (SFT) to 22.1 % (DPO) at the 8B scale

claim: The 75% share of gap problems with the same algorithm but a failed implementation is Sonnet 4.5's (112 gap problems). For the fine-tuned Qwen models the share was 40% (32B), 27% (8B) and 51% (4B), with 48%, 58% and 30% of gap problems using a different algorithm, so after fine-tuning the right-algorithm-wrong-code pattern is not three quarters of failures.
wiki_says: Three quarters of the failures were the right algorithm implemented wrongly.

claim: PyLang compares pass rates on the same problems in a known and an unseen language and reports the gap as a difference in percentage points; it does not propose a ratio as a headline metric.
quote: Our work differs from all of these by evaluating the same problems across two languages, one known, one unseen to directly isolate what fine-tuning contributes beyond pretraining.
wiki_says: Pass@1 on the same problems in the new language and in Python, the headline ratio the PyLang study suggests.

claim: PyLang pass rate saturated well below Python as SFT data grew: with 10%, 50% and 100% of the 2,250 examples, Qwen3-4B scored 19.9%, 30.4% and 34.7% and Qwen3-8B 28.1%, 36.6% and 38.4% (Python: 47.7% and 57.4%).
bears_on: how much distilled data a new language needs before returns flatten

claim: PyLang's GRPO used a fractional reward (tests passed over tests total; 0 for syntax errors and timeouts), 8 samples per step at temperature 0.7, 1,000 Codeforces problems for 4 epochs, β 0.1, learning rate 2 × 10^-6 and full fine-tuning. The paper chose partial credit because fully correct PyLang solutions are rare.
quote: At each training step, the model generates 8 candidate solutions at temperature 0.7 and receives execution-based rewards. The reward function is r = tests\_passed/tests\_total, yielding 1.0 for fully correct solutions, 0.0 for syntax errors, timeouts, or complete failure, and intermediate values for partial correctness. Training uses 1,000 Codeforces problems sampled from the training set, running for 4 epochs with β = 0.1, learning rate 2 × 10-6 , and full fine-tuning.
bears_on: partial-credit versus binary reward when correct samples are rare

claim: The dominant failure of fine-tuned Qwen models was algorithmic divergence: when implementation became hard they tended to produce a different approach rather than persist with the correct one.
quote: The dominant failure mode for fine-tuned models is algorithmic divergence (43-57 problems for 8B and 32B), consistent with the judge analysis in §4.1: when implementation becomes difficult, fine-tuned models tend to produce a different approach rather than persisting with the correct one.
bears_on: what a small distilled model does on a new language when implementation gets hard

claim: PyLang's headline gap figures do not all match its main table: the Combined objective at 32B leaves a 52.0 - 50.6 = 1.4-point overall gap, below the lower end of the stated range, reached by lowering Python rather than raising PyLang.
quote: The Combined objective appears to close the gap at 32B (50.6% PyLang vs. 52.0% Python), but this is because the multi-task objective hurts Python performance rather than helping PyLang.
bears_on: how to read PyLang's gap figures

claim: PyLang's data teacher could decline a problem it judged inexpressible (about 14% of failures) and got up to two more attempts per problem, each with a short tests-passed summary and the interpreter's actual error appended.
quote: The model may decline a problem with the literal token OOS when it cannot be expressed in PyLang, and such problems are dropped, accounting for about 14% of pool failures rather than wrong answers. On failure the model gets up to two more attempts, each with a short summary ("Tests failed: K/N passed") and the interpreter's actual error appended to the prompt.
bears_on: teacher-generation loop for verified lotml data

claim: Under direct generation, 83.9% (text-to-code) and 82.0% (code-to-code) of failed samples were labelled foreign syntax, against 30.0% and 27.2% with the syntax reference; the shares pool the six large models tested and label each failed sample by its first observed failure, assigned by an LLM annotator.
CangjieBench evaluated only models above 200B parameters because smaller models scored near-zero Pass@1 in pilot runs, leaving no headroom to compare methods.
quote: We restrict the selection to models above 200B parameters because smaller models bottomed out at near-zero Pass@1 in pilot runs, leaving no headroom to separate the methods
bears_on: whether prompting alone can carry a 0.5B-1.5B model on a language absent from pretraining

claim: About 9-10% of syntax-reference failures were duplicate definitions, mostly the model declaring its own main and conflicting with the test harness.
quote: About 9-10% of Syntax-Constrained failures are Duplicate def., where the model declares its own main and conflicts with the harness
bears_on: output contract between the model and the RL test harness

claim: Olausson et al. hypothesize that self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's feedback on its own code, and support it by substituting feedback from a stronger model, which gives substantially larger gains.
quote: We hypothesize that this is because self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on its own code; using a stronger model to artificially boost the quality of the feedback, we observe substantially larger performance gains.

claim: Every boosted-feedback configuration paired a weaker code model with a stronger feedback model; the paper never tests feedback from a smaller or weaker model than the one doing the repair.
quote: We thus set MP to be a weaker model (Code Llama on HumanEval, Code Llama or GPT-3.5 on APPS) and MF to be a stronger model
bears_on: whether a 0.5B guide's feedback can help a 1.5B writer

claim: On HumanEval, 9.1% of Code Llama 13B's sampled repairs passed with its own feedback, 20.1% with GPT-3.5's and 39.3% with GPT-4's (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 repairing their own code: 22.4% and 49.6%). The converted row carries a leading GPT-4 label and 10.8% that belong to the APPS overall row.
quote: | HumanEval | - | GPT-4 CodeLLama CodeLlama+GPT-3.5 CodeLlama+GPT-4 GPT-3.5 GPT-4 | 10.8% 9.1% 20.1% 39.3% 22.4% 49.6% |
bears_on: size of the feedback-quality effect for an open 13B model

claim: The study gives repair the full set of tests and makes no distinction between public tests used for filtering and private tests used to judge correctness.
quote: we do not make a distinction between public tests used for filtering and private tests used to determine correctness, since our method does not involve filtering the outputs.
bears_on: keeping the grader's tests hidden from a repair policy

claim: Agentless with GPT-4o resolved 96 of 300 SWE-bench Lite problems (32.00%) at an average cost of $0.70 and 78,166 tokens per issue.

Agentless ran GPT-4o for every step and evaluated no small model, so it shows that a fixed localize-repair-validate pipeline works with a frontier model, not that small models compete when the pipeline is split.
quote: We implement AGENTLESS using GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) [72].
wiki_says: Pipelines split into components are where small models compete. Agentless solved 32% of SWE-bench Lite for $0.70 per issue with a fixed localize, repair and validate flow.

claim: Of 300 issues, Agentless produced 213 reproduction tests that reproduced the issue, but only 94 of them reported the issue resolved after the ground-truth patch was applied.
quote: Out of the 300 problems in SWE-bench Lite, AGENTLESS is able to produce 213 reproduction tests that output the required reproduction message when evaluated on the original repository. However, these tests might still be incorrect as a correct reproduction should also be able to verify that the issue has been correctly resolved. To evaluate this, we directly apply the ground truth patch provided in SWE-bench 2 . We found that only 94 tests correctly output the Issues resolved message after applying the ground truth patches.
bears_on: model-written tests as verifiers

claim: SWE-bench Lite contains problems with the exact ground-truth patch in the description (4.3%), problems missing information needed to solve them (10.0%), and problems with misleading solutions in the description (5.0%).
quote: SWE-bench Lite contains problems with exact ground truth patch in the description (4.3%), problems with missing critical information needed to solve the issue (10.0%), and problems that include misleading solutions in the issue description (5.0%).
bears_on: task-pool quality for repair training and evaluation

claim: One greedy patch per location set already fixed 80 issues; adding samples helped until about 40 patches per issue, after which performance plateaued.
quote: First, we see that by just using 1 greedy sample for each location set, AGENTLESS can already achieve a significant number of correct fixes of 80. We can continue to improve repair performance by adding more samples. However, we observe that the performance plateaus at around 40 samples where adding additional candidate patches does not improve performance.
bears_on: sampling budget for repair at inference

claim: Real bad examples help even when few are available, and the learned breaker's advantage over training on real bad examples alone grows as they become scarcer.
quote: (ii) when the amount of real bad examples is small, BIFI exceeds FixerOnly by a larger margin, highlighting the usefulness of the bad examples generated by the learned breaker.
bears_on: a lotml repair corpus when real model errors are scarce

claim: On DeepFix, BIFI's fixer is applied repeatedly while the code still has errors, up to 5 times, so the 71.7% is a multi-pass repair result.
quote: At test time, following the original DrRepair, we repeatedly apply the fixer while the code still has errors, up to a maximum of 5 times.
bears_on: single-turn versus iterated repair with a compiler critic

claim: Real human errors differ from random perturbations in distribution: missing parentheses occur about 10x more often in a nested context than a non-nested one in GitHub-Python.
quote: real human-written code misses parentheses often in a nested context (e.g., 10x more than non-nested in our collected dataset GitHub-Python).
bears_on: building Python-habit mutants from observed model errors rather than random edits

claim: The syntax-only figure is not a measured grammar-constrained run: 'idealized Syntax' assumes every syntactically incorrect unconstrained output would compile under syntactic constraining, an upper bound. Both figures the survey pairs are HumanEval synthesis plus translation; MBPP is lower on both (mundler-syntax-ideal-9-4.9, mundler-types-cut-75-52), and the types result is an emulation (2504-09246-the-reported-types-results-are-an-emulation-becau).
quote: We measure the upper bound improvement of prior syntactic constraining methods [8, 57, 66] by assuming that all syntactically incorrect instances generated by Vanilla could be compiled under syntactic constraining.
wiki_says: In TypeScript only 6% of compile errors are syntactic, so grammar constraints removed about 9% of compile errors while type constraints removed 75%.

claim: In the repair task, unconstrained Gemma 2 2B made 33.5% (HumanEval) and 25.8% (MBPP) of non-compiling programs compile; type-constrained sampling raised this to 56.4% and 58.4%. These are compilation repairs, not functional ones.
quote: with Gemma 2 2B for example repairing only 33.5% and 25.8% of the non-compiling HumanEval and MBPP instances, respectively. This is substantially increased to 56.4% and 58.4% through type constraining.

claim: For the smallest model, Gemma 2 2B, type constraining raised HumanEval repair pass@1 from 11.6 to 20.9 (+79.4% relative), while its synthesis pass@1 rose only from 29.1 to 30.2.
bears_on: constrained decoding for a small repair model

claim: Across the evaluation only 3.5% of functional errors and 6% of compilation errors were syntactic, which caps what syntax-only constraints can add for models that already know the language.
quote: only 3.5% of the functional errors and 6% of the compilation errors in LLM-generated code are due to syntactic errors.
bears_on: grammar-only constraints versus type-aware constraints for lotml

claim: Many remaining compile errors under constraints were non-termination: when a constraint amends generation and the model cannot recover, it enters a generation loop until the token or time limit.
quote: We find this to be caused by generation loops, entered when generation is amended by constraints and the LLM is unable to recover.
bears_on: failure modes of constrained decoding with weak models

claim: The authors report that model quantization, essential for practical deployment, significantly amplifies programming-language confusion and degrades syntactic stability in complex tasks.
quote: Furthermore, model quantization-though essential for practical deployment-significantly amplifies PLC and degrades syntactic stability in complex tasks.

claim: Quantization did not simply strengthen the drift toward Python: on LiveCodeBench the quantized Llama-3.1-8B defaulted to C++ (89.55% dominant migration rate), and on BabelCode the quantized models' confusion spread over more target languages. Confusion has to be measured against every wrong language, not only Python.
quote: The FP models generally defaulted to Python (RQ1), but the Q version of LLaMA3.18B-Instruct now exhibits a strong bias towards C + + (89.55% DMR).
